title: self-improvement book|dealing with procrastination and perfectionism
text:
You sit down to work, open the document, and immediately check your email. Or scroll through social media. Or suddenly remember you need to reorganize your spice rack—right now. You tell yourself, “I’ll start in five minutes.” But five minutes becomes thirty. Then an hour. Then the day slips away, and you’re left with a quiet knot of guilt and self-criticism tightening in your chest.

This isn’t laziness. It’s not a character flaw. What you’re experiencing is often a collision between two powerful forces: procrastination and perfectionism—and they feed each other like fire and oxygen.

Perfectionism whispers in your ear: “If it’s not brilliant, it’s not worth doing. If it’s not finished perfectly, it’s better left undone. If someone might judge it—even just a little—you shouldn’t share it yet.” So you wait for ideal conditions: the perfect time, the perfect mood, the perfect level of clarity or energy. But those conditions never arrive. And waiting becomes safer than risking imperfection.

Procrastination, then, isn’t avoidance of work—it’s avoidance of discomfort: the discomfort of uncertainty, of making mistakes, of being seen trying before you’ve mastered it. You delay action because your nervous system has learned that starting feels threatening—not dangerous, but emotionally unsafe. Your brain chooses the short-term relief of distraction over the long-term reward of progress.

Here’s what you need to hear, clearly and kindly: Done is better than perfect. Started is better than flawless. Good enough is not a compromise—it’s the essential threshold for growth.

Begin by noticing your own patterns—not to shame yourself, but to understand. When do you stall? What thoughts arise right before you close the tab or walk away? Is it “This has to be amazing,” or “What if I get it wrong?” or “I don’t know where to begin, so I’ll do nothing”? Name it. Write it down. That simple act creates space between you and the impulse—and space is where choice lives.

Next, shrink the task until it feels physically impossible to resist. Instead of “write the report,” try “open the document and type one sentence.” Instead of “practice guitar for an hour,” try “pick up the guitar and play one chord.” These micro-actions bypass resistance because they ask almost nothing—and yet, they build momentum. Most importantly, they prove to your nervous system: “I can begin, and it won’t destroy me.”

Also, separate creation from evaluation. Give yourself permission to write badly, sketch messily, speak awkwardly, draft imperfectly. Set a timer for ten minutes and commit only to generating—not editing, not judging, not fixing. Let your first draft be gloriously flawed. You wouldn’t expect a sculptor to chisel the final form on the first strike. Why demand it of yourself?

And please, reconsider what “success” looks like—not as an outcome, but as a behavior. Success is showing up for five minutes. Success is sending the email even if the wording isn’t elegant. Success is sharing your idea before you’ve polished it into submission. Each time you choose action over idealism, you weaken perfectionism’s grip and strengthen your self-trust.

You are not behind. You are not broken. You are human—wired to seek safety, meaning, and connection. Perfectionism masquerades as high standards, but real excellence grows from iteration, feedback, and resilience—not from silence and delay.

So today, pick one small thing you’ve been avoiding—not because it’s urgent, but because it matters to you. Do it imperfectly. Notice what happens in your body when you finish. Breathe. That breath is proof you survived the risk. That completion is evidence your worth isn’t tied to flawless output.

Progress isn’t linear. Some days you’ll move forward in leaps. Others, you’ll circle back, revise, pause—or rest. All of it counts. What builds your life isn’t the absence of hesitation, but the presence of gentle, persistent return—to the work, to yourself, to the truth that you are enough—not after you finish, but right now, mid-sentence, mid-effort, mid-becoming. Keep going. Not perfectly. Just honestly.

title: leadership book for new managers|giving honest feedback without crushing morale
text:
So, you’ve just been promoted to manager. Congrats! Now comes the fun part—giving feedback. I remember my first time like it was yesterday. I was sweating bullets, fidgeting with my pen, and trying to figure out how to tell my team member, Mike, that his reports were a bit... well, let’s just say they needed some work. I didn’t want to crush his spirit, but I also knew I had to be honest. It’s a fine line, but fear not, I’ve got some tips and tales to help you navigate this tricky terrain.

First off, let me share a little story. When I started out, I had a boss who gave feedback like a sledgehammer. Every critique felt like a personal attack, and it left me feeling deflated and demotivated. That’s exactly what we don’t want. So, how do you give honest feedback without making someone feel like they’re about to be fired? Let’s dive in.

1. Start with the Positive: Always lead with something good. This sets a positive tone and reminds the person that you see their value. For example, “Hey, I really appreciate your enthusiasm and dedication. Your energy is infectious, and it makes the team feel motivated.”

2. Be Specific and Constructive: Vague feedback is like telling someone their cooking is “interesting.” It doesn’t help them improve. Instead, pinpoint exactly what needs to change. “In your last report, the data analysis section was a bit unclear. Maybe we can break it down into smaller, more digestible points?”

3. Use the Sandwich Method: You know, the old classic: compliment, critique, compliment. It’s like putting medicine between two delicious pieces of bread. It makes the tough stuff go down easier. “Your presentation skills are fantastic, and I love how you engage the audience. However, the slides could use a bit more clarity. But overall, you did a great job, and I’m confident you’ll nail it next time.”

4. Ask for Their Perspective: Sometimes, people have no idea they’re doing something wrong. Opening up a dialogue can make the conversation less one-sided. “What do you think about the project? Is there anything you’d like to improve or any challenges you faced?” This shows you value their opinion and are open to hearing their side.

5. Follow Up and Offer Support: Giving feedback isn’t a one-and-done deal. Check in regularly to see how things are going. “How’s the new approach working for you? Do you need any additional resources or training?” This shows you care about their growth and success.

Now, let’s talk about the elephant in the room—emotions. Yes, giving and receiving feedback can be emotional. Remember, it’s okay if someone feels a bit hurt or defensive. Acknowledge their feelings, and remind them that the goal is to help them grow. “I know this might be tough to hear, but I believe in you, and I want to see you succeed. We’re in this together.”

Lastly, practice makes perfect. The more you give feedback, the more natural it will become. And hey, even if you stumble a bit, it’s all part of the learning process. Just keep it real, keep it kind, and keep it focused on improvement. Your team will thank you, and you’ll build a culture of trust and growth. Good luck, and may the feedback force be with you!

title: Christian purpose-driven living book|serving others as the path to a meaningful life
text:
Let me tell you about the day I completely misunderstood purpose.  

It was a Tuesday—because, let’s be real, most of our epiphanies happen on Tuesdays, not mountaintops. I was sitting in my home office, scrolling through yet another “Find Your God-Given Purpose” quiz (yes, I took it—twice), trying to decode my spiritual GPS. I had a clear vision board: a published book, speaking gigs, maybe even a podcast with decent audio quality. All noble goals—until I got a text from my neighbor, Maria: *“My mom fell. Can’t get her up. She’s 82. I’m at work. Can you sit with her till 4?”*  

I stared at the screen. My internal monologue went full Hollywood: *But I have a deadline. And this chapter is due tomorrow. And what if I lose momentum? What if this little detour derails the whole plan?*  

I hesitated for exactly 47 seconds. Then I walked across the street.  

Maria’s mom, Mrs. Delgado, was sitting on the floor beside her recliner, holding a mug of cold tea like it was a lifeline. Her hip wasn’t broken—but her pride was bruised, her confidence shaky, her fear very real. So I didn’t fix anything right away. I sat on the floor *with* her—not above her, not rushing her—just there. We talked about her late husband’s rose garden, how she used to teach third grade in San Antonio, and why she still keeps a jar of butterscotch candies on her windowsill “for emergencies.” Two hours later, when Maria arrived, Mrs. Delgado squeezed my hand and said, “You didn’t just help me up. You helped me remember who I am.”  

That moment cracked something open in me. Not because it was dramatic—but because it was *ordinary*, tender, unglamorous—and yet it carried more weight than any milestone I’d been chasing.  

Here’s what Jesus didn’t say: “Go build your brand. Launch your ministry. Get your name known.” What He *did* say—over and over—is startlingly simple: *“Love your neighbor. Wash feet. Feed the hungry. Visit the prisoner. Welcome the stranger.”* Not as stepping stones to significance. As the very shape of significance itself.  

Serving others isn’t the *means* to a meaningful life—it *is* the meaningful life. It’s where heaven touches earth, not in lightning bolts, but in eye contact, in showing up, in remembering someone’s favorite soup or the name of their grandchild. Meaning isn’t found in the spotlight—it’s forged in the quiet furnace of faithful smallness.  

Think about it: When do you feel most *alive*? Not most accomplished—but most *anchored*, most *human*, most *like yourself*? For me, it’s not after a great talk. It’s when I’m chopping onions for the single mom down the block whose car broke down *again*. It’s when I listen—*really* listen—to my barista, who’s grieving her dad and hasn’t told anyone at work. It’s when I text my friend who’s struggling with depression not to “fix” her, but just to say, “I’m holding space for you today. No reply needed.”  

None of these things go viral. None earn me a trophy. But each one stitches me deeper into the fabric of love—God’s love made visible through my hands, my time, my attention. That’s where purpose breathes. Not in the grand declaration, but in the daily decision: *Will I look up—or look out? Will I protect my agenda—or enlarge someone else’s dignity?*  

And here’s the beautiful irony: The more I serve—not as a strategy, but as a surrender—the more my own life fills up. My anxiety softens. My gratitude deepens. My sense of calling becomes less about *what I’m supposed to do* and more about *who I’m becoming*: kinder, braver, quieter, more present. Purpose isn’t a destination we reach. It’s a posture we practice—one act of love at a time.  

So don’t wait for the big assignment. Start where you are. See the person in front of you—not as a project or a problem, but as a soul Jesus died for. Hand them the coffee. Hold the door. Ask, “How are you *really*?” Text the encouragement you were too busy to send. Serve like no one’s watching—because, in truth, Love is always watching… and smiling.  

That’s not just a path to meaning.  
That’s where meaning lives.

title: entrepreneurship book|launching a small business with almost no money
text:
Look. I’m not gonna hand you a glittery “hustle ladder” infographic or tell you to “monetize your passion” while sipping oat-milk lattes in a WeWork pod. You’re broke. Your bank account looks like a crime scene. Your “business plan” is scribbled on a napkin next to last night’s takeout order. Good. That’s where *real* small businesses start—not with seed funding, but with shame, stubbornness, and a $12.99 domain name.

First: ditch the “minimum viable product” nonsense. MVPs are for startups that already have engineers, lawyers, and a parent who’ll cosign a loan. You? You need an *MVP-0*: the version so bare-bones it’s basically just you, a phone, and one thing you can deliver *today*. My friend Lena started her copywriting gig by cold-emailing five local dentists—*not* with a fancy portfolio (she had none), but with this subject line: “Your website says ‘We Care.’ Yours actually does. Can I help?” She sent it at 7:13 a.m., before they’d checked email. Three replied. One said yes—for $150, cash, same day. She wrote his homepage in 93 minutes. Used that $150 to buy a $4.99 Canva Pro trial and made a single, ugly-but-clear PDF case study: *“How Dr. Patel Got 12 New Patients in 3 Weeks (Without Google Ads).”* That PDF got her four more clients in two weeks. Total startup cost? $17.98. Not $17,980. *Seventeen dollars and ninety-eight cents.*

You don’t need a logo. You don’t need business cards. You *do* need to answer the phone like you’ve done this a thousand times—even if your hands are sweating and you just Googled “how to say ‘invoice’ without stuttering.” Answer it *by the second ring.* Every second you let it ring is you telling the world, “I’m not serious yet.”

And stop waiting for permission. No one’s coming to approve your Instagram bio. No investor is going to tap you on the shoulder because your vision board has good feng shui. The only permission you need is from the first person who says “yes”—and even then, you’ll probably mess up the first invoice. (Lena did. Sent it with “$150.000” instead of “$150.00.” Client texted back: “Is this a typo or am I getting a bonus?” She apologized, fixed it, and offered to write his next three social posts free. He became her longest-running client.)

Here’s what costs money—and how to sidestep it:  
- Website? Use Carrd.co ($19/year) or even Linktree (free). Paste your phone number *twice*—top and bottom. Add one sentence: “I fix [X problem] for people like you. Text me.” Done.  
- Email list? Skip Mailchimp. Start with a free Gmail account labeled “hello@yourbusiness.com” (yes, you can do that—just set up forwarding from your personal email). When someone signs up, reply *within 9 minutes*. Not 9 hours. *Minutes.* That’s your “automation.”  
- Accounting? Use Wave Apps. Free. Takes 11 minutes to learn. If you spend more than 20 minutes setting up QuickBooks, you’ve already lost $87 in opportunity cost.  

Also—cut the “brand voice” obsession. Your brand voice is *you*, slightly louder and less apologetic. Say “I’ll get this to you Friday” instead of “I’ll endeavor to facilitate timely delivery.” People hire humans, not mission statements.  

One last thing: track *only* two numbers for the first 90 days. Not revenue per lead. Not CAC. Just:  
1. How many *actual conversations* you had (not DMs, not likes—voice-to-voice or face-to-face, minimum 3 minutes)  
2. How many of those ended with “Let’s do this” or “Send me the details”  

If you hit 5 conversations and 2 yeses in week one? You’re ahead of 83% of “entrepreneurs” who spent $4,200 on a Shopify theme and still haven’t sent one pitch.  

Oh—and delete your Pinterest board titled “Small Business Aesthetic.” It’s not helping. Neither is reorganizing your desk. Go call that florist. Text that yoga studio owner. Ask if they need help *right now* with something small, cheap, and urgent—like writing their holiday promo email or updating their Google Business profile. Charge $65. Take cash. Deposit it. Then do it again tomorrow.  

The money isn’t the barrier. The barrier is believing you need to look like you’ve got money *before* you make any. You don’t. You just need to show up—slightly unpolished, wildly available, and weirdly specific about what you’ll do *this week.*  

Now go. And if you reread this paragraph three times before acting? Stop. Pick up the phone. Dial. Say: “Hi, it’s [Your Name]. I help [X] with [Y]. Do you have 90 seconds?”  

That’s it. That’s the launch.

title: career advice book|quitting a stable job to do work you care about
text:
Chapter 3: The Leap of Faith: From Stability to Passion

 The Decision

In the quiet of my office, surrounded by the familiar hum of fluorescent lights and the soft clicking of keyboards, I found myself staring at a blank screen. It was a Monday, and like every other Monday for the past five years, I was at my desk, working on a project that no longer ignited any spark within me. I had a stable job, a steady paycheck, and a clear path to promotion. But something was missing. The passion, the drive, the sense of purpose—these were all fading, replaced by a gnawing emptiness.

I had always been a planner, someone who mapped out every step of their career with precision. I had followed the conventional wisdom: get a good education, land a stable job, work hard, and climb the corporate ladder. And yet, here I was, feeling like a stranger in my own life. The thought of spending the next thirty years in this same routine, doing work that didn't resonate with me, was suffocating.

It was during a late-night conversation with a close friend that the idea first took root. We were discussing our dreams, the things we wished we could do if money and stability weren’t factors. My friend, a passionate artist, talked about how she longed to paint full-time but was too afraid to leave her day job. As I listened, I realized that I, too, had a dream—a vision of a career that aligned with my values and brought me joy. I wanted to write, to share stories that could inspire and help others. But it seemed like an impossible dream, one that required a leap into the unknown.

 The Turning Point

The turning point came when I attended a workshop on personal development. The speaker, a successful entrepreneur, shared her journey from a stable but unfulfilling job to a career she loved. She spoke about the importance of aligning your work with your passions and the courage it takes to make that change. Her words resonated deeply with me. I left the workshop with a renewed sense of purpose and a growing conviction that it was time to take a leap.

But making such a significant decision is never easy. I knew I needed to be prepared, both emotionally and financially. I started by setting aside a portion of my salary each month, creating a financial cushion that would allow me to transition without immediate financial stress. I also began to research the field of writing, connecting with authors and editors, and taking online courses to hone my skills. I wanted to ensure that I was not just following a dream but was also equipped to succeed in it.

 The Transition

The process of quitting my stable job was not without its challenges. I had to navigate the expectations of family and friends, many of whom were concerned about the risks involved. "What if it doesn’t work out?" they asked. "What will you do then?" These questions were valid, and they made me pause. But I reminded myself that staying in a job that no longer fulfilled me was a risk in itself—a risk of living a life of regret.

I decided to have an honest conversation with my boss. I explained my decision, expressing gratitude for the opportunities I had been given and my desire to pursue a new path. To my surprise, he was supportive. He understood the importance of following one’s passions and even offered to provide references and support as I transitioned.

The day I handed in my resignation letter was a mix of emotions. There was a sense of relief, but also a twinge of fear. I was leaving behind the security of a stable job, but I was also stepping into a world of possibilities. The next few months were a whirlwind of activity. I spent my days writing, networking, and learning. I faced rejections and setbacks, but each one taught me something valuable. I learned to be persistent, to embrace failure as a part of the journey, and to trust in the process.

 Practical Advice

If you are considering quitting a stable job to do work you care about, here are some practical steps to guide you through the transition:

1. Clarify Your Vision: Before making any big changes, take the time to define what you truly want. What kind of work excites you? What impact do you want to make? Write down your goals and the reasons why you are making this change. This clarity will serve as your North Star throughout the transition.

2. Build a Financial Cushion: One of the biggest fears people have when leaving a stable job is financial insecurity. Start by assessing your current financial situation and create a budget that allows you to save a portion of your income. Aim to have enough savings to cover at least six months of living expenses. This will give you the financial breathing room you need to focus on your new venture.

3. Develop New Skills: If you are transitioning into a new field, it’s important to build the necessary skills. Take courses, attend workshops, and seek mentorship. Connect with professionals in your desired field and learn from their experiences. The more prepared you are, the smoother your transition will be.

4. Create a Plan B: Even with the best preparation, there may be unforeseen challenges. It’s wise to have a backup plan. This could be a part-time job, freelance work, or even a return to your previous field. Having a Plan B can alleviate some of the anxiety and provide a safety net.

5. Communicate Openly: Be honest with your employer, family, and friends about your decision. Explain your reasons and the steps you are taking to ensure a smooth transition. Their support can be invaluable, and open communication can help address any concerns they may have.

6. Embrace the Journey: The road to your dream career will likely be filled with ups and downs. Embrace the journey, and don’t be too hard on yourself. Celebrate small victories and learn from setbacks. Remember, every step forward, no matter how small, is a step toward your goal.

 Conclusion

Quitting a stable job to pursue work you care about is a bold and courageous decision. It requires self-reflection, planning, and a willingness to step into the unknown. But the rewards are immeasurable. For me, the leap from a stable but unfulfilling job to a career in writing has been one of the most rewarding experiences of my life. I wake up each day excited to work, and I am filled with a sense of purpose that I never felt before.

If you find yourself in a similar position, remember that it’s never too late to make a change. The world needs more people who are passionate about their work. Take the leap, and you might just find that the greatest adventure of your life is waiting on the other side.

title: personal finance book|negotiating a raise and why most people never ask
text:
I once asked for a raise by sending an email that said, “Hey, I’ve been killing it. Can we talk about my salary?” It was sent at 4:58 p.m. on a Friday. My manager replied at 9:03 a.m. Monday with: “Let’s circle back next quarter.” Which is corporate-speak for *“I will forget this ever happened and you will quietly resent your job until your therapist asks why you cry while folding laundry.”*

That was me—28, wearing shoes that pinched, eating lunch at my desk like it was a virtue, and absolutely terrified to ask for what I’d already earned. Not hoped for. *Earned.* Because here’s the uncomfortable truth no one tells you: most people don’t get raises because they don’t ask. Not because they’re underperforming. Not because budgets are tight (though yeah, sometimes they are). Mostly? Because they’ve convinced themselves that asking = being greedy, pushy, or—my personal favorite—*ungrateful*. As if showing up every day in sweatpants (under a blazer, of course) and pretending to understand Slack threads about “synergy levers” is some kind of charity.

I’ll never forget my friend Lena. Brilliant copywriter, calm under fire, once rewrote an entire product launch campaign in 36 hours after the original agency bailed. Her boss called it “heroic.” She got a handwritten thank-you note. And a $50 Amazon gift card. *Five. Zero.* Meanwhile, her counterpart at another firm—same experience, same portfolio—negotiated a 22% bump *before accepting the offer*. Same talent. Different script. Different courage. Different belief that her time, ideas, and emotional labor had actual dollar signs attached.

Why do we freeze? Because money feels weirdly sacred and deeply personal—like asking your dentist how much he charges per cavity. We overprepare or underprepare. We rehearse in the shower but panic in the elevator. We wait for “the right moment,” which—spoiler—is a myth invented by HR departments and people who’ve never had to choose between car insurance and groceries.

So let’s fix that. Here’s what actually works—not theory, but stuff I’ve tried, botched, refined, and taught to hundreds of people who later texted me screenshots of their new paystubs (some with celebratory taco emojis):

1. Anchor with data, not drama. Don’t lead with “I’m stressed” or “My rent went up.” Lead with “Based on market data from Payscale and Glassdoor, peers with my role, tenure, and impact average $X–$Y. I’m currently at $Z—and here’s exactly how I’ve moved the needle since last review.” (Bonus points if you attach a one-page “value summary”—three bullet points of wins, metrics, and outcomes. Keep it tight. Your manager has 73 unread emails. Be kind.)

2. Time it like a sitcom finale—not a season premiere. Ask *after* a win, not before. Just closed a big deal? Launched that feature everyone loves? Got unsolicited praise from a client? *That’s* your window. Not during budget-planning hell or when your boss’s Slack status reads “🧠🔥⚡️.”

3. Practice saying the number out loud—*alone*, preferably in your car. Seriously. Say it three times: “I’d like to discuss adjusting my base salary to $[exact number].” Not “maybe,” not “if possible,” not “whenever you have time.” Say it like you’re ordering coffee. Confident. Simple. Slightly bored, even. Your voice should sound like you’re stating weather, not committing treason.

And listen—this part matters—*don’t apologize for asking.* You wouldn’t apologize for checking your bank balance. Or for confirming your flight time. Asking for fair compensation isn’t rude. It’s professional hygiene. Like flossing, but for your career.

One last thing: If they say no? Don’t vanish into a cloud of shame. Say, “Thanks for your honesty. Can we agree on clear goals and a timeline to revisit this? Maybe in 90 days?” Then *hold them to it.* Document those goals. Hit them. Send a gentle follow-up. Most “no”s aren’t final—they’re just “not yet, and also I need you to make it easy for me to say yes next time.”

I still get nervous before these conversations. But now I know: the cost of silence isn’t just missed money. It’s compounding doubt. It’s eroded self-worth. It’s watching someone less skilled get promoted because they asked—and you didn’t.

So go ahead. Ask. Not greedily. Not desperately. Just clearly, calmly, and with receipts. And if your hands shake? Good. That means you care. And caring—that’s where real financial confidence begins.

title: negotiation book|finding out what the other side really wants
text:
Chapter 7: What They *Really* Want (Hint: It’s Not What They’re Asking For)

Let me tell you about Dave—the guy who almost cost his company $2.3 million… and didn’t even realize it.

Dave was negotiating a software integration deal with a midsize logistics firm. Their procurement team kept hammering on one thing: “We need a 45-day payment term.” Every meeting, every email, every redline in the contract—it all circled back to that number. Dave’s legal team pushed back hard. Finance said it was “untenable.” Dave spent three weeks building spreadsheets showing cash flow erosion, drafting compromise language, rehearsing his “reasonable but firm” tone. He thought he was being strategic. Turns out? He was negotiating blindfolded.

Then, over lukewarm coffee at a break in the fourth meeting, Dave asked something totally off-script—not about terms, not about timelines—but: “Hey, what’s keeping you up at night right now?”  

The CFO leaned in and said, “Honestly? Our CEO just got grilled by the board for missing Q3 delivery KPIs. We’re scrambling to prove this new system *works*—not just gets installed, but moves boxes faster. If we go live and it crashes during peak season? That’s a career-limiting event.”

Boom. The real ask wasn’t 45 days. It was *trust*. It was proof—fast, visible, low-risk—that the software wouldn’t blow up their operations. The payment term? Just a proxy. A safety net they’d grabbed because no one had offered them a better one.

So Dave scrapped the spreadsheet. Instead, he proposed a 90-day pilot—free of charge—with shared success metrics: “If your on-time delivery improves by 8% in Week 3, we waive the first month’s license fee. If it dips below baseline, we’ll stay onsite until it’s fixed—no bill.” The CFO’s shoulders dropped. He nodded. *That* was the deal they needed. The 45-day term? Dropped without a fight.

Here’s the uncomfortable truth most negotiators miss: People rarely negotiate *what they say they want*. They negotiate *what they think will get them what they really want*. And what they really want is almost always human—not transactional. Security. Recognition. Control. Relief from embarrassment. A win they can show their boss. Peace of mind.

I learned this the hard way early in my career—negotiating a vendor contract for a nonprofit I ran. The supplier insisted on “exclusive branding rights” on our annual report. I dug in. Argued about visibility, equity, mission alignment. Spent hours drafting clauses. Then, two days before signing, I called their account manager—not the VP—and asked, gently: “Help me understand—why does this matter so much *right now*?”  

Turns out? Her bonus was tied to landing one “prestigious nonprofit partnership” before quarter-end. She didn’t care about the logo placement. She cared about hitting her number—and proving she could land a “name-brand” client. So I cut her a letter—on official letterhead—calling her firm our “Strategic Technology Partner,” signed by our Executive Director. No exclusivity. No logo clause. Just credibility. She sent the signed contract back in 90 minutes.

So how do you uncover the real want? First—stop listening to demands. Start listening to *frustration*, *urgency*, and *pride*. Second—ask open, non-defensive questions that invite story, not position: “What would make this feel like a win for your team?” “If this went perfectly, what would change for you personally?” “What’s the biggest risk you’re trying to avoid?” Third—watch where people lean in. Where their voice softens. Where they pause and look down, then up again. That’s often where the real thing lives.

Remember: You’re not negotiating terms. You’re negotiating *meaning*. And meaning is never written into the contract. It’s whispered between the lines—if you know how to listen for it.

title: habit-building book|starting with habits so small you can't fail
text:
You've probably heard the advice to "dream big" or "aim for the stars." And sure, it's great to have grand visions and lofty goals. But when it comes to actually building habits that stick, I'm here to tell you: start small—so damn small that you can't possibly fail.

Let me give you an example. Say you want to get in shape. You might be tempted to sign up for a marathon, buy all the gear, and commit to running every day. That's a recipe for burnout and disappointment. Instead, start with something so tiny that it's almost laughable. How about just putting on your running shoes? That's it. No running required. Just put on the shoes. It sounds ridiculous, but it works.

Why? Because the biggest obstacle to forming a new habit is often just getting started. Once you're laced up, you might think, "Well, I'm already wearing these, might as well go for a short walk." And before you know it, you're out the door, maybe even jogging a bit. The key is to make the initial step so easy that your brain doesn't have a chance to resist.

Now, let's talk about reading. Maybe you want to read more, but you always find excuses. "I don't have time," "I'm too tired," "I'll do it tomorrow." Sound familiar? Here’s what you do: commit to reading one page a day. One page. That's it. It takes, what, 30 seconds? Anyone can do that. And if you find yourself getting into the story, you might keep going. But the goal is just one page. Over a year, that's 365 pages—almost a whole book. And you did it without even trying.

The beauty of starting small is that it builds momentum. When you consistently achieve a tiny goal, your brain gets a little hit of dopamine, and you start to feel good. You start to see yourself as someone who follows through. And that's a powerful shift in mindset. Before you know it, you're doing more than you ever thought possible.

But here's the thing: you have to be honest with yourself. If you set a goal that's too big, you're setting yourself up for failure. And failure feels bad. It makes you less likely to try again. So, if you want to meditate, don't start with 30 minutes. Start with 60 seconds. Yes, just one minute. Sit down, close your eyes, and breathe. That's it. It's so easy that you can't say no. And once you're in the habit, you can gradually increase the time.

Another important point: consistency is key. It's better to do a little bit every day than to do a lot sporadically. So, if you want to write a novel, don't set a goal of writing 10,000 words in a weekend. Set a goal of writing 50 words a day. It's manageable, and you can do it even on your busiest days. Over time, those 50 words will add up, and you'll have a manuscript.

Look, I get it. Starting small might feel like you're not making real progress. But trust me, it's the most effective way to build lasting habits. It's the difference between a flash in the pan and a lifelong change. So, pick something you want to do, break it down into the tiniest, most doable step, and get started. You won't regret it.

title: minimalism and focus book|clearing your desk, your inbox and your calendar
text:
Chapter 3: The Tuesday That Broke Me—And How I Learned to Clear, Not Conquer

It was a Tuesday. Not a dramatic, storm-lashed Tuesday—but the kind that arrives quietly, like fog rolling in at dawn: unremarkable until it’s suffocating.

My desk held three coffee rings (two fresh), a stack of unopened mail held together by a rubber band stretched to its breaking point, and a Post-it stuck to my monitor with the words *“CALL SARAH? (URGENT?)”*—written two weeks prior. My inbox sat at 1,247 messages. I’d stopped counting after 900. The “Important” label had long since lost meaning; everything felt urgent, nothing felt essential. And my calendar? A mosaic of back-to-back 30-minute meetings, color-coded like a hospital triage board—blue for “client,” red for “internal,” yellow for “follow-up (maybe?),” and one ominous black block labeled *“THINK?”*—scheduled for 11:58 a.m., lasting precisely two minutes.

At 10:47 a.m., my phone buzzed. A client needed a revised proposal *by noon*. Simultaneously, my laptop pinged: an automated reminder—*“Submit Q2 sustainability metrics (DUE IN 17 MINUTES).”* I opened my calendar to reschedule a call—and froze. There was no slot. Not even five minutes. My breath shortened. My fingers hovered over the keyboard, trembling—not from urgency, but from the sheer *weight* of unresolved, unsorted, unclaimed time and attention. I didn’t cry. I just… stopped. Sat very still. Stared at the blinking cursor on a blank document titled *“Proposal Draft_v12_FINAL_(ACTUAL).docx*.

That Tuesday didn’t break me because of the workload. It broke me because I’d confused *busyness* with *intention*, and *accumulation* with *capability*. My desk, inbox, and calendar weren’t tools—they were evidence rooms, each item a silent accusation: *You said yes. You saved it. You promised. You forgot.*

I walked away from the desk. Not dramatically—no slamming doors—but slowly, deliberately, to the small balcony outside my home office. I watched a sparrow land on the railing, hop twice, tilt its head, then fly off with absolute, uncomplicated purpose. No inbox. No calendar. No unread notifications. Just sky, wind, and the next necessary thing.

That’s when I understood: Clarity isn’t found by doing more. It’s reclaimed by removing what obscures your line of sight—even if that “what” is your own good intentions, your fear of missing out, or the polite “yes” you whispered six months ago.

So I began—not with a system, but with a vow: *No new input until the existing input has been honored, declined, or released.*

Here’s how I cleared the three anchors of modern distraction—not all at once, but in deliberate, daily acts of gentle excavation:

1. Your Desk: The Physical Threshold of Attention  
I started with one square foot—the space directly in front of my keyboard. Nothing else. I emptied it: pens, sticky notes, old receipts, a dried-out highlighter. Then I asked of each item: *Does this serve my current priority? Does it need action *today*? Or is it a relic of a past intention?* If the answer wasn’t a clear “Yes—right now,” it left the zone. Not thrown away (yet), but moved to a single “Hold” tray—out of sight, out of mind, but not out of accountability. I repeated this inch by inch, day by day. Within five days, my desk held only three things: my laptop, a notebook open to today’s single focus, and a ceramic mug. The emptiness wasn’t sterile—it was *resonant*. Space became a signal: *What deserves to live here?*

2. Your Inbox: Where Time Goes to Hide  
I disabled desktop notifications. Then I set a hard rule: *One inbox sweep per day—at 4:00 p.m., for 25 minutes.* No exceptions. Using the “Four Ds” (Delete, Delegate, Do, Defer), I processed every message—not to “get to zero,” but to get to *clarity*. Delete anything older than 30 days that hadn’t been acted upon. Delegate only if someone else truly owns the outcome (and I’d confirmed they’d receive it). “Do” meant *only* tasks taking under two minutes—reply, forward, schedule, archive. “Defer” went into a single, named folder: *“Waiting: [Name/Date].”* Crucially, I unsubscribed from *everything* that delivered information I didn’t actively seek—newsletters I skimmed, updates I never clicked, alerts I’d forgotten opting into. My inbox dropped from 1,247 to 43 in ten days. Not because I worked faster—but because I stopped letting other people’s rhythms dictate my attention.

3. Your Calendar: The Map of Your Finite Hours  
I blocked 90 minutes every morning as *“Focus Time”—non-negotiable, no-meeting, no-email.* Then I audited every existing meeting. For each, I asked: *If I couldn’t attend, would this still happen? Does it have a defined outcome? Who *must* be there—and why?* I declined or rescheduled 60% of them. I renamed vague blocks: *“Team Sync”* became *“Decide: Q3 Campaign Channels.”* I added a recurring 15-minute “Calendar Cleanse” every Friday at 4:45 p.m.—to delete ghosts, adjust buffers, and protect next week’s Focus Time. Most importantly, I started saying *“Let me check my calendar and circle back in 10 minutes”* instead of reflexively accepting invites. That pause alone reclaimed 8–12 hours a week.

Clearing isn’t about perfection. It’s about alignment. That Tuesday didn’t vanish my responsibilities—it revealed which ones were mine to carry, and which I’d merely agreed to hold. My desk, inbox, and calendar are no longer monuments to obligation. They’re quiet instruments—tuned, spare, ready—not for more, but for what matters *now*.

Start small. Start with one square foot. One 25-minute sweep. One 90-minute block. Not to conquer the chaos—but to remember who you are beneath it.

title: relationships advice book|staying faithful and keeping a long marriage alive
text:
You’ve been married for a long time—maybe twenty years, maybe forty. You’ve weathered job losses, illnesses, teenage rebellion, aging parents, quiet stretches where the days blur together. You’re not newly in love, and that’s okay. What you have is something quieter, deeper, and far more valuable: a shared life. But here’s what no one tells you outright: staying faithful and keeping that life vibrant isn’t about avoiding temptation—it’s about choosing each other, daily, with intention and tenderness.

Faithfulness isn’t just the absence of infidelity. It’s the presence of attention. It’s putting your phone face-down when your partner walks into the room. It’s listening—not to reply, but to understand—when they describe their day, even if it’s the same story you’ve heard three times this week. It’s noticing the small things: how they stir their coffee now, the way they sigh before answering a difficult question, the slight pause before they say “I’m fine” when they’re not. These are the quiet acts of fidelity—the ones that build trust brick by brick, year after year.

Long marriages don’t stay alive on autopilot. They require tending, like a garden that’s been there for decades. You wouldn’t expect it to flourish without occasional weeding, pruning, watering—even changing the soil now and then. So ask yourself: When was the last time you did something new *together*? Not just a vacation, but something that stretched you both—learning to bake sourdough, taking a pottery class, walking a different trail on Sunday mornings? Novelty doesn’t have to be grand. It can be as simple as cooking a recipe neither of you has tried, or turning off all screens for one evening a week and playing cards or talking about what you believed at age sixteen.

And let’s talk about conflict—because it will come. Not every disagreement needs resolution. Sometimes what matters most is not who’s right, but whether you still feel safe enough to be imperfect in front of each other. When you argue, notice your tone first. A softened voice, a pause before speaking, a hand gently placed on their arm—these aren’t signs of surrender. They’re lifelines thrown across the space between two people who refuse to let distance settle in.

Don’t underestimate the power of physical touch that isn’t sexual. A hand on the small of the back as you pass in the kitchen. Holding hands while watching TV. Sitting shoulder-to-shoulder on the porch swing, silent but close. These gestures whisper, “I’m still here. I still choose you.” Over time, they become the language of belonging—more reliable than words, especially when words fail.

You may feel invisible sometimes—like your role has blurred into caregiver, manager, fixer. That’s when you must protect your individual self. Not to escape the marriage, but to nourish it. Read that book you’ve been meaning to read. Call that old friend. Take a walk alone and listen to birdsong instead of your own thoughts looping. When you return to your partner replenished—not resentful, not depleted—you bring more love, not less.

And please, forgive yourselves—both of you—for the slow drifts, the missed cues, the years you didn’t prioritize connection the way you wish you had. Regret is useful only if it leads to change—not shame. What matters is what you do *now*. Today. This evening. The next time your partner says, “How was your day?” look up from your screen. Make eye contact. Ask one real follow-up question—and mean it.

Staying faithful isn’t about perfection. It’s about showing up, again and again, with humility and care. Keeping a long marriage alive isn’t about recreating early passion—it’s about cultivating reverence for the person who has seen you at your most ordinary, most tired, most tender, and loved you anyway. That kind of love doesn’t shout. It settles. It deepens. It stays.

So tonight, before you go to bed, say one true thing: “I’m glad you’re mine.” Not because everything is easy—but because you’ve chosen, every single day, to hold on—not to an idea of marriage, but to the real, breathing, imperfect, irreplaceable person beside you. That’s where faithfulness lives. That’s where love endures.

text:
Chapter 7: Single-Tasking in a World Built for Distraction

Have you ever found yourself sitting down to tackle an important project, only to be pulled away by the siren call of your inbox, or lured into the endless scroll of social media? I know I have. In fact, there was this one time when I had a deadline looming over me like a dark cloud, and instead of focusing on my work, I spent half the day jumping from one task to another, feeling more anxious with every passing minute. By the end of the day, I realized I hadn't made any meaningful progress, and the guilt of wasted time weighed heavily on me. It's a story that resonates with many of us, as we navigate a world designed to distract.

But why is it so hard to stay focused? The answer lies in how our brains are wired and the environment we've created. Our ancestors didn't have to deal with constant notifications, emails, and the allure of the internet. They lived in a world where single-tasking was the norm, and their survival often depended on it. Today, however, we live in a digital age where multitasking has become the default mode, and the idea of doing just one thing at a time seems almost counterintuitive.

Let's talk about the science behind it. When you switch between tasks, your brain has to go through a process called "context switching." This means that every time you jump from one task to another, your brain needs to reorient itself, which takes time and energy. Imagine you're driving on a highway, and every few minutes, you have to take an exit, find a new road, and get back on the highway. It's not very efficient, is it? That's exactly what happens when you try to juggle multiple tasks. You end up wasting precious mental resources and making more mistakes.

So, how can we reclaim our focus in a world that seems to be conspiring against it? The key is to embrace single-tasking, and here’s how you can do it:

First, create a distraction-free environment. Turn off notifications on your phone and computer. If you need to, use apps that block distracting websites during certain times of the day. For me, I found that putting my phone in another room and using a website blocker like Freedom really helped. It might feel uncomfortable at first, but trust me, the peace of mind is worth it.

Second, set clear goals and priorities. Before you start your day, make a list of the most important tasks you need to accomplish. Focus on one task at a time, and give it your full attention. I like to use the Pomodoro Technique, where you work for 25 minutes, then take a 5-minute break. It's a simple but effective way to keep your focus sharp and prevent burnout.

Third, practice mindfulness. Being present in the moment can help you resist the urge to check your email or social media. Take a few deep breaths before you start a task, and remind yourself why it's important. When you notice your mind wandering, gently bring it back to the task at hand. Mindfulness isn't just about meditation; it's about being fully engaged in whatever you're doing.

Finally, be kind to yourself. We all have days when we struggle to stay focused, and that's okay. Don't beat yourself up if you find yourself getting distracted. Instead, acknowledge the distraction, and gently guide yourself back to the task. Over time, you'll build the muscle of single-tasking, and it will become easier.

Remember, the goal isn't to be perfect; it's to make progress. By embracing single-tasking, you'll not only get more done, but you'll also enjoy the process more. So, the next time you sit down to work, take a deep breath, turn off those notifications, and dive into that one task. You might be surprised by how much you can accomplish.

title: writing-craft memoir|the daily routine of a working novelist
text:
6:17 a.m. Alarm goes off. I hit snooze. Not the “gentle, nurturing, mindfulness-approved” kind—just the brutal, jarring *BRRRRT* from my ancient Samsung flip phone I keep solely for this purpose. Why? Because if it’s on my iPhone, I’ll scroll TikTok for seventeen minutes pretending I’m “researching Gen Z voice” and then panic when I realize it’s 7:03 and my coffee’s cold and my dog’s staring at me like I’ve personally betrayed the covenant of breakfast.

Coffee first. Black. Two heaping scoops in the French press. Not “artisanal single-origin”—it’s Folgers Classic Roast, $4.99 at Walmart. Don’t judge. It works. The bitterness wakes up the part of my brain that remembers how to spell *separate* instead of *seperate*. (I still get it wrong in first drafts. Always.)

By 7:22, I’m at the desk—the one with the wobble in the left front leg, fixed with a folded Post-it note from 2018. Laptop open. No fancy writing software. Just Word. With Track Changes *off*, thank god. I used Scrivener for three months in 2019. Wasted 87 hours learning how to tag “character motivation” before realizing I’d rather stab myself in the ear with a bent paperclip than organize a scene by “emotional arc.” So: Word. Font: Calibri. Size: 12. Margins: narrow. That’s it.

I write from 7:45 to 11:15. *Exactly.* Not “until inspiration strikes.” Inspiration is a myth sold by people who don’t have rent. I write 1,200 words. Some days it’s 1,183. Some days it’s 1,247. If I hit 1,200 at 10:52? I stop. Walk away. Let the sentence hang. Let the character stew. Let my lower back scream. I do *not* “push through.” Pushing through gives you prose that smells like burnt toast and regret.

At 11:15 sharp, I close the laptop. Even if the sentence is mid—*“She reached for the—”* —I close it. I’ve trained my brain to treat that cutoff like a physical door slamming. It works. The subconscious does its thing while I’m folding laundry or arguing with my teenager about why yes, she *can* wear ripped jeans to her AP Bio exam, but no, she cannot text during dinner.

Lunch is whatever’s in the fridge that doesn’t require cooking. Yesterday: half a block of cheddar, two saltines, and a pickle spear. I ate it standing over the sink. My agent says I should “optimize wellness.” I told her I optimize *output*. She sighed. I sent her a screenshot of my word count. She stopped asking.

Afternoon is for the *real* work: revision. Not “polishing.” Not “tightening.” *Surgery.* I print pages. Red pen only. Not gel ink—actual cheap-ass Bic red ballpoint. The kind that bleeds through. I circle every “very,” cross out every “just,” slash every adverb ending in *-ly* unless it’s doing something violent or unexpected (e.g., “she laughed *hysterically*” → stays; “she walked *quickly*” → dies). I count dialogue tags. If there are more than three “he saids” in a paragraph, I rewrite the whole damn exchange. People don’t *say* things. They *do* things while speaking. They spill coffee. They crack their knuckles. They lie.

I read aloud. Every. Single. Page. Even the boring exposition about municipal zoning laws in Chapter 12. If my tongue stumbles, it stays cut. If I yawn? Cut. If I check my watch? Cut. My editor once asked why I kill so many darlings. I said, “Because they’re not darlings. They’re corpses wearing silk pajamas.”

Emails? Answered between 3:30 and 4:15 p.m. Only the ones that can’t wait until tomorrow. My assistant handles the rest. She’s brilliant. I pay her what she asks. Not a cent less. Writers who underpay their assistants deserve every bad review they get.

5:00 p.m. Dog walk. No headphones. Just me, the leash, and the fact that I haven’t thought about plot for 22 minutes. That’s the point.

I don’t journal. I don’t meditate. I don’t “find my center.” I find my next line. And if it takes three tries, and I curse, and I throw a pen across the room (which I did Tuesday), fine. The pen bounced. The line eventually came. Not elegant. Not profound. But *true*. For this book. Right now.

My husband asks sometimes, “What’s the book *about*?” I say, “It’s about a woman who lies to her sister and then has to fix the leaky faucet.” He nods. He knows better than to ask again.

And yeah—I skipped lunch twice last week. And yes, my left knee clicks like a Geiger counter. And yes, the manuscript currently lives in a folder labeled “FUCKTHISV2_FINAL_REALLY.”  

That’s how it goes.
