Chapter 3: The Coffee Cup That Broke My Multitasking Habit  

It happened on a Tuesday. Not a dramatic Tuesday—no fire alarms, no missed flights—but one of those ordinary, over-scheduled mornings where my to-do list had metastasized into three color-coded documents, my inbox blinked with 47 unread messages (12 marked “URGENT”), and my calendar was a mosaic of back-to-back Zoom calls, each titled with an acronym I couldn’t decipher without Googling. I’d just finished “quickly” drafting an email while half-listening to a team stand-up, then opened a new tab to research vendor pricing while simultaneously scrolling through LinkedIn “for inspiration.” My brain felt like a browser with 23 tabs open—two frozen, one playing audio from a forgotten YouTube tutorial, and the rest slowly leaking memory.

Then, I reached for my coffee.  

The mug was ceramic, warm, slightly chipped at the rim—the same one I’d used every morning for seven years. As I lifted it, my elbow nudged my laptop. The screen tilted. The coffee cup wobbled. And in that suspended half-second—before the spill, before the reflexive jerk of my wrist—I *felt* it: a sudden, startling clarity. Not about the coffee. Not about the laptop. But about the sheer, exhausting *noise* I’d been carrying inside my skull for months. The constant context-switching wasn’t making me faster. It was making me brittle. Fragile. Like a mug held too tightly, too long, by someone who’d forgotten how to feel its weight.  

I set the cup down. Unplugged my earbuds. Closed all but one tab. And sat—just sat—with the steam rising from the coffee, watching it curl and vanish. No agenda. No timer. No intention to “optimize” the moment. Just presence. For ninety seconds.  

That tiny pause didn’t solve my workload. But it cracked something open. It was the first time in years I’d noticed the *texture* of my own attention—not as a tool to deploy, but as a living thing: tender, finite, easily frayed. And it led me, reluctantly at first, to single-tasking—not as austerity, but as stewardship.

Let’s be clear: single-tasking isn’t about perfection. It’s not locking your phone in a safe and retreating to a cabin for six weeks. It’s the quiet, daily practice of choosing *one thing*—and giving it your unbroken attention—for a defined, humane span of time. In a world engineered to fracture us—to ping, scroll, interrupt, and hijack—single-tasking is the most radical act of self-respect you can perform.

Here’s how to begin—not with willpower, but with design:

1. Start with the “Anchor Task”: Identify *one* non-negotiable activity each day that anchors your sense of competence or calm. For me, it’s writing the first 300 words of my manuscript—no email, no Slack, no news. Not the whole chapter. Just 300 words. I protect this like sacred ground: same time (8:15 a.m.), same physical space (the corner armchair, no laptop—pen and paper only), same ritual (coffee in *that* mug, no distractions). Anchor tasks build neural trust. They whisper: *You are capable of focus. You are allowed to begin.*

2. Design Your Environment, Not Just Your Schedule: Distraction isn’t a failure of discipline—it’s a failure of environment. Your brain doesn’t choose distraction; it *responds* to cues. So remove the triggers. Put your phone in another room during anchor time. Use a physical timer (not your phone’s alarm) so you’re not tempted to glance at notifications. Close your email client *completely*—not just the window, but the app. Studies show it takes an average of 23 minutes to fully re-engage after an interruption. Protect your attention like the irreplaceable resource it is.

3. Embrace the “Five-Minute Reset”: When your mind wanders—and it will—don’t scold yourself. Gently name what pulled you: “Ah, planning dinner,” or “Worrying about that meeting.” Then, without judgment, return to your anchor task. If the pull is strong, give it five minutes *after* your session: “I’ll write down that grocery list *right now*, but only after these next ten minutes of writing.” This isn’t suppression; it’s compassionate redirection.

4. Measure Depth, Not Duration: Forget “hours worked.” Track *moments of flow*: when time dissolved, when ideas connected unexpectedly, when you looked up and realized you’d been fully immersed for 25 minutes. These aren’t flukes—they’re evidence of your attention’s natural capacity. Celebrate them. Note what conditions made them possible (light? silence? pen vs. keyboard?). Build more of *those* conditions.

That Tuesday didn’t change my workload. But it changed my relationship to it. Single-tasking didn’t make me faster—but it made me *clearer*. Decisions felt less frantic. Emails became shorter and kinder. I started finishing things—real things—instead of perpetually “in progress.” Most importantly, I stopped mistaking busyness for contribution.

The world won’t slow down. Notifications won’t stop pinging. But you *can* reclaim the quiet sovereignty of your attention—one anchored cup of coffee, one protected 25-minute block, one gentle return to the task at hand. You don’t need to eliminate distraction. You just need to remember what it feels like to hold something—your work, your breath, your coffee—with both hands. Fully. Without rush. Without apology.  

That’s where real productivity begins: not in doing more, but in being wholly *here*.

title: entrepreneurship book|launching a small business with almost no money
text:
Starting a small business with almost no money is a journey that requires creativity, resilience, and a dash of audacity. You're not just building a company; you're crafting a dream from the ground up, often with little more than your wits and a relentless drive to succeed. But fear not, because many have walked this path before you, turning their visions into thriving enterprises. Let's dive into how you can do it too.

First, embrace the lean startup philosophy. This approach, championed by Eric Ries, advocates for launching your product or service as quickly as possible, using the minimum resources necessary. The goal is to learn and iterate based on real customer feedback, rather than perfecting your offering in isolation. It means you start small, test your assumptions, and scale only when you've validated your business model. This way, you minimize waste and maximize your chances of hitting the market need right on target.

Next, focus on what you already have. Take stock of your skills, experiences, and connections. Often, the most valuable resources are the ones you don't even realize you possess. For instance, if you have a background in marketing, you can leverage that to promote your business without spending much. If you're great at coding, you can build your own website or app. Your network, too, is a treasure trove. Reach out to friends, family, and former colleagues. They might offer advice, help spread the word, or even become your first customers.

Bootstrap your operations by being resourceful. Look for free or low-cost tools and services. There are countless online platforms that offer free trials or freemium models, which can be enough to get you started. Use social media to build your brand and engage with potential customers. Platforms like Instagram, Facebook, and Twitter are powerful marketing channels that require time, not necessarily money. Additionally, consider bartering services. If you need a logo, perhaps you can trade your expertise in exchange for design work. This kind of creative collaboration can save you a lot of cash.

When it comes to funding, explore all your options. While traditional loans and investors might seem out of reach, there are other ways to secure the capital you need. Crowdfunding platforms like Kickstarter or Indiegogo allow you to pitch your idea directly to the public, who can contribute small amounts in exchange for early access to your product or other perks. Another option is to look into microloans, which are smaller, more accessible loans designed specifically for entrepreneurs with limited financial history. Grants and competitions can also provide non-dilutive funding, meaning you don't have to give up equity in your business.

As you grow, stay lean and agile. Keep your overhead low by working from home, co-working spaces, or even coffee shops. Hire freelancers or part-time employees instead of full-time staff, and only bring on team members when you absolutely need them. This flexibility will help you weather the ups and downs of running a new business.

Finally, never stop learning. The entrepreneurial journey is one of continuous improvement. Stay curious, read books, listen to podcasts, and attend workshops and webinars. Join online communities and forums where you can connect with other entrepreneurs and share experiences. Every piece of knowledge you gain is an investment in your future success.

Launching a small business with almost no money is challenging, but it's also incredibly rewarding. By leveraging your existing resources, embracing a lean mindset, and staying adaptable, you can turn your dream into a reality. Remember, the most successful entrepreneurs are those who see obstacles as opportunities and never give up. So, take that first step, and keep moving forward. Your journey to success starts now.

title: small-business marketing guide|getting your first hundred customers through word of mouth
text:
Okay, confession time: my first hundred customers didn’t come from a fancy funnel, a LinkedIn ad campaign, or even a “strategic influencer collab” (which, in 2013, meant asking my cousin Dave if he’d mention my handmade leather notebook sleeves on his very active MySpace page). They came from people *telling other people*—while eating lunch, while waiting for the bus, while pretending to listen to their partner complain about the Wi-Fi. Word of mouth. The OG growth hack. And honestly? It felt less like marketing and more like accidentally starting a rumor that everyone decided was true—and helpful.

I remember standing in line at that tiny coffee shop near my apartment—the one with the perpetually broken pastry case—and overhearing two strangers debating whether my $12 “Stress-Proof To-Do List Pad” was worth it. One said, “My therapist recommended it.” (She hadn’t. But bless her.) The other said, “My neighbor’s dog walker uses it and hasn’t cried since March.” (Also untrue. But *also* kind of true? The dog walker *had* stopped crying, but that was after her third espresso shot.) Point is: they were talking. About *my thing*. And I nearly dropped my oat-milk latte.

Here’s what I learned—not from books, but from awkwardly eavesdropping, sending too many thank-you texts, and once accidentally texting my mom the wrong order confirmation (she still hasn’t let me live down the “Your ‘Serenity Sock Bundle’ has shipped! 🧦✨” message she got at 3 a.m.).

First: Stop trying to *get* word of mouth. Start trying to *deserve* it. People don’t spread things because they’re cleverly branded. They spread things because they feel *delighted*, *relieved*, or mildly obsessed. Was your customer’s problem actually solved? Did your packaging make them laugh out loud? Did your follow-up email include a terrible pun and a GIF of a dancing cactus? That’s the stuff that gets forwarded.

Second: Make it *ridiculously easy* for people to talk—and not just in vague, polite ways. Give them language. Not “It’s great!”—but “It fixed my spreadsheet chaos in under 90 seconds.” Not “I love it!”—but “I told my boss it was magic, and now we use it for all our team stand-ups.” Bonus points if you hand them a little card that says, “If this made your Tuesday better, tell someone who’s still using Excel as a calendar. (And yes, we’ll send you a free sticker.)”

Third: Pay attention to *who* talks—and why. Early on, I noticed three people kept referring friends: a high-school art teacher, a freelance graphic designer, and a retired librarian who ran a very opinionated neighborhood newsletter. They weren’t my “ideal customer” (I’d drawn up some nonsense persona named “Chloe, 34, wellness-adjacent, owns 4 reusable water bottles”). They were just *real humans* who cared deeply about good tools and bad systems. So I stopped trying to “target” and started trying to *serve*. I sent the librarian a custom-printed bookmark. I asked the teacher if she wanted early access to our classroom version. I didn’t pitch—I *listened*, then surprised them with something small and thoughtful. And guess what? Their referrals came with built-in credibility. (“Ms. Delaney says it works. She also says your website font is ‘unforgivably cheerful.’”)

Also—this is critical—*respond to every single referral like it’s a Nobel Prize nomination.* When someone sends you a friend, don’t just say “Thanks!” Say, “Wow—thank you for trusting me with [Friend’s Name]’s time and attention. That means more than you know.” Then *follow up* with the new person—not with a sales pitch, but with, “Hey, [Name] mentioned you might be wrestling with [specific pain point]. Here’s a 60-second video I made just for that moment.” (Spoiler: it’s 58 seconds long and ends with me holding up a slightly burnt cookie.)

And finally: stop obsessing over the *first* hundred. Obsess over the *first ten*. Because those first ten will tell you what’s working, what’s confusing, and which of your jokes land (and which ones should be buried in a landfill with last year’s fidget spinners). They’ll give you real stories to share—not case studies, but human moments: “Sarah from Portland used our planner to finally schedule her dentist appointment *and* her existential crisis. Both happened. Both went fine.”

Word of mouth isn’t lightning—it’s compost. Slow, messy, occasionally smelly, but *incredibly fertile*. You feed it with honesty, consistency, and the courage to be slightly weird in service of being genuinely helpful. And one day, you’ll be standing in line somewhere, heart pounding, listening to strangers talk about your thing… and realize you didn’t build a business. You built a quiet little ripple. And ripples? They keep going. Even when you’re busy Googling “how to unsend a text to your mom.”

title: startup memoir|the early days of a search-engine company and its odd culture
text:
We launched SearchHive on a Tuesday. April 12th, 2016. Not because it was auspicious—no one believed in auspicious dates—but because our AWS bill hit $387.42 that Monday and we panicked. So we pointed the DNS, tweeted “It’s live (maybe?)”, and immediately unplugged the office router to stop ourselves from refreshing the analytics dashboard every 93 seconds.

The office wasn’t an office. It was a converted dental suite on 3rd and Hoyt in Brooklyn. Still had the sink with the foot pedal. We kept it. Used it to rinse coffee mugs, then occasionally our hands after someone spilled Sriracha on the server rack (that was Derek. He also licked the rack once. Said it tasted like burnt almonds and regret.)

Our “culture” wasn’t designed. It accreted. Like mold behind the fridge—but tastier, somehow. We banned PowerPoint before Day 3. Not with a memo. With a fire drill. Someone yelled “PPT INCOMING!” and we all sprinted into the stairwell while Derek held the door open with a fire extinguisher he’d never actually read the manual for. We still do it. Every time someone opens Keynote. Works every time.

We paid ourselves $1,800/month. *Each.* Not “equity plus stipend.” Just $1,800. Cash. From a single Chase account named “SearchHive Payroll (DO NOT TOUCH UNLESS IT’S TUESDAY).” We almost didn’t make payroll in July. I personally drove a U-Haul full of vintage Mac Minis to a data center in Newark and traded them for two months of hosting. The guy who took them wore Crocs with socks and asked if we’d considered “a more spiritual approach to indexing.”

Our search algorithm? Started as a Python script named `jank_search.py`. Ran on a 2012 MacBook Pro with the battery swollen enough to lift the trackpad 3mm off the chassis. It returned results in 2.7 seconds—*if* you searched for “cats” or “why is my laptop hot.” For “quantum entanglement,” it crashed. Then emailed me a haiku:  
> *Your query is deep.*  
> *My RAM is full of cat GIFs.*  
> *Restarting now. Sorry.*

We hired people based on three criteria:  
1. Could they fix a leaky faucet without calling a plumber? (Derek passed. Maya failed but brought us a bag of sour gummies and got hired anyway.)  
2. Did they own at least one pair of shoes with Velcro? (Non-negotiable. We lost three interns to “shoelace-related existential crises.”)  
3. Had they ever cried in a CVS parking lot? (Turns out, yes. All of us. Even Raj, who claims it was “allergies + wind + existential dread re: supply chain logistics.”)

Our “onboarding” was a laminated index card taped to the monitor:  
> *Welcome.*  
> *1. Your password is “honeybadger” (lowercase, no space, period at end).*  
> *2. The coffee maker is sacred. If you use it, you must refill the water *and* wipe the drip tray *and* whisper “thank you” to the thermal carafe.*  
> *3. If the search bar returns “404: Query too sad,” just type “help” and it’ll suggest therapy podcasts or a list of nearby bodegas that sell pickles.*  

We had zero HR. Just Margo, who ran payroll and also did our taxes using TurboTax Deluxe and a bottle of Jameson she kept in the filing cabinet labeled “Q4 Compliance.” She once filed our 941 form *twice*, triggering an IRS audit that ended with her sending them a handwritten note: “We’re trying. Also, here’s a photo of our dog, Biscuit, wearing sunglasses. He believes in you.” They replied with a postcard. No fine. Just a sticker of a smiling eagle.

Our first real user wasn’t a VC or a journalist. It was Mrs. Gable from Staten Island. She typed “how do i get glitter out of my grandson’s ear canal” and got back three results:  
- A 2008 CDC PDF on foreign-body removal  
- A Yelp review for “Ear Candy Ear Cleaning Spa” (4.2 stars, “they used tweezers *and* jazz”)  
- A link to our internal Slack channel titled glitter-emergencies (password: “sparkle”).  

She emailed us. Subject line: “URGENT: Glitter is *crunching*.” We called her. Spent 22 minutes on speakerphone while she held the phone near her grandson’s ear so we could hear the crunch. Derek Googled “ear glitter acoustics.” Maya ordered saline drops from Amazon Prime Now. Raj built a real-time glitter-detection API in 4 hours. Mrs. Gable sent us a tin of homemade rugelach. Still in the breakroom. Unopened. We’re saving it for “the day we get acquired.” Or until it grows sentient.

We didn’t believe in “disruption.” We believed in fixing one weird problem at a time—even if the solution involved duct tape, a Raspberry Pi, and an apology letter written in Comic Sans.

And yeah, sometimes the servers caught fire. (Once. In October. Caused by a rogue cron job and Derek’s habit of charging his phone *inside* the server rack.) But the fire alarm was broken, so we just opened all the windows and played Spotify’s “Chill Vibes for Data Centers” playlist until the smoke cleared.

That’s how we knew we were building something real. Not because it scaled. Because it *smelled* like burnt plastic and hope and slightly stale rugelach.

title: negotiation book|finding out what the other side really wants
text:
Chapter 5: Unveiling the True Desires: The Art of Listening and Probing

 The Story of the Hidden Motive

A few years ago, I was working with a mid-sized tech company that was looking to acquire a smaller, innovative startup. The startup, let's call it BrightSpark, had developed a groundbreaking software solution for predictive analytics. My client, TechGiant, was eager to integrate this technology into their existing product line, and they believed that an acquisition would be the fastest and most efficient way to do so.

The initial meetings between the two companies were cordial but somewhat tense. BrightSpark's founder, Alex, was clearly passionate about his creation and had built a strong team. However, he seemed hesitant to sell, even though TechGiant was offering a generous sum. The negotiations were at a standstill, and it was clear that something more than money was at play.

I decided to take a step back and focus on understanding what Alex really wanted. During our next meeting, I made a point to ask open-ended questions and listen carefully to his responses. It turned out that Alex was not just interested in the financial aspect; he was deeply concerned about the future of his team and the legacy of his product. He feared that once acquired, his team would be disbanded, and the software would be shelved or significantly altered.

This revelation was a turning point. We realized that the key to a successful negotiation lay in addressing Alex's deeper concerns. We proposed a deal that included not only a competitive financial offer but also a commitment to keep the team intact and to allow Alex to continue playing a significant role in the development of the software. This approach resonated with Alex, and we were able to reach a mutually beneficial agreement.

 Practical Advice: Uncovering the True Desires

1. Ask Open-Ended Questions

One of the most effective ways to uncover what the other side truly wants is by asking open-ended questions. These are questions that cannot be answered with a simple "yes" or "no." Instead, they encourage the other party to share their thoughts, feelings, and motivations. For example, instead of asking, "Do you want to sell your company?" you might ask, "What are your long-term goals for your company, and how do you see this acquisition fitting into those plans?"

2. Listen Actively

Listening is a critical skill in any negotiation. Active listening involves not just hearing the words the other person is saying but also paying attention to their tone, body language, and emotional cues. When you listen actively, you can pick up on subtle signals that may reveal their true desires. For instance, if the other party seems particularly animated when discussing a certain topic, it might indicate that it is a high-priority issue for them.

3. Probe for Underlying Concerns

Sometimes, the other side may not be fully aware of their own underlying concerns, or they may be reluctant to share them openly. In such cases, probing questions can help you get to the root of the issue. For example, if the other party expresses hesitation about a particular term, you might ask, "Can you tell me more about why this term is a concern for you? What specific outcomes are you worried about?"

4. Empathize and Validate Their Perspective

Empathy is a powerful tool in negotiation. By putting yourself in the other party's shoes and validating their perspective, you can build trust and create a more collaborative environment. Acknowledge their concerns and show that you understand their point of view. For example, you might say, "I can see why you're concerned about the future of your team. Let's discuss how we can ensure that their roles and contributions are valued and preserved."

5. Look for Nonverbal Cues

Nonverbal communication can provide valuable insights into what the other side is thinking and feeling. Pay attention to their facial expressions, gestures, and body language. If the other party leans forward and nods while discussing a particular topic, it might indicate that it is important to them. Conversely, if they cross their arms and look away, it could signal discomfort or disagreement.

6. Use Silence as a Tool

Silence can be a powerful tool in negotiation. When you ask a question, give the other party time to think and respond. Often, people will fill the silence with additional information or insights that they might not have shared otherwise. For example, after asking about their long-term goals, you might pause and wait, giving them the space to elaborate.

7. Be Patient and Persistent

Uncovering the true desires of the other side is not always a quick process. It may require multiple conversations and a willingness to dig deeper. Be patient and persistent, and don't be afraid to revisit topics or ask follow-up questions. Over time, you will gain a clearer picture of what is truly important to the other party.

8. Offer Creative Solutions

Once you have a good understanding of the other side's desires, you can start to craft creative solutions that address their needs. Think outside the box and consider non-monetary incentives, such as strategic partnerships, leadership roles, or continued involvement in the project. By offering solutions that align with their true desires, you increase the likelihood of reaching a mutually beneficial agreement.

 Conclusion

In the world of negotiation, success often hinges on your ability to uncover and address the true desires of the other side. By asking open-ended questions, listening actively, and probing for underlying concerns, you can gain valuable insights that will guide you toward a win-win outcome. Remember, the goal is not just to reach an agreement, but to build a relationship based on mutual understanding and respect. As my experience with Alex and BrightSpark demonstrated, when you take the time to understand what the other side really wants, you can unlock new possibilities and achieve a more satisfying and sustainable agreement.

title: motivational book|achieving long-term goals by managing your energy, not your time
text:
You’ve tried the time management tactics. You’ve color-coded your calendar, set alarms for every thirty minutes, blocked off “focus time,” and tracked every minute like it was gold. And yet—here you are, exhausted at noon, scrolling mindlessly at midnight, watching your long-term goals recede like a shoreline in fog. That’s not because you’re lazy or undisciplined. It’s because you’ve been solving the wrong problem. Time is fixed. Twenty-four hours. Everyone gets the same. But energy? That’s yours to shape. Your focus, resilience, creativity, emotional steadiness—they all flow from energy, not minutes. And energy isn’t just physical. It’s mental, emotional, and spiritual. Managing your energy—not your time—is how you actually move mountains.

Let’s start with a hard truth: pushing through fatigue doesn’t build momentum—it erodes it. When you ignore your body’s signals—the heaviness behind your eyes, the shallow breath, the irritability that flares over small things—you’re borrowing from your future self. That loan comes with compound interest: diminished clarity, poor decisions, fractured relationships, and eventually, burnout that halts everything. You don’t need more hours. You need deeper, more intentional pulses of energy—moments when you’re fully present, aligned, and capable of doing work that matters.

So how do you manage energy? First, notice your natural rhythm. Are you sharpest in the early morning, or does your mind truly wake up after lunch? Do you think best while walking, or only in silence? Stop fighting your biology. Schedule your most demanding cognitive work—writing that proposal, strategizing your next career move, having that difficult conversation—during your personal energy peaks. Protect those windows fiercely. Guard them like sacred ground. Let go of the myth that discipline means grinding at 8 p.m. when your brain has already shut down. Real discipline is choosing rest when you need it—not as surrender, but as strategy.

Second, treat your attention like a muscle—not a switch. You can’t expect to focus for four hours straight without recovery. Build in micro-renewals: three minutes of deep breathing between meetings, a five-minute walk outside without your phone, closing your eyes and naming three things you feel grateful for before starting your next task. These aren’t distractions. They’re recalibrations. They restore your nervous system, replenish your mental bandwidth, and keep your emotional thermostat steady. Over time, these tiny acts compound into extraordinary stamina.

Third, examine what drains you—and be ruthless about reducing it. Not all tasks drain equally. Some deplete your mental energy (like back-to-back Zoom calls), others your emotional energy (like constant conflict resolution), and still others your spiritual energy (like pretending to care about work that contradicts your values). Audit your week honestly. Where are you spending energy on things that don’t serve your long-term vision? That weekly meeting that goes nowhere? The habit of checking email first thing, hijacking your calm? The people who leave you feeling smaller, not stronger? Energy management means saying no—not out of scarcity, but out of reverence for what you’re building.

And finally, remember: energy is renewable—but only if you invest in its sources. Sleep isn’t downtime; it’s maintenance. Movement isn’t optional exercise; it’s neural lubrication. Connection isn’t “nice to have”; it’s emotional oxygen. Purpose isn’t abstract inspiration; it’s the fuel that turns effort into meaning. You don’t need to overhaul your life overnight. Start with one thing: tonight, put your phone in another room an hour before bed. Tomorrow, take one real lunch break—no screens, no agenda—just food and quiet. Next week, say no to one request that doesn’t align with your goal. Small, consistent choices like these don’t just conserve energy—they multiply it.

You’re not racing against the clock. You’re cultivating a life force. Every choice you make—to rest, to move, to disconnect, to reconnect, to protect your focus—is a vote for the person you’re becoming. Long-term goals aren’t achieved in bursts of heroic effort. They’re built in the quiet, daily stewardship of your energy. So stop watching the clock. Start listening to your body. Trust your rhythm. Honor your limits. And move forward—not faster, but fuller. Because the life you want isn’t waiting for more time. It’s waiting for you, fully charged.

title: relationships advice book|staying faithful and keeping a long marriage alive
text:
So. You’re married. Maybe twenty years in. Maybe thirty. Maybe you’ve just caught yourself wondering, *Wait—did I lock the front door? Or did I just mentally rehearse my resignation email while folding socks?* And you think: *Is this what forever feels like? Like a slightly warm cup of coffee left on the counter too long?* I get it. I once spent seventeen minutes Googling “is it normal to fantasize about a barista who remembers your order” while my husband microwaved lasagna for the third night in a row. (Spoiler: It’s normal. The barista was *not* the problem.)

Let me tell you about the Great Sock Incident of 2018. My husband and I had gone six weeks without a real conversation—not the “Did you feed the cat?” kind, but the “What actually makes your chest feel tight when you wake up?” kind. Then one Tuesday, he held up a lone argyle sock and said, deadpan, “This is our marriage.” Not romantic. Not poetic. But weirdly accurate. Because here’s the thing no one tells you: fidelity isn’t just about not kissing someone else. It’s about showing up—even when you’re tired, even when you’d rather rewatch *The Bear* than make eye contact, even when you’re both silently competing to see who can sigh louder during tax season.

I used to think love was a bonfire. Big, bright, crackling with drama and grand gestures. Turns out, long-term love is more like a well-tended campfire—low, steady, occasionally needing a poke and some dry twigs, and absolutely *requiring* that someone remembers to bring marshmallows. Not every day has to be fireworks. Some days, it’s just two people sharing a slightly burnt s’more and agreeing that yes, the dog *does* look suspiciously guilty about the shredded couch.

Here’s what actually works—no guru nonsense, just hard-won, laundry-basket-overflowing wisdom:

1. Schedule “boring intimacy.” Yes, I said boring. Text each other at 3 p.m. saying, “Just thought of the time you tried to assemble IKEA furniture blindfolded.” Laugh. Remember the ridiculous. Touch—on the shoulder, the small of the back, the hand resting on the counter while you both chop onions. Not always sex. Just *contact*. Our hands have forgotten how to hold each other’s wrists sometimes, so we started doing it deliberately—like a ritual. “Wrist check-in,” we call it. Sounds dumb. Feels like coming home.

2. Fight *with* your spouse, not *against* them. Early on, I’d keep score: *He forgot the milk. Again.* Now I ask, “What’s underneath the milk thing?” Turns out, he was drowning in work stress and the milk felt like the only thing he *could* forget without consequences. We stopped arguing about groceries and started arguing about exhaustion—and then, miraculously, *solved* something.

3. Protect your “us” like it’s the last slice of pizza at a family dinner. Say no. To extra shifts. To “just one more episode” when your partner’s already in bed. To scrolling until your eyes feel like raisins. One tiny boundary—“No phones after 9 p.m. unless the house is literally on fire”—saved us more than three couples’ therapy sessions.

Also? Stop comparing your behind-the-scenes to everyone else’s highlight reel. That couple who posts sunset walks and matching linen sets? Their DMs probably contain screenshots of a parking ticket and a passive-aggressive note from their HOA. I know. I saw it. (Not on purpose. Okay, *slightly* on purpose.)

And please—please—stop waiting for passion to magically return like a lost cat who suddenly shows up at the door with a dead bird. Passion doesn’t wait. It *builds*. Brick by awkward, vulnerable, slightly sweaty brick. Sometimes the brick is admitting you cried watching a commercial about rescue dogs. Sometimes it’s asking, “Can I hold your hand *right now*, even though we’re paying bills?”

We’re not perfect. Last week, I snapped at him for using my favorite mug. He retaliated by putting the milk back in the cupboard. (Yes, really.) We made up over frozen yogurt and admitted we were both hangry and emotionally jet-lagged from parenting teens. Forgiveness isn’t grand—it’s handing him the spoon and saying, “You pick the topping. I’ll stop judging your life choices.”

Staying faithful isn’t about white-knuckling temptation. It’s about choosing, daily, to find the person you fell for *inside* the person who now leaves wet towels on the bathroom floor. It’s remembering that love isn’t the absence of boredom—it’s the presence of curiosity. Even if the question is, “Why do you *still* chew with your mouth open?” (Answer: because he’s 52 and apparently immune to social cues. Also, I kind of love it.)

So go ahead—hold the sock. Light the fire. Eat the slightly-squished marshmallow. Your marriage isn’t failing because it’s quiet. It’s breathing. And breathing, my friend, is wildly underrated.

title: writing-craft memoir|the daily routine of a working novelist
text:
Every morning, I wake up to the sound of my alarm clock blaring an old jazz tune. It's a little ritual I've developed over the years, a way to start the day with something familiar and comforting. As I stretch and shuffle towards the kitchen, I'm already thinking about the characters in my latest novel, their voices mingling with the hiss of the coffee maker. Writing is a part of my life that never really stops; it follows me from the moment I open my eyes until I drift off to sleep, sometimes even invading my dreams.

My workspace is a cozy nook in the corner of our living room, a desk cluttered with notes, sticky tabs, and a stack of books I’m always meaning to read. The first thing I do when I sit down is light a scented candle—something soothing like lavender or vanilla. It’s a small act, but it helps me transition into the world of my story. I’ve found that creating a space that feels safe and inviting is crucial for me to dive deep into my writing.

The truth is, being a working novelist isn’t all about the glamour of book signings and literary festivals. Most of the time, it’s just me, my laptop, and a lot of hard work. I aim to write at least 1,000 words a day, which can be a challenge on those days when the muse decides to take a vacation. But I’ve learned that consistency is key. Even if what I write isn’t perfect, I can always go back and revise. The important thing is to keep the momentum going.

One of my favorite parts of the day is taking a mid-morning break. I’ll often head to the local café, where the baristas know my order by heart. There’s something about the hum of conversation and the clinking of cups that sparks my creativity. I’ll usually bring a notebook and jot down ideas or character sketches while I sip my latte. These moments away from my desk are like mini-recesses, allowing my mind to wander and come up with new angles for my story.

Afternoons are typically reserved for research. I might spend hours reading articles, watching documentaries, or even visiting places that inspire my setting. For my last novel, which was set in a small coastal town, I spent a week in Maine, walking along the cliffs and talking to locals. Immersing myself in the environment not only helped me create a more authentic setting but also gave me a deeper understanding of the characters who would inhabit it.

As the day winds down, I try to wrap up my writing session by 5 PM. This gives me time to cook dinner, catch up with my family, and maybe watch a movie or read a book. It’s important to me to have a balance between my work and personal life. Sometimes, I’ll sneak in a bit of writing after everyone goes to bed, especially if I’m on a roll. But generally, I try to respect the boundaries I’ve set for myself.

One of the most rewarding aspects of being a novelist is the feedback I get from readers. Whether it’s a glowing review or a thoughtful email, hearing how my stories have touched someone’s life is incredibly fulfilling. It reminds me why I started writing in the first place: to connect with others and share a piece of myself through the power of storytelling.

So, there you have it—a glimpse into the daily routine of a working novelist. It’s not always glamorous, but it’s a life I wouldn’t trade for anything. Each day brings new challenges and opportunities, and I’m grateful for every word I get to put on the page.

title: productivity book|single-tasking in a world built for distraction
text:
Chapter 3: The Coffee Cup That Changed Everything  

I was sitting in a sunlit corner booth at *The Grind*, laptop open, notebook beside it, phone face-down (but vibrating—*again*). My to-do list had seven items. I’d already checked email three times, scrolled through two news alerts, and drafted half a reply to a Slack message about a meeting that wasn’t for another four days. My “deep work” block? Forty-seven minutes in—and I hadn’t written a single sentence of the client proposal due that afternoon.

Then my coffee cup slipped.  

Not dramatically—just a quiet tilt as I reached for my phone again. A slow, amber arc of cold brew spilled across my notebook, soaking through three pages of bullet points, blurring my careful outline into Rorschach-like stains. I froze. Not because of the mess—but because, for the first time in hours, my mind was utterly still. No internal pressure to “catch up,” no phantom buzz in my pocket, no mental rehearsal of what I *should* be doing next. Just the damp paper, the sharp smell of coffee, the hum of the espresso machine, and the startling clarity of *this moment*.  

That spill didn’t ruin my afternoon. It rescued it.  

I closed the laptop. Wiped the table with a napkin. Took out a fresh page. And wrote—not on the proposal, but on the blank sheet: *What is the one thing this document needs to do before 3 p.m.?* Not “draft section 2,” not “review citations,” not “check formatting.” Just *one thing*: *Persuade the CFO that this solution saves $180K annually.*  

I wrote only that sentence. Underlined it. Then I opened the document—and wrote *only* the paragraph that proved it. No tangents. No research rabbit holes. No editing. Just that one argument, cleanly made, in 22 minutes. I printed it. Walked to the CFO’s office. Handed him the single page. He read it, nodded, and said, “Send me the full deck by Friday.”  

That day, I didn’t “get more done.” I got *the right thing done*—deeply, decisively, and without residue. And it began with surrendering the illusion that multitasking was efficiency. It began with a single, ruined notebook page.  

This is the quiet rebellion of single-tasking: not rigidity, not austerity—but *intentional gravity*. In a world engineered to scatter our attention—notifications that hijack dopamine, interfaces designed for infinite scroll, workplaces that reward visible busyness over quiet impact—choosing one thing, and holding space for it, is an act of profound resistance. And it works—not because it’s harder, but because it’s *aligned* with how our brains actually function.  

Neuroscience confirms it: when we switch tasks, even briefly, our prefrontal cortex—the brain’s executive control center—must disengage from one context and re-engage in another. This “switch cost” isn’t trivial. Studies show it can take *up to 23 minutes* to fully regain deep focus after an interruption. And most of us interrupt ourselves *every 40 seconds*. We’re not working faster. We’re running a marathon on quicksand.  

So how do you begin—not with willpower, but with design?  

Start with the “Anchor Task”:  
Each morning, identify *one* task that moves your most important goal forward—not the most urgent, not the easiest, but the one with the highest *leverage*. Write it on a sticky note. Place it where you’ll see it first: your laptop lid, your notebook cover, your bathroom mirror. Make it visual, physical, non-negotiable. Mine reads: *“Draft the opening story for Chapter 5.”* Not “Work on book.” Not “Edit.” Just that. One anchor.  

Create a “Distraction Contract” with Yourself:  
Before beginning, name *exactly* what you’ll ignore for the next 25–50 minutes. Not “I’ll avoid distractions.” Be surgical: *“For the next 35 minutes, I will not check email, open new browser tabs, or respond to non-urgent messages—even if my phone lights up.”* Say it aloud. Then silence notifications *at the system level* (not just “Do Not Disturb”—turn off app badges, disable desktop alerts, close Slack). If your work requires email access, schedule two 10-minute blocks *later*—and close the inbox tab now.  

Embrace the “Pause-and-Pivot” Ritual:  
When your mind wanders (and it will), don’t scold yourself. Pause. Breathe once. Then ask: *“Is this thought serving my Anchor Task *right now*?”* If not—gently return. No drama. No self-judgment. This isn’t about perfection; it’s about *reconnection*. Each pause strengthens the neural pathway for attentional control—like flexing a muscle you didn’t know you had.  

End with a Micro-Review (90 seconds):  
When your timer ends, stop. Don’t rush to the next thing. Ask: *“What did I learn about this task? What felt clear? Where did resistance show up—and what does that tell me?”* Jot one line. This builds metacognition—the awareness of *how* you think—and turns every session into data, not just output.  

Single-tasking isn’t about doing less. It’s about doing *with presence*. It’s the difference between skimming the surface of ten things and diving deep enough to change one. It’s how a coffee stain became a compass.  

The world won’t slow down. But your attention doesn’t have to race with it. You hold the pen. You hold the cup. You hold the choice—to pour your focus, deliberately, into one vessel at a time. Start small. Start with one sentence. One paragraph. One breath before you begin.  

The rest will follow—not faster, but truer.

title: personal finance book|why you should stop feeling guilty about lattes and focus on big wins
text:
You’ve probably heard the advice before: skip your daily latte, and in ten years you’ll have enough to buy a house. Or at least pay off student loans. Or fund your retirement. It sounds logical—until you actually do the math. And when you do, you realize something uncomfortable: blaming your $5 latte for your financial stress is like blaming a single raindrop for the flood. It’s not wrong, exactly—but it’s wildly disproportionate to the real problem.

Let’s be honest: you don’t feel guilty about lattes because they’re objectively expensive. You feel guilty because they’re visible, frequent, and easy to point to—and because guilt feels like action. But guilt without clarity is just emotional noise. It distracts you from what actually moves the needle in your financial life: your income, your major expenses, and your long-term decisions.

Think about your rent or mortgage. If you pay $1,800 a month and you could find a place for $1,500—or negotiate a $200 reduction—you’d save $3,600 a year. That’s 600 lattes. One conversation with your landlord might do more than six months of skipping coffee. Or consider your car payment. A $400 monthly loan adds up to $4,800 a year. Refinancing to a lower rate, or choosing a less expensive model next time, could free up thousands—not pennies.

What about insurance? Many people overpay on auto, home, or health coverage simply because they haven’t shopped around in years. A 15-minute comparison could save $500–$1,200 annually. That’s not “giving up” anything—it’s keeping money already yours. Same with credit card interest. Carrying a $5,000 balance at 22% APR costs you over $1,100 a year in interest alone. Paying that down—even by redirecting just $200 extra per month—cuts years off repayment and saves thousands. That’s not austerity. That’s arithmetic.

And then there’s income. This is the biggest lever most people ignore. Raising your salary by 10%—whether through negotiation, certification, a side project, or a strategic job change—can add more in one year than cutting every discretionary expense for five. Yet we spend hours optimizing our grocery list while avoiding the far scarier but higher-impact conversation about asking for a raise.

None of this means your latte is “fine” in every context. If you’re drowning in debt, working three jobs, and skipping meals to afford coffee, then yes—pause and reflect. But if you’re employed, relatively stable, and still beating yourself up over a small daily ritual, you’re misplacing your energy. Guilt doesn’t build wealth. Clarity does. Intention does. Strategy does.

So stop auditing your coffee. Start auditing your biggest three expenses—the ones that account for 70% or more of your spending. Open your bank statements. Sort by category. Look for the line items that make your breath catch—not because they’re shameful, but because they’re significant. Then ask: Can I reduce this? Negotiate this? Replace this? Automate a better version of this?

Also ask: What’s one thing I can do in the next 30 days to increase my income or reduce a major cost? Not “I’ll try,” but “I’ll email HR about the raise timeline on Tuesday,” or “I’ll call two insurers Thursday afternoon.” Small, concrete actions—not self-reproach—are what compound over time.

Your latte isn’t the villain. It’s neutral. What *is* costing you freedom, security, and peace is the illusion that tiny sacrifices are enough—and the avoidance of bigger, bolder choices. You don’t need perfection. You need proportion. You need focus. You need to stop shrinking your attention down to the espresso shot and start expanding it to the whole café—and then the whole city.

So take a breath. Enjoy your coffee. And then turn your full attention to where your money *really* lives—and where it *could* go. That’s where your power is. Not in denial. In direction.

text:
Hey there, folks! So, you want to build a company culture that's all about delivering happiness? Awesome! I’ve been on this journey myself, and let me tell you, it’s not just about making customers smile—it’s about creating an environment where your team feels like they’re part of something truly special. And when your team is happy, guess what? Your customers will be too.

First things first, let me share a little story. A few years back, I was running a small startup, and we were so focused on growth that we almost forgot why we started in the first place. We were working crazy hours, and the stress was palpable. One day, a customer sent us a thank-you note for going above and beyond. It was a simple gesture, but it reminded us of the joy we felt when we helped someone. That moment was a wake-up call. We decided to make happiness our top priority, not just for our customers, but for everyone in the company.

So, how do you build a culture of happiness? Here are a few tips:

1. Start with your mission. Make sure your mission statement isn’t just a bunch of corporate jargon. It should be something that resonates with everyone. For example, ours is “To spread joy, one interaction at a time.” Simple, right? But it works. When your team knows what they’re working towards, it’s easier to stay motivated and aligned.

2. Hire for values, train for skills. This is huge. You can teach someone how to use a new software or how to handle a tricky customer, but you can’t teach them to be kind or empathetic. During interviews, ask questions that reveal their values. Do they genuinely care about making others happy? If the answer is yes, you’ve found a keeper.

3. Celebrate the wins, big and small. We have a tradition called “Happy Hour” (not the drinking kind, though that happens too). Every Friday, we gather and share stories of the week—funny moments, customer compliments, and even personal milestones. It’s a great way to end the week on a high note and remind everyone that we’re in this together.

4. Empower your team. Trust your people to make decisions. If a customer has a problem, give your team the authority to solve it without having to run it up the chain. Not only does this make the customer experience smoother, but it also shows your team that you trust them. And trust, my friends, is the foundation of a happy workplace.

5. Lead by example. As a leader, you set the tone. If you’re stressed out and grumpy, your team will follow suit. So, take care of yourself. Practice mindfulness, get enough sleep, and don’t forget to laugh. When your team sees you happy and balanced, they’ll feel more comfortable doing the same.

Now, let’s talk about the fun stuff. One of the best things we did was create a “Culture Book.” It’s basically a scrapbook filled with photos, notes, and memories from our team. It’s a tangible reminder of all the good times we’ve had, and it’s always growing. New hires love flipping through it, and it helps them feel connected to the team right from the start.

And here’s a little secret: sometimes, it’s the small things that make the biggest difference. Like the time we surprised everyone with ice cream on a hot summer day. Or when we organized a silly costume contest. These little moments of joy add up and create a culture where people look forward to coming to work.

In the end, building a culture of happiness is about creating a place where people feel valued, supported, and inspired. It’s not always easy, but it’s worth it. Because when you focus on happiness, everything else falls into place. Your team is more productive, your customers are happier, and your business thrives. So, go ahead, spread some joy, and watch the magic happen. 🌟

Until next time, keep smiling and spreading happiness!

title: relationships advice book|staying faithful and keeping a long marriage alive
text:
Chapter 7: Faithfulness Isn’t Just About Not Cheating — It’s About Showing Up, Every Single Day  

Let me tell you about my friend Carla. Twenty-eight years married to the same man, two grown kids, a cozy house with mismatched mugs and a perpetually overwatered fern on the kitchen counter. Last year, at her 50th birthday dinner, she leaned across the table, fork hovering mid-air, and said something that stuck with me like glue: “The hardest part of staying faithful isn’t resisting temptation—it’s resisting indifference.”  

I blinked. Then I wrote it down on a napkin. Because she was absolutely right.  

We’ve been sold this narrow, dramatic version of fidelity: white-knuckled willpower, midnight phone checks, moral fortresses built against temptation. But real, lasting faithfulness—the kind that survives mortgage payments, menopause, teenage rebellion, and the sheer, grinding weight of *routine*—is quieter. It’s softer. And frankly, it’s way more demanding.  

Think about it: You don’t fall out of love in one grand betrayal. You drift. You stop asking, “How was your day?” and start hearing the answer while scrolling through your phone. You forget how your partner takes their coffee—and then forget to ask again. You stop touching—not just intimately, but casually: a hand on the small of their back as they pass the salt, a squeeze of the shoulder when they’re stressed, a forehead kiss before bed even when you’re exhausted. These aren’t “extras.” They’re the daily deposits into your emotional bank account. Skip too many, and suddenly you’re overdrawing—and wondering why you feel so lonely in your own marriage.  

I’ll be honest: My husband and I hit a wall around Year 12. We weren’t fighting. We weren’t cheating. We were just… parallel. Two responsible adults sharing a life, a calendar, and a Netflix password—but not much else. One night, after yet another silent dinner (me reading emails, him watching highlights), I snapped—not angrily, but sadly—and said, “I miss us.” He looked up, surprised. “Me too,” he whispered. That tiny admission cracked something open.  

So we started small. Ridiculously small. We instituted “no screens after 8 p.m.”—not as punishment, but as permission to be present. We revived our “walk-and-talk” ritual from early dating: 20 minutes, no phones, no agenda—just noticing things. The way the oak tree across the street finally dropped its first acorn. How his laugh sounds different when he’s genuinely relaxed. We also made a pact: if either of us felt emotionally distant for more than three days, we’d say it—no blame, no drama—just, “I’m feeling far. Can we reconnect?”  

Here’s what changed: the fidelity deepened *because* we stopped treating it like a boundary to guard—and started treating it like a garden to tend. Faithfulness became less about *not going elsewhere*, and more about *choosing, daily, to stay right here*. To notice the person beside you—not the idea of them, not the version you married, but the actual, evolving, slightly tired, wonderfully imperfect human who still chooses you, too.  

And yes—temptation still shows up. A charming colleague, an old flame sliding into your DMs, that fleeting, irrational fantasy about someone else’s life. That’s normal. What matters isn’t whether those thoughts flicker; it’s what you do with the space *after* the flicker. Do you fan the spark? Or do you gently blow it out—and turn your full attention back to the person whose hand you’re holding?  

Long marriages don’t survive on perfection. They survive on repair. On showing up—even when you’re bored, frustrated, or just plain tired—with kindness, curiosity, and the quiet courage to say, “You matter. This matters. *We* matter.”  

So tonight, put your phone down. Make eye contact. Ask one real question—and listen to the answer like it’s the most important thing you’ll hear all day. That’s not just keeping a promise. That’s keeping love alive. One ordinary, extraordinary moment at a time.

title: happiness and meditation guide|a ten-minute daily breathing practice for beginners
text:
Look. Ten minutes. Not twelve. Not “as much as you can.” Ten. Set your damn phone timer—*not* the one that buzzes like a startled pigeon, but the kind with a soft chime or, better yet, silence. And put it *across the room*. Because if it’s in your hand, you’ll scroll Instagram for 47 seconds thinking, *Just one more post*, then wonder why your “meditation” felt like wrestling a greased ferret.

Sit. Chair. Cushion. Floor. Doesn’t matter—but *don’t lie down*. I’ve watched too many beginners nod off mid-breath and wake up convinced they “did it,” when really they just took a nap with spiritual branding. Sit upright—not ramrod-stiff, not slumped—but like you’re gently holding yourself together. Hands on knees or folded loosely in your lap. Eyes closed. Or, if that freaks you out (it did for me, first six months), soften your gaze on a spot on the floor about three feet ahead. No blinking contests. Just… rest.

Now—breathe. Not “deeply.” Not “from your diaphragm” like some yoga influencer whispering secrets. Just *breathe*. Like you’ve been doing since you were born. In. Out. That’s it. Your breath isn’t broken. It doesn’t need fixing. You’re not trying to *do* breathing right. You’re just noticing it. The coolness at the tip of your nose on the inhale. The slight warmth on the exhale. The tiny pause—yes, there *is* one—between breaths. That half-second where nothing happens? That’s where you start learning how quiet actually feels.

Your mind *will* bolt. Guaranteed. At 1:23, you’ll remember you forgot to reply to Dave’s email about the quarterly report. At 3:11, you’ll suddenly calculate how many calories are in that leftover slice of cake in the fridge. At 5:48, you’ll rehearse an argument with your partner that hasn’t even happened yet. This isn’t failure. This is the *point*. Your brain is a rescue dog who’s never been off-leash—it *will* sprint toward every squirrel, every dropped chip, every phantom text vibration. Every time you notice you’ve left the breath? Gently—*no scolding, no sighing, no “Ugh, I’m so bad at this”*—just guide attention back. Like you’d hand a toddler back their stuffed rabbit. Not “good job!” Not “bad toddler!” Just… here. Breathe.

Don’t count breaths. Counting is a trap. By breath 7, you’re already negotiating with yourself: *Is that seven or eight? Did I skip six? Should I restart?* Nope. Let numbers go. If thoughts come with words—“I’m stressed,” “This is boring,” “My knee itches”—label them *softly*: “thinking,” “judging,” “sensing.” Not “Oh god, my knee is on fire and I’m doomed.” Just “itching.” Then back to breath. Like flicking dust off a lens.

And yes—your body will protest. A foot will fall asleep. Your jaw will clench. Your lower back will stage a minor uprising. Fine. Notice *that* too. “Tightness.” “Pressure.” “Warmth.” Don’t fix it. Don’t curse it. Just name it, and return. This isn’t about comfort. It’s about showing up for what’s *actually* happening—not what you wish was happening.

If tears come? Let them. If laughter bubbles up for no reason? Let it. If you feel nothing but impatience and the crushing weight of your own to-do list? Good. That’s data. That’s real. That’s where the work lives.

You won’t feel “blissed out” after day one. Or day seven. Maybe not even day thirty. What you *will* get: a split-second gap between stimulus and reaction. That moment *before* you snap at your kid. Before you refresh your inbox for the fourth time. Before you reach for the wine bottle at 7:03 p.m. sharp. That gap is where choice lives. Where breath becomes backbone.

Do it daily. Not “when I have time.” Not “after I finish this project.” *Before* you check email. *After* you brush your teeth. Same time. Same place. Even if you do it standing in the shower because you overslept. Especially then. Consistency beats duration. Ten minutes, same time, same way, for ten days straight—*that’s* the magic. Not enlightenment. Just showing up. Breathing. Returning. Again. And again. And again.  

(Your timer just chimed. Open your eyes. Don’t rush. Blink twice. Then go make coffee. Or don’t. Just be here.)

title: habit-building book|starting with habits so small you can't fail
text:
Imagine for a moment that you've set out to climb the highest mountain in the world. It's an incredible goal, one that fills you with both excitement and a touch of fear. But what if, instead of starting at the base, you began your journey by simply walking around your neighborhood park every day You might think it's too small, too insignificant to matter. Yet, this is exactly where the magic of building lasting habits begins.

When it comes to creating new habits, the key is to start so small that you can't possibly fail. This approach may seem counterintuitive, especially when we're often told to dream big and aim high. But the truth is, the smaller the step, the more likely you are to take it, and the more consistently you'll stick with it. Over time, these tiny actions add up, leading to significant changes in your life.

Let's say you want to read more books. Instead of setting a goal to finish a book a week, which might feel overwhelming, how about committing to reading just one page per day That's it. One page. It takes no more than a couple of minutes. So minimal, in fact, that on even the busiest days, finding time for one page seems entirely doable. And here's the beautiful part: once you start, you might find yourself reading two pages, then three, and before you know it, you're well into chapter two. The initial barrier was so low that you barely noticed it, and now, you're making real progress.

Or perhaps your goal is to become more physically active. Rather than jumping straight into an hour-long workout routine, begin with something as simple as doing five squats or going for a 5-minute walk each day. These activities require such little effort that they almost guarantee success. As you get comfortable, you can gradually increase the duration or intensity, but the important thing is to keep the initial commitment as effortless as possible.

The power of starting small lies not only in its simplicity but also in the psychological boost it provides. Every time you complete your tiny task, you experience a sense of accomplishment. This positive reinforcement makes it easier to stay motivated and continue. Over time, these small victories build confidence, making it more likely that you'll tackle bigger challenges down the road.

Another benefit of beginning with small steps is that it helps you overcome the fear of failure. When the stakes are low, there's less pressure, and thus, less room for disappointment. If you miss a day, it's not a big deal; you can easily pick up where you left off. This resilience is crucial for long-term habit formation, as it teaches you to be kind to yourself and to view setbacks as temporary rather than catastrophic.

Remember, the goal isn't to make huge, immediate changes but to create a foundation upon which you can steadily build. Think of it like planting a seed. At first, all you see is a tiny sprout, but with consistent care and attention, that sprout grows into a strong, flourishing plant. Your habits work the same way. Start with the smallest, most manageable action, and watch as it grows into something substantial over time.

So, as you embark on your journey to build new habits, remember to keep your steps small. Celebrate each tiny victory, and don't be afraid to adjust your pace as needed. With patience and persistence, those seemingly insignificant actions will lead to profound, lasting change.

title: motivational book|achieving long-term goals by managing your energy, not your time
text:
I used to keep a time-tracking app on my phone like it was a holy relic. I’d log every 12-minute Instagram scroll, every 47-minute “researching podcast mics” detour (spoiler: I bought three mics and recorded one voice memo), every 90-second stare into the fridge like it owed me money. I thought if I just *squeezed* hard enough—cut coffee breaks, mute Slack, wake up at 4:47 a.m. with a gratitude journal and a kale smoothie—I’d finally write that book, launch that course, or at least remember where I left my keys *consistently*. Spoiler again: I didn’t. I wrote 37 half-finished chapters, launched a course nobody enrolled in (my mom signed up twice—bless her—and asked if the “bonus meditation” came with snacks), and once spent 22 minutes searching for my keys… only to find them in my coat pocket. Which I was wearing. At 3 p.m. On a Tuesday.  

Here’s what cracked me open: I wasn’t running out of *time*. I was running on fumes. My brain felt like a laptop with 3% battery and 14 Chrome tabs open—including one titled “How to fix low battery anxiety.” Time is fixed. Energy? That’s wildly negotiable. It’s the difference between trying to drive a car with no gas versus trying to drive a car with a full tank but the parking brake on. You’re not lazy—you’re *leaking*.  

I learned this the hard way during my “Year of the Big Goal”—the one where I swore I’d finish my first manuscript *and* run a half-marathon *and* learn Spanish *and* finally organize the junk drawer (RIP, loose batteries and mystery USB cables). By March, I was napping in the shower, saying “yes” to things while mentally drafting my obituary, and crying softly while folding laundry because a sock had *no partner*. Not dramatic. Just… depleted. Then my therapist said, very gently, “What if you stopped scheduling your *hours*, and started scheduling your *humanity*?” I blinked. She handed me a highlighter and said, “Mark when you feel *alive*, not just awake.” So I did. Turns out, I’m not a morning person—I’m a *11:23 a.m. after two sips of coffee and one real laugh* person. And my best writing happens not at dawn, but at 8:17 p.m., after dinner, when my brain stops yelling and starts humming. Who knew? Not me. I assumed genius only struck between 5–7 a.m. while whispering affirmations to a ficus.  

So here’s what actually works—not as theory, but as lived, slightly messy, occasionally snack-fueled practice:  

1. Map your energy, not your calendar. For one week, jot down *how you feel* every 90 minutes—not what you’re doing, but *what state you’re in*: “zombie-mode,” “curious-but-tired,” “weirdly brilliant,” “mentally filing divorce papers from my to-do list.” You’ll spot patterns. Mine? I crash hard after Zoom calls. Like, “need to lie on floor and hum showtunes” hard. So now I schedule those calls right before lunch—not right before my most important creative hour. Obvious? Yes. Practiced? Rarely.  

2. Protect your “golden 90.” Everyone has a window—usually 60–120 minutes—where focus feels effortless, ideas click, and you forget to check your phone. Mine is 8:17 p.m. Yours might be 6:03 a.m. or 2:15 p.m. after a walk. Guard that time like it’s the last slice of pizza at a family reunion. No emails. No “quick calls.” Just you, your goal, and zero performance pressure. Progress isn’t loud. It’s quiet. It’s showing up for *one* deep thing, consistently, in your own rhythm.  

3. Rest isn’t the reward—it’s the engine. We treat rest like dessert: “If I finish everything, *then* I get a nap.” But your nervous system doesn’t run on willpower—it runs on recovery. Try this: set a daily “non-negotiable pause.” Five minutes. No screens. Just sit. Breathe. Stare at a wall. Pet a dog. Let your brain reboot. I do mine at 3:30 p.m. every day—even if I’m mid-sentence in an email. My team knows the “3:30 wall-stare” is sacred. They’ve even started joining me. (We don’t talk. We just… exist. It’s weirdly beautiful.)  

Look, long-term goals aren’t marathons run at sprint speed. They’re slow dances—with yourself. With your limits. With your weird, wonderful, inconsistent human body. You don’t need more hours. You need more *honesty* about when you’re lit up—and when you’re just pretending to be awake while Googling “how to reattach eyebrows.” Your energy is your compass. Your time is just the map. Stop forcing the map to tell you where to go. Listen to the compass. Even if it whispers, “Hey. Go eat a cookie. Then try again tomorrow.” You’ve got this. And also, maybe go eat that cookie. I’ll wait.

title: leadership book for new managers|giving honest feedback without crushing morale
text:
Chapter 7: The Sandwich Trap Is a Lie (And What to Serve Instead)  

Let me tell you about the first time I ruined someone’s week. Not on purpose—never on purpose—but I did. Her name was Maya. Brilliant coder, quiet, always the first to spot a bug no one else saw. I’d just been promoted to team lead, and I was *determined* to be “the kind of manager people actually like.” So when I noticed Maya had missed two deadlines—and worse, hadn’t flagged the risks—I decided to “handle it gently.”  

I sat her down, smiled warmly, and opened with: *“Maya, you’re such a strong technical thinker—your work on the login module was outstanding!”*  
Then came the middle layer—the “filling”: *“But lately, timelines have slipped, and stakeholders are getting anxious.”*  
And I finished with: *“I know you’ll nail this next sprint—you’ve got so much potential!”*  

She nodded politely. Left my office. And didn’t speak to me for three days. Later, over coffee, she told me the truth: *“I heard ‘you’re great’… then ‘you’re failing’… then ‘just try harder.’ It felt like praise was just the wrapping paper for criticism. I spent that whole week wondering: Did she even see what I *did* do? Or just what I messed up?”*  

That moment rewired my brain. I’d fallen hard for the “feedback sandwich”—a well-meaning but deeply flawed idea that cushioning criticism with compliments makes it safer. Here’s what I’ve learned since: honesty doesn’t need padding. It needs clarity, care, and courage—not camouflage.  

First, ditch the script. Feedback isn’t a performance; it’s a conversation between humans who both want the same thing: for the person to succeed. So start with *intent*, not structure. Ask yourself: *What do I hope Maya walks away knowing—and feeling?* Not “that she’s late,” but “that her voice matters in planning, and we’ll figure out how to protect her time together.”  

Second, anchor feedback in observable behavior—not interpretation. Instead of *“You’re disorganized,”* try *“I noticed the API docs weren’t updated before last Friday’s demo, and the QA team couldn’t test auth flows.”* That’s factual. It’s neutral. It leaves room for Maya to add context (“Oh—the docs template broke, and I didn’t flag it because I thought devops would fix it by noon”). Suddenly, you’re solving a problem—not judging a person.  

Third, make it *two-way*—within 60 seconds. After you state the observation, pause. Say: *“What’s your take on what happened?”* Not as a trap. As an invitation. This does two things: it signals respect, and it reveals the real bottleneck—maybe it’s tooling, maybe it’s unclear priorities, maybe it’s burnout masked as apathy. You won’t know unless you ask.  

And yes—this feels riskier than the sandwich. It means sitting with discomfort. It means sometimes hearing, *“Honestly? I’m overwhelmed and haven’t known how to ask for help.”* Good. That’s the gold. That’s where real support begins.  

I still mess up. Last month, I gave rushed feedback to a junior designer after a client presentation went sideways. I led with “You were nervous,” which sounded like judgment—not observation. She blinked, and I saw it: that familiar flicker of shame. So I stopped mid-sentence, took a breath, and said: *“Wait—I’m going to restart. What I meant was: Your hands shook slightly when you clicked through the wireframes, and your voice got quieter at slide five. That tells me something felt high-stakes. Can we talk about what that was?”* Her shoulders dropped. She sighed. And then she told me the client had interrupted her twice—and she’d rehearsed only once, because she’d spent 12 hours fixing handoff files from engineering. We fixed *that*. Not her confidence. The system.  

Honest feedback isn’t about being blunt. It’s about being *present*. It’s choosing precision over politeness, curiosity over assumption, and partnership over performance review. When you do that—when you treat feedback as an act of faith, not correction—you don’t crush morale. You build trust. And trust? That’s the only foundation strong enough for people to grow, stumble, learn, and leap.  

So next time you brace for that tough conversation—breathe. Drop the sandwich. Bring your humanity instead. The rest will follow.

title: leadership book for new managers|giving honest feedback without crushing morale
text:
Let me tell you something, new manager. Giving feedback is one of the most critical and, let's be real, one of the most uncomfortable parts of your job. But it’s also where you can make a huge difference. I’ve seen too many managers either sugarcoat everything or go in with guns blazing, leaving a trail of bruised egos and broken spirits. Neither approach works. You need to find that sweet spot where honesty meets compassion.

First off, understand that 80% of employees actually want more feedback from their bosses. They crave it. It’s like water in a desert. But here’s the catch: they don’t just want any kind of feedback. They want the kind that helps them grow, not the kind that makes them feel like they’re being attacked. So, how do you do that?

Start by setting the right tone. When you sit down with an employee, make sure they know this isn’t a witch hunt. “Hey, I wanted to chat with you about some things. No big deal, but I think there are a few areas where we can both improve.” Notice the “we” there? That’s important. It’s not just about them; it’s about the team, and you’re part of that team too.

Now, when you get into the nitty-gritty, be specific. Vague feedback is worse than no feedback at all. If someone’s been consistently late, don’t just say, “You need to be on time.” Instead, say, “I’ve noticed you’ve been late three times this week. Can we talk about what’s going on?” Specificity shows you’re paying attention, and it gives the person a clear idea of what needs to change.

But here’s the thing: for every negative, throw in a positive. The 3:1 ratio is a good rule of thumb. For every one piece of constructive criticism, give three pieces of positive feedback. This isn’t about padding the blow; it’s about recognizing that everyone has strengths and weaknesses. Highlighting the good stuff reinforces the behavior you want to see more of.

Also, don’t wait for the annual review. Those things are archaic. Regular, informal check-ins are way more effective. A quick, “Hey, great job on that presentation. Just a thought, maybe next time we could add a bit more data to back up the points,” is much better than saving it all up for one big, overwhelming conversation.

And listen. Really listen. Feedback should be a two-way street. If you’re doing all the talking, you’re missing out on valuable insights. Ask questions, and give the person a chance to share their perspective. Maybe there’s a reason they’ve been late, or maybe they have a different take on why that project didn’t go as planned. You might learn something, and they’ll feel heard, which is a big morale booster.

Lastly, follow up. Don’t just drop a bomb and walk away. Check in a week later, a month later. See if the changes are happening, and if not, figure out why. Maybe they need more support, or maybe the issue is deeper than you initially thought. Either way, showing that you care and that you’re invested in their success is key.

Look, giving feedback isn’t easy. It takes practice, and you’ll probably mess up a few times. But the more you do it, the better you’ll get. And trust me, your team will thank you for it.
