Chapter 7: Automating Your Savings So You Never Have to Think About It

Hey there! Remember the last time you tried to save money, and it felt like climbing a mountain? Every step was a struggle, and you kept wondering if you'd ever reach the top. Well, I've got some great news for you. There's a way to make saving feel more like taking an elevator to the summit—effortless and almost automatic. Let me share a story with you.

A few years back, I was just like you. I had good intentions of saving, but life always seemed to get in the way. Rent, bills, groceries, and the occasional night out with friends—all these expenses added up, and before I knew it, my savings account was looking pretty sad. I'd set aside a little here and there, but it never felt like enough. Sound familiar?

One day, I stumbled upon a simple yet powerful idea: automating my savings. I thought, "What if I could set it and forget it, just like my favorite streaming service?" That's when everything changed.

Here's how I did it, and how you can do it too:

1. Open a Separate Savings Account: First things first, I opened a high-yield savings account. This is different from your checking account, where all your transactions happen. The savings account is specifically for your goals, whether that's a down payment on a house, an emergency fund, or a vacation. I chose an online bank that offered a higher interest rate, which meant my money would grow faster.

2. Set Up Automatic Transfers: Next, I set up an automatic transfer from my checking account to my savings account. I decided to start small, transferring just $50 every payday. It wasn't a huge amount, but it was something. Over time, as I got more comfortable, I increased the amount. The key is to start with what feels manageable and then build from there.

3. Use Apps and Tools: There are some fantastic apps and tools out there that can help you automate your savings even further. For example, I use an app called Acorns, which rounds up my purchases to the nearest dollar and invests the spare change. It's like finding loose coins in your couch, but instead of spending them, they go straight into your savings.

4. Pay Yourself First: This is a golden rule. Before you pay anyone else, pay yourself. Make sure that your savings transfer happens right after you get paid. This way, you're prioritizing your financial future, and it becomes a non-negotiable part of your budget.

5. Review and Adjust Regularly: Finally, don't set it and completely forget it. Check in on your savings every few months. See how much you've saved, and if you can afford to increase your contributions. Life changes, and so should your savings plan. Maybe you got a raise, or you found a way to cut back on some expenses. Use those opportunities to boost your savings.

Let me give you a real-world example. My friend Sarah, who's also in her early 30s, started with a modest goal of saving $100 a month. She set up an automatic transfer and forgot about it. A year later, she had over $1,200 in her savings account, and she didn't even notice the money missing from her checking account. She was so thrilled that she decided to bump up her monthly contribution to $150. Now, three years later, she has a solid emergency fund and is well on her way to buying her first home.

Automating your savings is like having a personal finance assistant who works 24/7, making sure you stay on track. It takes the stress and guesswork out of saving, and it helps you build wealth without even thinking about it. So, why not give it a try? Set it up today, and watch your savings grow effortlessly. Trust me, your future self will thank you.

title: personal memoir with life lessons|a year of travel after a painful divorce
text:
I got the divorce papers on a Tuesday. Not dramatic—just a FedEx envelope, no tracking number, like my marriage had been downgraded to Standard Ground. My ex’s lawyer wrote “amicable dissolution” in the cover letter. I laughed so hard I choked on a stale almond from the office snack drawer. Amicable? We hadn’t shared a toothbrush in seventeen months. We’d shared a mortgage, a terrier named Gary (who chose her), and exactly one conversation about the weather since last October.  

So I booked a one-way ticket to Lisbon. No itinerary. Just a backpack, $4,283 in savings (I counted it three times), and a stupid vow: *Don’t sleep in the same country for more than 21 days.*  

First stop: a hostel in Alfama with bunk beds that smelled like damp wool and regret. My top bunk squeaked every time I rolled over. On night three, a Dutch guy named Sven offered me half his *pastel de nata* and asked, “Why you run?” I said, “I didn’t run. I walked out. Slowly. With good posture.” He nodded like that made sense. It didn’t. But he didn’t ask again. That was lesson one: most people don’t actually want your backstory. They want your ear, or your spare Wi-Fi password, or—rarely—your last slice of cake. Give them the cake. Keep the story.  

I spent eleven days in Oaxaca learning to make mole from Doña Lupe, who smoked Marlboros through a bent silver holder and called my first attempt “a tragedy with cinnamon.” She made me chop onions until my eyes streamed—not from sadness, just raw onion juice—and then she handed me a knife with a chipped tip and said, “Again. Your tears are free. Your time is not.” I burned three batches. Wasted twelve avocados. Cried once, quietly, behind the compost bin, because the heat reminded me of our old kitchen, where I used to stand at the stove while he scrolled through sports scores on his phone. Doña Lupe caught me. Didn’t say anything. Just slid a fresh tortilla across the counter, still warm, steam rising like a small, stubborn prayer.  

In Hoi An, I stayed in a guesthouse where the shower was a hose attached to a rusty pipe, and the owner, Mr. Binh, charged me $6.50 a night—including breakfast, which was always rice, fried egg, and a single wedge of lime. He never asked why I was alone. Never offered pity. Once, when my phone died for three days straight, he smiled and said, “Good. Now you see the light on the water. Not the light on the screen.” I sat on his dock at dawn for four mornings straight, watching fishing boats bob like corks, listening to the clank of nets, the low hum of motorbikes waking up miles inland. My therapist back home would’ve called it “grounding.” Mr. Binh called it “breakfast time.”  

I missed flights. Twice. Once in Athens because I got lost in Monastiraki buying a ceramic owl that looked mildly judgmental (still on my shelf). Once in Marrakech because I followed a stray cat into an alley and ended up sharing mint tea with three women who taught me how to braid hair but not how to speak Arabic—just how to laugh at my terrible pronunciation of *shukran*.  

I cried on a train between Budapest and Vienna—not ugly, snot-smeared crying, but quiet, steady, like rain on a windowpane. A woman across from me, maybe seventy, slid a tissue across the aisle without looking up from her book. *The Book Thief.* Irony noted. She didn’t offer advice. Didn’t pat my knee. Just kept reading. And that—that quiet, unperformative kindness—was the first thing in eight months that didn’t feel like a performance.  

I learned how much I hated hostels after day 17. How many times I could say “I’m fine” before my jaw ached. That silence isn’t empty—it’s full of everything you stopped saying aloud. That grief doesn’t shrink. It just changes shape: sometimes a stone in your shoe, sometimes the air you breathe, sometimes just the way your hand hovers over the passenger seat when you rent a car.  

I didn’t “find myself.” Found a lot of other people, though. A Bolivian nurse who stitched up my thumb after I sliced it open on a broken bottle in La Paz. A Georgian grandmother who fed me *khachapuri* and told me, “Men come. Men go. Cheese stays hot if you eat it fast.” A bus driver in Laos who drove 90 minutes off-route so I could see a waterfall no guidebook mentioned—then refused payment, just winked and said, “You look like you need water falling down.”  

I came home on a Thursday. My apartment smelled like dust and forgotten takeout menus. The lease was up. I signed a new one—for six months only. No promises. No plans. Just a key, a suitcase still half-packed, and a single, slightly smudged postcard from Doña Lupe: *Mole gets better with time. So do you. (But next time, less cinnamon.)*  

I stuck it on the fridge with a magnet shaped like a chili pepper. Still there. Still smudged.

title: startup memoir|the early days of a search-engine company and its odd culture
text:
Chapter 3: The Day We Indexed a Squirrel (And Why That Was Our First Real Breakthrough)  

It was late October, and the air in our rented garage smelled of burnt coffee, soldering iron flux, and existential dread. My co-founder, Lena, stood barefoot on a stack of *Wired* magazines—her “elevation platform,” she called it—waving a USB cable like a conductor’s baton. On the battered iMac beside her, our search engine prototype, codenamed *Whisper*, had just returned its first non-catastrophic result for the query *“how to fix a leaky faucet.”* Not perfect—its top hit was a 2003 forum post titled *“My faucet weeps. Is it sentient?”*—but it *worked*. Sort of.

Then the squirrel happened.

It wasn’t metaphorical. A young gray squirrel, startled by the whine of our overtaxed server rack (a repurposed Dell PowerEdge we’d bought off Craigslist for $89), darted across the garage floor, skidded on a spilled bag of organic lentils, and launched itself—tail-first—into our primary index drive’s intake vent. There was a high-pitched *whirr-click-hiss*, a puff of static, and silence. The lights on the rack blinked out. Whisper went dark.

We didn’t panic. We *documented*. Lena grabbed her Moleskine. I filmed the squirrel’s slow, dazed exit from the vent with my flip phone (yes, 2012). We named him *Indexer-7*. And when the drive rebooted—miraculously intact, though now emitting a faint nutty aroma—we discovered something strange: Whisper had cached not just the squirrel’s thermal signature and the sound of its claws on aluminum, but also the *entire contents* of the garage whiteboard behind it: our half-written user flow diagrams, Lena’s doodle of a sad cloud labeled *“VC Pipeline,”* and, crucially, my handwritten note: *“People don’t search for answers. They search for relief.”*

That accidental, absurd indexing of context—not just keywords, but *ambient human intention*—became our first cultural axiom: Search is not about words. It’s about wounds.

Our early culture wasn’t built on ping-pong tables or free kombucha. It was forged in the quiet chaos of that garage, where failure wasn’t a pivot point—it was data with fur. Here’s what stuck, and why it matters:

1. Celebrate the Squirrel, Not Just the Search Bar  
Most startups optimize for the “ideal user journey.” We optimized for the *interrupted* one. When a user typed *“why does my head hurt after Zoom calls”* and got back clinical papers on digital eye strain, they weren’t failing *us*—we were failing *their exhaustion*. So we built “context layers”: optional, lightweight signals (time of day, device type, recent app usage) that didn’t track, but *inferred*. If someone searched at 2:17 a.m. on a phone, Whisper would gently surface “quick fixes” before academic journals. This wasn’t AI magic—it was humility. *Practical advice: Before you add a feature, ask: “What real-world squirrel just crashed into this?” Identify the friction your users are too tired or embarrassed to name—and design the relief first.*

2. The “Three-Minute Rule” for Hiring  
We once interviewed a brilliant NLP researcher who aced every technical question… then spent 47 seconds staring blankly at our whiteboard when asked, *“How would you explain ‘indexing’ to your grandmother while she’s stirring soup?”* We didn’t hire her. Instead, we hired Maya, a former librarian who, in her first interview, drew a beautiful, slightly lopsided diagram of how a library catalog *feels* when it fails—and then made us all laugh about Dewey Decimal trauma. Culture isn’t vibe. It’s shared vocabulary. *Practical advice: Replace “culture fit” with “clarity fit.” In every interview, force a 3-minute explanation of your core product *without jargon*. Hire the person who makes complexity feel warm, not the one who makes simplicity sound sterile.*

3. Ship the Ugly Truth, Then Polish the Humanity  
Our first public beta launch included a bug where typing *“help”* returned a single line: *“Breathe. We’re figuring this out too.”* We meant to hide it. But a user screenshot went viral on Hacker News. People wrote in saying it was the first tech interface that hadn’t made them feel stupid. So we kept it—and expanded it. Every error page included a tiny, hand-drawn icon (Lena’s squirrel, later joined by a confused owl and a patient teapot) and one sentence of unvarnished empathy. *Practical advice: Your first version doesn’t need to be polished. It needs to be *honest*. Users forgive broken code. They don’t forgive condescension. Build the apology *into* the architecture—not as an afterthought, but as a first principle.*

The squirrel left no permanent damage. But it left a legacy: Whisper never became the fastest or most comprehensive search engine. It became the one people whispered about in group chats when they were overwhelmed, when they needed clarity without judgment, when they just wanted to know if their weird, specific, squirrel-level problem had ever been solved before.

We sold Whisper to a larger platform five years later—not for its algorithms, but for its *ethos*. The acquiring CEO told me, “You didn’t build a search engine. You built a way to say, ‘I see you, even when you’re covered in lentils.’”  

That’s the odd truth of early days: the breakthroughs rarely come from the boardroom. They come from the garage floor, mid-spill, when you stop trying to control the chaos—and start listening to what the chaos is trying to teach you.  

And sometimes? The teacher has a fluffy tail and terrible aim.

title: small-business marketing guide|getting your first hundred customers through word of mouth
text:
Congratulations on taking the first step towards growing your small business. Getting those initial customers is a thrilling yet challenging journey, and one of the most effective ways to start is through word of mouth. This guide will walk you through some practical strategies to help you reach that milestone of 100 customers.

First, let's talk about why word of mouth is so powerful. People trust recommendations from friends, family, and even strangers online more than they do traditional advertising. A satisfied customer can be your best advocate, sharing their positive experience with others who are likely to become your next customers.

To kick things off, focus on delivering an exceptional product or service. Quality is the foundation of any good word-of-mouth campaign. Make sure every interaction with your business, from the moment a potential customer discovers you to after they make a purchase, is top-notch. Go above and beyond to ensure satisfaction. When people have a great experience, they're naturally inclined to share it with others.

Next, engage with your community. Attend local events, join chambers of commerce, and participate in industry-related meetups. These activities not only put your business in front of potential customers but also help you build relationships. Personal connections often lead to more genuine recommendations. Don't just hand out business cards; take the time to listen and understand the needs and challenges of the people you meet. This shows that you care, and it makes a lasting impression.

Leverage social media to amplify your message. Platforms like Facebook, Instagram, and LinkedIn offer fantastic opportunities to connect with your audience. Share stories, behind-the-scenes looks, and customer testimonials. Encourage your existing customers to tag your business in their posts and leave reviews. You can even run a referral program, offering incentives for both the referrer and the new customer. For example, a discount on their next purchase or a free product. Just make sure the reward is something that adds value without breaking the bank.

Another key strategy is to partner with complementary businesses. Look for companies that offer products or services that align with yours but don't directly compete. For instance, if you own a coffee shop, consider partnering with a local bakery. You can cross-promote each other's businesses, perhaps by featuring each other's products or co-hosting events. This kind of collaboration can introduce you to a whole new set of potential customers.

Don't underestimate the power of excellent customer service. Make it easy for people to get in touch with you, whether it's through email, phone, or social media. Respond promptly and professionally to any inquiries or concerns. Happy customers are more likely to spread the word, and addressing issues quickly and effectively can turn a dissatisfied customer into a loyal one. Remember, a single negative review can be as impactful as several positive ones, so always aim to resolve problems to the best of your ability.

Finally, ask for feedback and act on it. Regularly check in with your customers to see how you can improve. Send out surveys, ask for reviews, and pay attention to what people are saying about your business online. Use this information to refine your offerings and address any areas where you might be falling short. Showing that you value and act on customer feedback demonstrates that you're committed to providing the best possible experience.

By focusing on these strategies, you'll be well on your way to reaching your first 100 customers through word of mouth. It may take some time and effort, but the results will be worth it. Your early customers can become your biggest advocates, helping you grow your business in a sustainable and authentic way. Good luck, and remember, every great business started with a single customer.

title: happiness and meditation guide|a ten-minute daily breathing practice for beginners
text:
Let me tell you about the day I cried in my car—parked, thankfully, not moving—after a particularly brutal morning of back-to-back Zoom calls, a spilled coffee on my favorite sweater, and a text from my kid’s teacher that began with “We need to talk.” I sat there, gripping the steering wheel, heart racing, breath shallow, feeling like I’d been running on a treadmill set to ‘hurricane.’ That was the moment I realized: I wasn’t just tired. I was *unmoored*. My nervous system had no idea where home was anymore.

That afternoon, instead of scrolling or grabbing another espresso, I sat on my living room floor—no cushion, no fancy mat, just me and a kitchen timer—and tried something ridiculously simple: ten minutes of breathing. Just breathing. Not fixing, not optimizing, not even *doing* anything except noticing the air moving in and out. And honestly? The first time, I lasted 92 seconds before my mind hijacked me into planning dinner, rehearsing an apology, and wondering if I’d left the stove on. But I kept showing up. Not perfectly. Not even consistently at first—some days I did it, some days I forgot, some days I did it while half-watching a cooking show (guilty). But slowly—like light returning after a long overcast day—I started to notice tiny shifts. Less reactivity. More space between a stressful email and my response. A quiet little laugh that came out of nowhere while folding laundry. That, my friend, is where real happiness begins—not as a grand fireworks display, but as a gentle, steady warmth you start to recognize as *yours*.

So here’s your ten-minute daily breathing practice—designed for beginners, built for real life, zero experience required:

First, find a seat—not a throne, just a chair or cushion where your spine can be comfortably upright (no slouching, no stiffening—think “tall and soft”). Set a timer for ten minutes. Yes, *actually* set it. Your phone’s alarm works fine—just silence all other notifications. This isn’t multitasking. It’s *you*, fully invited.

Close your eyes—or soften your gaze downward, resting on the floor a few feet ahead. Take three slow, full breaths: inhale through your nose, letting your belly gently rise; exhale through your mouth, like fogging a mirror. No force. No agenda. Just a gentle reset.

Now, let your breath return to its natural rhythm. Don’t change it. Don’t deepen it. Just notice it—where you feel it most: cool air at your nostrils? Warmth at your upper lip? A soft rise and fall beneath your ribs? Pick one anchor point and rest your attention there.

Here’s the beautiful, messy truth: your mind *will* wander. Constantly. That’s not failure—that’s your brain doing its job. Every time you notice you’ve drifted (to your to-do list, a memory, that weird noise outside), simply say *“Ah, wandering”*—not with judgment, but with the kindness you’d offer a friend who just tripped over a rug. Then, gently guide your attention back to your breath. That *noticing-and-returning*? That’s the entire practice. That’s the muscle you’re building.

No need to clear your mind. No need to feel blissful. Some days you’ll feel calm. Some days you’ll feel restless, bored, or even frustrated—and that’s 100% part of the practice. One woman I coached told me she cried during her third session—not from sadness, but because she hadn’t *felt* her own breath so clearly in over a decade. Another man, a firefighter, said his first week felt like “watching paint dry”—until day eight, when he paused mid-argument with his wife, took one breath, and chose to ask, “Can we try that again?” instead of reacting. That’s the magic: not changing your life, but changing your relationship to it.

When your timer chimes, don’t jump up. Sit quietly for ten more seconds. Notice how your body feels. Notice the quality of your mind. Then open your eyes—slowly—and carry that gentle awareness with you, like holding a warm cup of tea.

You don’t need ten perfect minutes. You need ten *real* minutes—with all the mess, the wandering, the soft returns. Because happiness isn’t found in a silent mind—it’s found in the quiet courage to come back, again and again, to the breath that’s always here, always steady, always yours. Start today. Just ten minutes. Just you. Just breathing. That’s enough.

title: negotiation book|finding out what the other side really wants
text:
Let’s get one thing straight: *listening* doesn’t mean waiting for your turn to talk while mentally rehearsing your next rebuttal. I’ve watched senior VPs—people who’ve closed $47M deals—sit across from a supplier and nod along like they’re at a TED Talk, then walk out thinking the vendor just wanted “better terms.” Meanwhile, the vendor’s CFO had quietly told his team *two weeks earlier*: “If we don’t lock in that 18-month volume guarantee by Friday, we’re cutting 23 headcount in logistics.” That wasn’t on the agenda. It wasn’t in the RFP. It was buried in a throwaway line about “capacity planning”—and the VP missed it because he was already drafting his counteroffer in his Notes app.

Here’s what actually works: stop asking *what* they want—and start hunting for the *why behind the why*. Not the polite, boardroom-ready why (“We value long-term partnerships”). The real one. The one that keeps someone up at 2:17 a.m., scrolling LinkedIn job listings while their kid’s fever spikes to 102.4°F.

I’ll tell you how I found it once—with a midsize SaaS client negotiating with a cloud infrastructure provider. Their ask? A 12% discount off list. Standard. Boring. We spent 90 minutes *not* talking price. Instead, I asked the provider’s procurement lead:  
*“If this deal falls apart tomorrow, what’s the first thing your boss asks you?”*  

Silence. Then: *“How much revenue did we lose in Q3?”*  
Okay. So we dug deeper:  
*“What’s the number that makes your CFO’s eyebrow twitch?”*  
*“$1.8 million.”*  
*“And if you miss it…?”*  
*“My bonus gets cut. And my team’s Q4 roadmap gets axed.”*  

Boom. There it was—not “discount,” but *certainty*. Not “price,” but *predictability*. They weren’t negotiating cost—they were negotiating risk transfer. So we flipped the script: instead of arguing over 12%, we offered a *guaranteed minimum spend*—$2.1M over 15 months—with automatic escalation tied to usage (not inflation). No discount. Just ironclad revenue. They signed in 4 days. Our client got better uptime SLAs *and* faster support response times as part of the trade. Everyone won—because nobody tried to sell “value” or “synergy.” We sold *sleep*.

You think that’s rare? Try this: In 2022, I audited 41 enterprise procurement negotiations. Only *7* involved even one question about personal consequences—like “What happens to your team if this drags past September?” Or “Who else in your org is watching this deal closely—and what are *they* measuring?” The rest? All about clauses, caps, and carve-outs. Like rearranging deck chairs on the *Titanic* while ignoring the iceberg shaped like your counterpart’s unspoken KPI.

And don’t fall for the “relationship” trap. “We have a great relationship!” means *nothing* unless you know what that relationship is *for*. Is it for speed? For cover? For political capital? Last month, a hospital system’s supply chain director told me, “We love working with MedTechX.” I said, “Cool. What does ‘love’ get you when your CEO asks why ortho inventory’s up 37%?” She blinked. Then whispered: *“It buys me three extra weeks to fix the ERP integration before the audit.”* There it was. Not loyalty. A buffer. A lifeline. So we built in a 21-day grace period on delivery tolerances—and added real-time inventory dashboards *they* could show the audit team. Done.

Stop treating negotiation like a puzzle where the answer is hidden in the contract language. It’s not. It’s in the pause before they answer. In the way their foot taps twice when you say “Q4.” In the fact they brought *three* people to the call—but only two spoke, and the third kept checking her watch every 92 seconds.

Your job isn’t to be clever. It’s to be *curious enough to feel uncomfortable*. To ask the question that makes them shift in their chair. To sit with the silence—not to fill it, but to *listen to what the silence says*. Because the thing they really want? It’s rarely written down. It’s usually sweating through their shirt collar. You just have to stop talking long enough to hear it.

title: writing-craft memoir|the daily routine of a working novelist
text:
Chapter 5: The Daily Grind: Finding Routine in the Chaos

The sun had barely begun to paint the sky with its soft, golden hues when I woke up. My alarm clock, set for 5:30 AM, was a gentle nudge, a reminder that the day was already in motion, and I needed to be, too. This was my routine, a carefully crafted schedule that had evolved over years of trial and error, one that I hoped would help me balance the demands of writing with the rest of my life.

I stumbled out of bed, still half-asleep, and made my way to the kitchen. The first order of business was always coffee. A strong, black cup, brewed just right, was my fuel. As the coffee percolated, I took a moment to stretch, letting my body wake up. I opened the windows, letting in the cool morning air, and the distant sound of birds chirping. It was a small ritual, but it grounded me, setting the tone for the day ahead.

By 6:00 AM, I was at my desk, a cluttered space that somehow felt like home. My laptop, a stack of notebooks, and a few pens were all I needed. The screen glowed softly, and I opened my manuscript, the cursor blinking expectantly. For the next two hours, I wrote. No distractions, no interruptions. Just me and the words. 

This was the most sacred part of my day. The world outside was still asleep, and I could lose myself in the story. I found that this early-morning session was often the most productive. My mind was fresh, and the ideas flowed more freely. I didn't worry about word count or perfection; I just focused on getting the words down. Later, I could refine and polish, but for now, the goal was to make progress.

At 8:00 AM, I took a break. By this time, the house was starting to stir, and the day's responsibilities were creeping in. I made breakfast, usually something simple like oatmeal or scrambled eggs, and sat down with my family. These moments were precious, a chance to connect before the day pulled us in different directions. After breakfast, I helped get the kids ready for school, and by 9:00 AM, they were out the door, and I was back at my desk.

The mid-morning hours were a bit more challenging. The initial burst of creativity had waned, and the distractions of the day began to pile up. Emails, social media, household chores—all clamored for my attention. To combat this, I set a timer for 25 minutes and focused on writing in short, intense bursts, followed by 5-minute breaks. This technique, known as the Pomodoro Technique, helped me stay focused and avoid burnout. I could tackle smaller tasks during the breaks, like checking emails or doing a quick load of laundry, without losing the momentum of my writing.

By noon, I usually took a longer break. I might go for a walk, read a chapter of a book, or even take a nap. This was a crucial part of my routine, a chance to recharge and reset. Writing is a marathon, not a sprint, and taking care of my mental and physical well-being was essential. I learned the hard way that pushing too hard can lead to burnout, and once you hit that wall, it's tough to climb back over.

In the afternoon, I shifted gears. If I had any administrative tasks, like responding to emails or managing my website, I tackled them then. I also used this time for research, reading, and planning. Sometimes, I would work on a different project, like a short story or an article, to keep things fresh. Variety was key to keeping my creative juices flowing.

By 4:00 PM, the kids were back from school, and the evening routine began. Homework, dinner, and family time filled the next few hours. I tried to be fully present during these moments, knowing that the day was almost over, and the quiet of the morning would return soon enough.

After the kids were in bed, I often spent another hour or so at my desk, reviewing what I'd written earlier, making notes, and planning for the next day. This was a more relaxed session, a chance to reflect and adjust. I found that ending the day with a clear plan for the next morning made it easier to jump back into the story.

As I write this, I realize that my routine is not perfect. There are days when everything goes off the rails, and I have to adapt. But having a structure, a framework to fall back on, has been invaluable. It gives me a sense of control and purpose, even when the chaos of life threatens to overwhelm me.

For anyone looking to establish their own routine, I offer this advice:

1. Start Small: Don't try to overhaul your entire day at once. Begin with one or two changes, like waking up 30 minutes earlier or setting aside 15 minutes for writing. Build from there.
   
2. Be Flexible: Life happens. Kids get sick, deadlines change, and unexpected events occur. Be prepared to adjust your routine as needed, but don't let it fall apart entirely. Find a way to get back on track as soon as possible.

3. Prioritize Self-Care: Writing is a demanding task, both mentally and emotionally. Make sure to take care of yourself. Exercise, eat well, and get enough sleep. Your best work will come when you're at your best.

4. Set Realistic Goals: It's easy to get caught up in the idea of writing thousands of words a day, but that's not sustainable for everyone. Set goals that are achievable and meaningful to you. Even a few hundred words a day can add up over time.

5. Celebrate Small Wins: Every step forward, no matter how small, is a victory. Celebrate your progress, whether it's finishing a chapter, hitting a word count, or simply showing up to write. These small wins build confidence and motivation.

In the end, the daily grind is what makes the dream of being a working novelist a reality. It's the small, consistent actions, day after day, that turn a passion into a profession. And while it's not always easy, it's always worth it.

title: habit-building book|starting with habits so small you can't fail
text:
You’ve tried before. You’ve set big goals—lose twenty pounds, write a novel, meditate daily—and you’ve watched them crumble by day three. Not because you lack willpower, not because you’re lazy or broken—but because you started too big. You aimed for the summit before learning to stand up straight. Here’s the truth no one tells you: lasting change doesn’t begin with heroic effort. It begins with something so small you literally cannot fail.

Right now, pause and ask yourself: What’s the tiniest version of the habit you want—so tiny it feels almost silly? Not “exercise for 30 minutes.” Not “read 20 pages.” Not “wake up at 5 a.m.” Those are outcomes. We’re after the smallest, most frictionless action—the absolute floor of what counts.

If you want to floss daily, start with flossing *one tooth*. Yes—one. That’s it. Not even the whole arch. Just one tooth. If you want to run, start with putting on your running shoes and standing outside for ten seconds. If you want to write, open a blank document and type the words “I am here.” That’s the entire habit. No pressure to continue. No judgment if you stop there.

Why does this work? Because your brain isn’t wired to trust grand promises. It’s wired to notice patterns—and consistency builds trust. When you do something tiny every single day, your nervous system starts whispering: “This is safe. This is normal. This is who we are.” That quiet whisper—repeated—rewires your identity long before any visible result appears.

You might think, “But that’s not enough!” And you’re right—it’s not enough *for results*… yet. But it *is* enough for belief. Every time you follow through on something ridiculously small, you prove to yourself: “I keep my word—even to myself.” That proof accumulates. It becomes the bedrock of self-trust. And self-trust is the only real foundation for discipline.

There’s another hidden benefit: starting small eliminates the need for motivation. Motivation is unreliable—it’s weather, not compass. But showing up for one tooth, ten seconds, or two typed words requires no pep talk, no perfect mood, no cleared schedule. It fits into the cracks of your life—the thirty seconds while your coffee brews, the pause between texts, the moment you sit down at your desk. It asks nothing of you but presence.

And here’s what happens when you do it: you’ll often *want* to do more. You’ll floss one tooth—and realize you’re already holding the floss, so you floss two more. You’ll stand outside in your shoes—and feel the sun, hear the birds, and take three steps down the sidewalk. You’ll type “I am here”—and suddenly remember an idea, and write another sentence. That’s fine. But crucially: it’s *not required*. The habit is complete the moment you do the tiny thing. Everything extra is bonus—not obligation.

Don’t track streaks. Don’t add points. Don’t post about it. This isn’t performance. It’s practice. It’s showing up like you’d show up for a friend who just needs you to sit beside them—not fix anything, just be there. Your job is simply to honor the agreement you made with yourself, however small.

If you miss a day? No problem. Just return the next day—and do the tiny thing. No guilt, no catch-up, no penance. A missed day isn’t failure; it’s data. It tells you the habit was still slightly too big—or your environment got in the way. Next time, make it smaller. Floss half a tooth? Okay. Stand in your shoes *inside* the house? Fine. Type just the letter “I”? Done.

This isn’t about speed. It’s about sustainability. Real change isn’t a sprint—it’s the quiet accumulation of hundreds of tiny yeses. Each one strengthens the neural pathway just a fraction. Over weeks, those fractions become habits. Over months, they become reflexes. Over years, they become your character.

So today—right now—choose one thing you want to build. Then shrink it. Shrink it again. Keep shrinking until it feels laughably easy. That’s your starting point. Not tomorrow. Not Monday. Today. Do it. Then stop. Celebrate the doing—not the outcome. Because the magic isn’t in the habit itself. It’s in the unbroken thread of trust you’re weaving between who you are and who you’re becoming. You don’t have to be ready. You just have to be willing—to start impossibly small. And then do it again tomorrow.

title: motivational book|achieving long-term goals by managing your energy, not your time
text:
I used to keep a time-tracking app on my phone like it was a holy relic. I’d log every 12-minute Instagram scroll, every 47-minute “researching podcast mics” detour (spoiler: I bought three mics and recorded one 37-second voice memo). My calendar looked like a Tetris board designed by a stressed-out owl—color-coded, hyper-scheduled, and quietly judging me at 3 a.m. when I’d wake up wondering why my “deep work block” felt more like deep napping with guilt as a side dish.

Here’s what no productivity guru told me until I crashed *hard*: I wasn’t running out of time. I was running on fumes—emotional, mental, physical fumes—and then blaming the clock for my exhaustion. Time is neutral. It doesn’t care if you’re typing a grant proposal or reorganizing your spice rack by vibrational frequency (yes, I tried that. Cumin *does* hum, apparently).

Let me tell you about the Great Book Deadline Debacle of 2022. My editor gave me six months to write this very book. I spent four months “prepping”: outlining, researching, interviewing experts, buying fancy notebooks, and learning calligraphy so my chapter titles would *feel* literary. Then, two months before deadline, I sat down to write—and my brain served me a blank screen with a tiny, sarcastic pop-up: *“Surprise! You’ve been conserving energy for a project you haven’t actually started.”* Turns out, I’d been treating focus like a battery I could charge once and use forever. Nope. Focus is more like a campfire—you’ve got to tend it, feed it the right kind of wood, and step back when it flares too hot.

So I stopped scheduling hours. I started scheduling *energy*. Not “9–11 a.m. write,” but “9–11 a.m. write *only if* I’ve had breakfast, walked outside, and not checked email first.” And guess what? On the days I honored that? I wrote 1,800 words before lunch—and didn’t need a nap afterward. On the days I ignored it? I wrote 180 words, deleted 179, and Googled “can existential dread be cured with kombucha?”

Energy isn’t just “feeling awake.” It’s the quiet hum beneath your ribs when you’re doing something that matters *to you*, not just something that’s due. It’s the difference between scrolling TikTok because your brain is fried versus scrolling TikTok because you’re avoiding a hard conversation—and yes, those feel *radically* different in your shoulders, your breath, your gut. Your body keeps score long before your to-do list does.

A few things I learned the messy, coffee-stained way:

1. Name your non-negotiables—not tasks, but *conditions*. For me: 7 hours of sleep (not 6:52), 10 minutes of silence before checking my phone, and zero “urgent” emails before noon. These aren’t luxuries. They’re the operating system my goals run on.

2. Protect your peak energy like it’s a rare orchid you inherited from your eccentric aunt. Mine is 8:30–11:30 a.m., post-coffee but pre-lunch fog. That’s when I tackle the thing that scares me most—the writing, the hard call, the idea that feels too big. Everything else gets slotted *around* that window, not inside it.

3. Schedule rest like it’s a board meeting with Elon Musk. Seriously. Put “recharge” in your calendar. Block it. Decline invites to it. I have a recurring “Do Nothing (Genuinely)” slot every Tuesday at 3 p.m. Sometimes I stare at clouds. Sometimes I fold laundry while humming off-key. The point isn’t output—it’s recalibration.

And here’s the gentle, slightly embarrassing truth: some days, your energy will show up wearing sweatpants and holding a half-eaten granola bar. And that’s okay. Long-term goals aren’t built on heroic sprints. They’re built on showing up—tired, distracted, mildly confused—*and still choosing the next small, sustainable thing.* Not the perfect thing. Not the impressive thing. Just the next thing your energy can carry without dropping it.

I’m not saying skip deadlines. I’m saying stop confusing discipline with self-punishment. You wouldn’t expect a racehorse to gallop uphill on an empty stomach, yet we ask our brains to sprint through burnout daily. So try this: today, notice *one* moment when your energy dipped—not because you ran out of time, but because you ran out of *you*. Then ask yourself: What did my body need *just then*? Water? A walk? A laugh? A hard boundary? That question—asked gently, repeatedly—is where real momentum begins. Not in the clock. In the quiet, stubborn, beautifully human pulse of your own aliveness. Now go drink some water. Or don’t. But know that either choice is part of the work.

title: personal finance book|why you should stop feeling guilty about lattes and focus on big wins
text:
Let’s get one thing straight: you do not need to feel guilty about that latte. You read that right. Stop beating yourself up over a five-dollar coffee, and let's talk about the real game-changers in your financial life.

I’ve seen it too many times. Someone reads a blog post or watches a YouTube video, and suddenly they’re on a guilt trip every time they step into a café. "If I skip my daily latte, I could save... let me see, 365 days a year, $5 a day, that’s... $1,825 a year!" And then the self-righteousness kicks in. "Wow, look at me, I’m practically a millionaire!"

Here’s the truth: if you're serious about building wealth, cutting out lattes is a drop in the ocean. It’s like trying to drain a bathtub with a teaspoon. Sure, it’ll work eventually, but there are way more efficient ways to get the job done.

Let's break it down. The average American spends around $1,000 a month on housing. Now, imagine you refinanced your mortgage and managed to shave off just half a percent from your interest rate. On a $300,000 loan, that could mean saving $75 to $100 a month—way more than what you’d save by skipping lattes. And we haven’t even touched on the long-term benefits of paying less interest over the life of the loan.

Now, let’s talk about your car. The average car payment in the U.S. is over $500 a month. What if, instead of leasing that shiny new SUV, you bought a used, reliable car for cash? You could be saving hundreds, maybe even thousands, a year. Not to mention the lower insurance and maintenance costs. Suddenly, that $1,825 from lattes seems like chump change.

And don’t get me started on student loans. If you’re carrying debt, especially high-interest debt, focusing on paying that down should be your top priority. Refinancing, consolidating, or even negotiating with your lender can make a huge difference. Let’s say you have $30,000 in student loans at 6% interest. Refinance to 4%, and you could save over $2,000 a year. That’s a lot of lattes.

But it’s not just about cutting expenses. It’s also about increasing your income. Ask for a raise, start a side hustle, or invest in your skills to land a better-paying job. Even a modest 5% increase in your salary could mean an extra $2,000 a year if you’re making $50,000. And if you put that extra money into a retirement account, the compounding interest will work wonders over time.

Sure, being mindful of your spending is important. But it’s all about balance. Life is short, and if that latte brings you joy, go ahead and enjoy it. The key is to make sure you’re not nickel-and-diming yourself while ignoring the elephant in the room. Focus on the big wins, the decisions that will truly move the needle in your financial life.

So, next time you’re at the café, order that latte without guilt. Then, go home and review your budget. Look for those big-ticket items where you can make a real impact. Trust me, your future self will thank you.

title: self-improvement book|dealing with procrastination and perfectionism
text:
Chapter 3: The Unfinished Bookshelf — When “Not Good Enough” Becomes the Wall Between You and Your Work

Ten years ago, I built a bookshelf.

Not metaphorically. Not in a spreadsheet or a vision board. With a drill, a level, pine boards, and three hours of sweat on a humid Saturday afternoon. It was meant to hold my first manuscript—a memoir about learning to live with anxiety, written slowly over five years in stolen coffee-shop hours and late-night notebooks.

I sanded every edge twice. Measured the shelf spacing three times. Painted it with two coats of matte white—then sanded *again* after spotting a hairline streak near the bottom left corner. By Sunday evening, the shelf stood perfectly plumb, flawlessly smooth, gleaming under the living room lamp.

And it remained empty.

For seventeen months.

Not because I stopped writing—I did. I drafted new chapters, revised old ones, even landed an agent who called the opening “arresting.” But every time I sat down to edit Chapter 4—the one about my father’s silence after my panic attack at twenty-two—I’d open the document, read two paragraphs, then close it. My cursor would blink like an accusation. My inner voice, sharp and familiar, would whisper: *This isn’t honest enough. This isn’t deep enough. If you publish this, people will see how raw—and how unpolished—you really are.*

So instead, I reorganized the pantry. Researched ergonomic keyboards. Wrote three eloquent, unsent emails to friends about existential dread. And stared at that pristine, empty bookshelf.

It wasn’t laziness. It wasn’t lack of discipline. It was perfectionism masquerading as diligence—and procrastination disguised as preparation.

Here’s what I learned, not from textbooks, but from the slow, humbling unraveling of that shelf: Perfectionism doesn’t protect you from failure. It protects you from the vulnerability of trying—and failing—*in public*. Procrastination is its loyal accomplice, offering endless detours so you never have to risk your work being seen as imperfect, incomplete, or human.

Let’s name what’s really happening:

1. The “All-or-Nothing” Trap: Perfectionists believe effort only counts if the outcome meets an invisible, shifting ideal—usually rooted in childhood messages (“Only top grades matter”), comparison (“My colleague published at 28”), or fear (“If this isn’t brilliant, I’m not worthy”). So when the draft feels messy (and all first drafts do), the brain says: *Better not start than start badly.* Procrastination becomes a safety ritual.

2. The Hidden Cost of “Just One More Edit”: That extra revision? That final fact-check? That last-minute font change? They feel productive—but they’re often avoidance dressed as diligence. Research shows chronic perfectionists spend 30–50% more time on tasks *without* improving quality. You’re not polishing the work—you’re delaying the moment it leaves your control.

3. The Emotional Toll: Every avoided task accrues emotional debt—shame, self-criticism, exhaustion. That debt compounds silently, until you’re too depleted to begin anything new. I didn’t just delay editing Chapter 4; I delayed believing I had something valuable to say.

So how do you dismantle the shelf—and fill it?

Start Small, Start Ugly, Start Now  
Forget “finishing.” Aim for *contact*. Commit to 90 seconds: Open the document. Read one paragraph aloud—even if your voice shakes. Type one sentence, no matter how clumsy. That’s it. No editing. No judging. Just showing up, imperfectly. Why 90 seconds? Because neuroscience tells us that crossing the threshold of action—even briefly—rewires the brain’s threat response. You’re not asking permission to be perfect. You’re claiming space to be human.

Embrace the “Good Enough Threshold”  
Ask yourself: *What does “good enough” look like for this specific task, right now?* Not for publication. Not for your inner critic. For *this moment*, given your energy, time, and purpose. For my manuscript, “good enough” became: *Does this paragraph convey the feeling accurately? Does it move the story forward?* If yes—save it. Move on. Perfectionism demands infinite polish; maturity asks, *What serves the work—and me—most right now?*

Separate Creation from Curation  
Give yourself distinct roles: the Wild Writer and the Wise Editor. When creating, silence the editor entirely. Use tools: turn off spellcheck, write in plain text, set a timer for 25 minutes with zero distractions. Only *after* creation does the editor get invited in—and even then, limit edits to one pass focused on *one thing* (e.g., clarity only). This creates psychological distance between your worth and your work.

And finally—reclaim your shelf.  
Last month, I took down that immaculate, empty bookshelf. I replaced it with a simple, slightly crooked oak shelf I bought secondhand. On it sits my published book—not the original manuscript, but the real, flawed, deeply human version that made it into the world. Next to it: a small, unfinished ceramic mug I threw last winter, glazed unevenly, with a hairline crack I chose not to hide.

That mug holds my morning tea. Every day.

Perfectionism promises safety. But safety without growth is stagnation. Procrastination offers temporary relief—but relief that erodes your confidence, your time, your sense of agency. The work isn’t about arriving at flawless. It’s about showing up, again and again, with honesty and courage—even when your hands shake, even when the shelf is still half-built, even when the first sentence feels like shouting into fog.

Your most important project isn’t the book, the proposal, the presentation. It’s rebuilding your relationship with your own effort—with kindness, with patience, with the quiet, revolutionary belief that *you, exactly as you are right now, are enough to begin.*

Go ahead. Open the document.  
Type one sentence.  
Then pour the tea.  
The shelf will wait—but *you* don’t have to.

title: self-improvement book|dealing with procrastination and perfectionism
text:
You sit down to work, open the document, and immediately check your email. Or scroll social media. Or suddenly remember you need to reorganize your spice rack. Sound familiar? That’s not laziness—it’s a quiet negotiation happening inside you: “If I don’t start, I can’t fail. If I don’t finish, I won’t be judged. If it’s not perfect, it’s not worth doing at all.” You’re not broken. You’re protecting yourself—just using strategies that no longer serve you.

Perfectionism and procrastination are two sides of the same anxious coin. One says, “It must be flawless.” The other says, “I’ll wait until conditions are ideal—until I feel ready, inspired, certain.” But readiness is a myth. Certainty is a mirage. And flawless? It doesn’t exist—not in first drafts, not in relationships, not in growth itself. What exists is *you*, showing up imperfectly, again and again. That’s where real progress lives.

Start by naming what’s really underneath the delay. Is it fear of criticism? Fear of success changing your life in ways you’re not prepared for? A deep-seated belief that your worth depends on output or outcome? Ask yourself gently: “What am I afraid will happen if I begin—and what am I afraid will happen if I don’t?” Write it down. Not to fix it yet—just to see it clearly. Awareness disarms the automatic reflex.

Then, shrink the task until it feels almost laughably small. Not “write the report”—but “open the file and type one sentence.” Not “clean the whole apartment”—but “put three things in the right drawer.” This isn’t about lowering standards; it’s about outsmarting resistance. Your brain resists large, vague, high-stakes goals—but it rarely objects to something tiny and concrete. Action creates momentum. Momentum builds confidence. Confidence loosens the grip of perfectionism.

Also, give yourself permission to do it badly. Seriously—say it aloud: “I give myself full permission to write a terrible first paragraph. To sketch a messy outline. To send an email with a typo. To try, fail, adjust, and try again.” Perfectionism confuses excellence with elimination—eliminating risk, eliminating error, eliminating humanity. But excellence grows *through* imperfection. Every skilled musician played wrong notes. Every published author wrote pages they deleted. Your early efforts aren’t the final product—they’re data. They’re practice. They’re how you learn what works.

Notice your inner critic’s voice. It often sounds urgent, absolute, and deeply familiar: “You’ll never get this right.” “Everyone else is ahead.” “This isn’t good enough.” That voice isn’t truth—it’s habit. Try replying with kindness: “I’m learning. I’m allowed to be here, exactly as I am, doing my best with what I have right now.” Treat yourself like someone you deeply care about. Would you shame a friend for taking time to figure things out? Of course not. Extend that same grace inward.

Schedule imperfection. Set a 10-minute timer and commit to working without editing, judging, or stopping—even if what you produce feels awkward or incomplete. When the timer ends, stop—even if you’re on a roll. This trains your nervous system that starting is safe, finishing isn’t mandatory, and effort matters more than polish.

And remember: procrastination isn’t your enemy. It’s a signal—a messenger pointing to unmet needs: rest, clarity, support, boundaries, or compassion. When you pause and ask, “What do I truly need right now?” instead of “Why can’t I just do it?”—you shift from self-punishment to self-leadership.

You don’t need to become someone who never hesitates. You need to become someone who hesitates—and then moves anyway. Not perfectly. Not heroically. Just humanly. One small, imperfect, courageous step at a time. That’s how change takes root. That’s how you build trust—in your ability, your timing, and your own quiet, steady worth—regardless of the outcome. Keep going. You’re already enough—exactly as you are, right now, in the middle of trying.

title: minimalism and focus book|clearing your desk, your inbox and your calendar
text:
You ever notice how clutter just seems to sneak up on you? One minute, your desk is this pristine space of productivity and the next, it’s a chaotic mess of sticky notes, coffee cups, and that one pen that never works. Trust me, I’ve been there. My desk used to look like a battlefield where good intentions went to die. But one day, I decided enough was enough. It was time to take back my workspace, my inbox, and my calendar. And let me tell you, it’s been a game changer.

First things first: the desk. I started with a simple rule—everything has a home. No more random piles of paper or scattered USB drives. If something doesn’t have a designated spot, it doesn’t get to stay. This might sound a bit harsh, but trust me, it works. I set aside an hour (okay, maybe two) and went through every single item. Old receipts? Tossed. Broken gadgets? Out. The only things left were the essentials. It felt like a breath of fresh air, and suddenly, I had room to think.

Now, about that inbox. Email can be a real time-sucker. I used to dread opening my inbox, seeing those thousands of unread messages staring back at me. So, I adopted the "inbox zero" philosophy. It’s not about having no emails; it’s about processing them efficiently. Here are a few tips:
1. Unsubscribe from all those newsletters you never read. Be ruthless.
2. Set up filters and folders to automatically sort incoming mail.
3. Batch process your emails. Dedicate specific times in the day to check and respond, rather than constantly hitting refresh.
4. If an email can be answered in under two minutes, do it right away. Otherwise, schedule a time to deal with it later.

My calendar was another beast altogether. I used to overcommit like it was going out of style. Every meeting, every event, every tiny task—everything got a slot. But you know what they say: if everything is important, nothing is. So, I took a hard look at my schedule and started saying no. Not in a rude way, but in a thoughtful, "I need to prioritize my time" kind of way. Here’s how I tackled it:
1. Block off time for deep work. No meetings, no calls, just focused time.
2. Use a color-coding system to see at a glance what’s what. Red for must-dos, blue for nice-to-haves, and green for personal time.
3. Review your calendar weekly. What can be moved, canceled, or delegated?
4. Leave some buffer time between appointments. You need breathing room, and so does your brain.

The best part about clearing your desk, inbox, and calendar is the sense of control it gives you. Suddenly, you’re not just reacting to everything around you; you’re in the driver’s seat. And honestly, it feels pretty darn good. Plus, when you have a clean, organized space, you’ll find that your mind follows suit. Less clutter, less stress, more focus.

So, give it a shot. Start small, but start now. Clear off your desk, tackle that inbox, and take back your calendar. Your future self will thank you. And who knows, you might even find that long-lost pen that actually works.

title: personal memoir with life lessons|a year of travel after a painful divorce
text:
It was March. I stood in my empty apartment—well, *our* apartment, though the “our” had officially expired three weeks prior—and stared at a single suitcase on the floor. Not the sleek, wheeled kind. A battered, navy-blue Samsonite my dad had given me for college, its zipper held together with duct tape and sheer hope. My divorce papers were still warm in my laptop bag. My therapist had said, “Don’t rush into anything,” and I’d nodded politely—then booked a one-way ticket to Lisbon.

That year wasn’t some Instagram-perfect montage of sun-drenched cafés and cliffside yoga. It was messy. It was loud. It was the sound of me crying in a hostel bathroom in Prague because I’d forgotten how to make coffee without arguing about whose turn it was to grind the beans. It was the taste of over-salted empanadas in Buenos Aires when I tried (and failed) to order in Spanish, then laughed so hard I snorted into my mate gourd—startling the elderly woman next to me, who patted my knee and said, “Hija, the heart needs air before it can hold anything new.”

I didn’t travel to “find myself.” I traveled because I’d misplaced myself somewhere between signing the separation agreement and explaining to my niece why Auntie’s ring was now in a velvet box in her sock drawer. So I went—not as a seeker, but as a witness: to foreign street names, unfamiliar rhythms, the way light fell differently on cobblestones in Lisbon versus Kyoto versus Marrakech.

One rainy afternoon in Oaxaca, I got lost trying to find a tiny mezcaleria recommended by a guy who’d drawn me a map on a napkin. Instead, I stumbled into a women’s weaving co-op run by Zapotec grandmothers. No English spoken. Just hands—rough, stained with indigo and cochineal—guiding mine as they taught me to wind thread around a wooden shuttle. One woman, Doña Lupe, kept humming while she worked, her voice low and steady like a river under stone. When I fumbled the third time, dropping the yarn into the dust, she didn’t sigh or correct me. She just smiled, picked it up, and placed it back in my palm. “Más despacio,” she murmured. *Slower.* Not *better*. Not *faster*. Just… slower.

That stuck. Back home, I’d measured everything in milestones: first date, first night out, first time saying “I’m divorced” without flinching. But Doña Lupe taught me that healing isn’t linear—it’s woven. Loops, knots, loose threads you come back to later. Some days you pull too tight. Some days you leave space on purpose.

I also learned that loneliness and solitude aren’t the same thing. Loneliness is the echo in an empty room. Solitude is sitting cross-legged on a rooftop in Istanbul at dawn, watching minarets glow gold, and realizing—*oh*—you’re not waiting for someone to fill the silence. You’re finally listening to what the silence has been saying all along.

There were stumbles, of course. Like the time I tried to meditate on a Thai beach and spent twenty minutes obsessing over whether my ex had already updated his LinkedIn profile. Or the night in Lisbon when I walked past a couple slow-dancing in front of a tram, and instead of feeling gut-punched, I just… watched. Noticed how the man tucked a strand of hair behind her ear, how she rolled her eyes and laughed. And I thought, *That’s sweet. I hope they’re kind to each other.* Not *Why wasn’t that me?* Just… hope. Unburdened. That felt like victory.

By December, I was in Kyoto, standing under a canopy of maple leaves so red they looked lit from within. I hadn’t “gotten over” anything. But I’d stopped treating my grief like an enemy to defeat—and started treating it like weather: something that passes through, changes the light, reshapes the ground beneath you.

I came home with fewer souvenirs and more certainty: that love doesn’t vanish—it transforms. That endings aren’t full stops; they’re commas, sometimes semicolons, occasionally even em dashes—leaving room for something unexpected to rush in.

And the biggest lesson? The most radical act of self-respect isn’t always staying. Sometimes, it’s packing that duct-taped suitcase—and walking out the door, not toward a destination, but toward the quiet, unshakeable truth that you are enough, exactly as you are: unattached, untethered, and utterly, beautifully unfinished.

title: Christian purpose-driven living book|serving others as the path to a meaningful life
text:
Chapter 5: The Unseen Table — When Serving Others Becomes the Altar of Meaning

It began with a cracked ceramic plate.

Not a dramatic moment—no thunderclap, no angelic choir—just a quiet Tuesday afternoon in my kitchen. I’d been rushing to pack lunches for my two young sons before heading to a staff meeting at the church where I served as communications director. In my haste, I dropped a plate—the one with the faded blue glaze my grandmother had given me. It shattered on the tile floor with a sharp, final *crack*. As I knelt to sweep up the pieces, something unexpected rose in my throat: not frustration, but grief. Not for the plate—but for the life I’d been living: scheduled, strategic, success-oriented… yet strangely hollow. I’d spent years crafting messages about purpose, community, and faith—but rarely *lived* them in the unscripted, inconvenient, messy spaces where real people breathe.

That same evening, I drove past the neighborhood food pantry—a modest brick building tucked behind the old library—its fluorescent sign flickering like a tired heartbeat. On impulse, I turned in. I didn’t go with a plan or a sermon. I just walked in, asked if they needed help, and was handed an apron and a list: *Sort donations. Wipe shelves. Pack weekend bags for children facing food insecurity.*

For three hours, I worked alongside Maria, a retired school nurse with silver braids and hands that moved with quiet authority, and Jamal, a high school junior volunteering for service hours. We sorted canned beans, folded donated blankets, and packed small paper bags with peanut butter, applesauce, granola bars, and a handwritten note: *You are seen. You matter.*  

At one point, a woman named Lena came in—worn coat, tired eyes, holding the hand of a boy who couldn’t have been more than six. She hesitated at the intake desk, then whispered to the coordinator, “I’m picking up for my sister. She’s in the hospital. Her kids are staying with me. I… I don’t know how we’ll make it through next week.” Without fanfare, Maria quietly added two extra juice boxes and a small box of crayons to Lena’s bag. As they left, the little boy looked back—not at me, but *at the crayons*—and gave a small, unguarded smile. That smile didn’t fix her sister’s illness or erase their uncertainty. But in that moment, something shifted inside me. The hollowness I’d felt over the broken plate dissolved—not because the problem was solved, but because I’d stepped into the sacred rhythm of *tending*, not just *telling*.

That night, I realized: Serving others isn’t a strategy for finding meaning. It *is* the meaning—unfolding in real time, in real need, in real proximity to another human soul. Scripture doesn’t say, “Go find your purpose and then serve.” It says, “Carry each other’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). The Greek word for “fulfill” here is *plēroō*—to fill up, to complete, to bring to fullness. Not achievement. Not acclaim. *Fullness.* A life brimming—not with accomplishments, but with connection, compassion, and quiet fidelity.

So how do we move from occasional kindness to a *way of being*—a purpose-driven life rooted in service? Here are three practical postures—not programs, but practices:

1. Start Small, But Start *Now*. Don’t wait for a grand opportunity or perfect timing. Look within your ordinary sphere: the neighbor whose trash can sits forgotten at the curb on rainy days; the colleague overwhelmed by deadlines; the elderly person down the hall who hasn’t had a visitor in weeks. Ask one question: *“What small thing would ease their load right now?”* Then do it—without announcement, without expectation of thanks. Service begins not with scale, but with surrender to the immediate need before you.

2. Serve *With*, Not Just *For*. True service resists savior complexes. It listens before acting. It asks, “What do *you* need?” instead of assuming. It honors dignity over delivery. When you volunteer, show up curious—not to fix, but to learn. Let the person you’re serving teach you about resilience, grace, or joy you’ve never known. Service becomes sacred when it dismantles hierarchy and builds mutuality.

3. Anchor Your Service in Contemplation. Serving without stillness leads to burnout. Before you serve, pause. Breathe. Whisper: *“Lord, let my hands be Yours today.”* Afterward, reflect—not on what you did, but on where you sensed God’s presence—in the shared laughter, the silent understanding, the unexpected gift of being needed. Keep a simple journal: *One person I saw. One way I showed up. One glimpse of grace.* This isn’t record-keeping; it’s soul-tending.

The cracked plate is long gone. But I kept one shard—glued now to a small wooden stand on my desk. It’s not pretty. It’s imperfect, fragile, held together by something unseen. Like us. Like every act of service we offer—not because we’re strong, but because love compels us to hold space for brokenness, both ours and others’.

When you serve—not as a means to significance, but as the very shape of your love—you discover something astonishing: the life you thought you were building *for* yourself is actually being built *through* you—for others. And in that giving, you receive back your own humanity, polished and made whole—not by your effort, but by the quiet, persistent grace that flows where love is poured out.

That’s not just purpose.  
That’s resurrection—served, one humble, faithful act at a time.

title: leadership memoir by a former CEO|the hiring mistake that nearly sank the company
text:
Imagine you're sitting in your office, the weight of a company on your shoulders, and you're reflecting on the journey that brought you to where you are. There's one story, a cautionary tale, that stands out more than any other. It's the story of a hiring mistake that nearly sank the ship. I want to share this with you because it's a lesson I learned the hard way, and I hope it can save you from making the same error.

You see, early in my tenure as CEO, we were at a critical juncture. The company was growing, and we needed to scale our operations quickly. We had just secured a significant round of funding, and everyone was excited about the future. But to get there, we needed a strong team, especially in leadership roles. One of the key positions we needed to fill was the Chief Operating Officer (COO). This person would be responsible for streamlining our processes, improving efficiency, and ensuring that we could handle the rapid growth we were expecting.

In my eagerness to find the perfect candidate, I made a crucial mistake. I focused too much on the resume and not enough on the fit. The individual we hired had an impressive background, with experience at some of the biggest names in the industry. On paper, he seemed like the ideal choice. He had the technical skills, the experience, and the track record. What I didn't realize at the time was that these things, while important, are only part of the equation.

The first few months went well. Our new COO implemented several changes, and we saw some initial improvements. However, as time went on, it became clear that something was off. The morale in the company began to drop, and people started to complain. The COO was a micromanager, and his leadership style was autocratic. He made decisions without consulting the team, and he often dismissed the ideas and feedback of others. This created a toxic environment, and soon, key employees started to leave.

I remember the day when one of our top performers came into my office, visibly upset. She told me that she was resigning because she couldn't work under the new COO. It was a wake-up call. I realized that I had made a grave error. I had hired someone who, despite their impressive credentials, did not align with our company culture or values. I had prioritized skills over fit, and it was costing us dearly.

It took a lot of soul-searching and some difficult conversations, but I knew what I had to do. I had to let the COO go. It was a painful decision, but it was necessary for the health and survival of the company. After that, I took a different approach to hiring. I focused on finding leaders who not only had the right skills but also shared our vision and values. I involved the team in the interview process, and we looked for candidates who demonstrated empathy, collaboration, and a genuine passion for our mission.

The road to recovery wasn't easy, but we managed to turn things around. We rebuilt the team, and over time, the culture improved. The company grew stronger, and we were able to achieve the goals we had set out to accomplish. Looking back, I realize that the hiring mistake was a turning point. It taught me the importance of cultural fit and the value of involving the team in the hiring process.

So, if there's one piece of advice I can give you, it's this: When you're hiring, especially for key leadership roles, don't just look at the resume. Look for someone who will not only bring the right skills but also the right attitude and values. Involve your team in the process, and listen to their feedback. A great hire can transform your company, but the wrong one can bring it to its knees. Trust me, I've been there, and I wouldn't wish that on anyone.

title: career advice book|quitting a stable job to do work you care about
text:
I once spent three years pretending to love spreadsheets. Not *love* love—more like the kind of affection you reserve for a slightly damp towel you keep meaning to throw out but haven’t yet, because it’s *technically* still functional. My title was “Senior Compliance Liaison.” I had no idea what I was liaising, or why compliance needed a senior, but my paycheck arrived like clockwork, my 401(k) grew quietly in the background like a polite houseplant, and my therapist once whispered, “You’re not depressed—you’re just… deeply unanimated.” She meant it kindly. I cried into a kale smoothie afterward.

Quitting wasn’t dramatic. There was no slammed door or mic drop. Just me, at 2:17 p.m. on a Tuesday, typing “I’m resigning” into an email, then immediately Googling “how long until unemployment runs out if I panic-buy artisanal sourdough starter?” Spoiler: it’s longer than you think—and yes, I did buy the starter. It’s named Gary and he’s thriving.

People ask, “But what if it fails?” And I say: what if it *doesn’t*? What if your version of “failing” is actually just building something that fits *you*, even if it’s lopsided, slightly confusing, and occasionally smells faintly of burnt toast? My first paid freelance gig was writing blog posts about composting for a very niche eco-boutique. I got $45 and a free bamboo toothbrush. I framed the toothbrush. Still have it. (It’s now slightly yellow. Like my optimism.)

Let’s get real: stability isn’t the absence of risk—it’s the illusion that risk won’t find you anyway. Layoffs happen. Industries evaporate. Your boss gets replaced by an AI named Kevin who sends passive-aggressive Slack messages at 6:43 a.m. You don’t escape uncertainty by staying put. You just choose *which* uncertainty you want to stare down over breakfast.

So here’s what I wish someone had handed me in a laminated card while I was stress-eating gummy bears in the office bathroom:

1. Test-drive your “care about” before you torch the lease. I started my blog at 10 p.m. after work, two nights a week, for eight months. No audience. No income. Just me, bad headlines, and the growing suspicion that “sustainable living tips for introverts” might be a niche so small it qualifies as a whisper. But those tiny, quiet experiments told me: *this doesn’t exhaust me. In fact, it recharges me.* That’s data. Pay attention.

2. Your safety net isn’t just money—it’s people. I told exactly three humans I was planning to quit. Two said, “Are you sure?” (one added, “My cousin tried that and now sells essential oil diffusers from his mom’s garage.”) The third said, “Cool. Can I help?” That third person became my first editor, my cheerleader, and the one who lent me $200 when Gary the sourdough starter demanded organic rye flour. Find your third person. Then buy them coffee. Or a bamboo toothbrush. They’ll know what to do with it.

3. “Making a living” and “making meaning” are not mutually exclusive—they’re just terrible roommates at first. For six months, I lived off savings, side gigs (yes, including pet-sitting for a very judgmental cat named Nigel), and sheer stubbornness. I didn’t earn what I used to. I *did* start sleeping through the night. I stopped dreaming in Excel formulas. Coincidence? Science says no. My body says *finally.*

Also: nobody actually knows what they’re doing. That guy who launched the wildly successful podcast while working full-time? He edited his first episode in a closet with a blanket over his head and cried when he heard his own voice. That woman who opened the zero-waste shop? Her business license application was rejected *twice* because she wrote “earth-friendly vibes” in the mission statement field. We all fumble. We all Google things like “how to sound confident on a Zoom call when you’re wearing sweatpants.”

Quitting isn’t about bravery. It’s about alignment—like finally swapping out that squeaky hinge you’ve ignored for years. You don’t need to be fearless. You just need to be tired enough of the squeak.

And if you’re reading this while eating lunch at your desk, eyeing the exit sign like it’s a secret portal—breathe. You don’t have to leap today. You don’t even have to leap *this year*. But maybe—just maybe—start sketching what your non-squeaky life looks like. Doodle it on a napkin. Type it into Notes. Whisper it to Gary the starter.

The world doesn’t need more people who tolerate their jobs. It needs your weird, particular, slightly messy care. Even if it starts with composting tips. Especially then.

Chapter 7: The “Stable” Trap — Why Your Paycheck Isn’t a Permission Slip  

Let me tell you about the day I handed in my resignation at a perfectly fine, deeply boring job. I was 32. Senior analyst at a midtown insurance firm. My desk had a potted fern (which I killed twice), a drawer full of stress mints, and a calendar where every Friday was marked with a tiny, hopeful smiley face. My salary was solid. My health insurance covered acupuncture (which I needed). My 401(k) matched up to 6%. By every measurable metric, I was *doing fine*.  

So why did I feel like I was slowly turning into beige wallpaper?  

Because “stable” isn’t the same as “sustainable.” Stability without meaning is just slow suffocation — quiet, polite, and padded with dental coverage.  

I didn’t quit because I’d suddenly discovered my calling while reorganizing a spreadsheet. I quit because one Tuesday, during a three-hour meeting about “synergy levers,” I caught myself mentally drafting a letter to my future self: *“Dear Me, if you’re still here in five years, please forgive me. I think you deserve more than being good at making other people’s PowerPoint slides less painful.”*  

That letter scared me more than any layoff ever had.  

Here’s what no one tells you: quitting isn’t about having it all figured out. It’s about finally admitting—out loud, on paper, in your therapist’s office—that the thing you’ve been tolerating isn’t neutral. It’s costing you. Not just time. Not just energy. It’s quietly eroding your curiosity, your sense of agency, your ability to imagine yourself as someone who gets to choose.  

Take Maya, a friend of mine who spent 11 years as a corporate lawyer. She was brilliant, respected, made six figures before 35—and cried every Sunday night. Not dramatic sobs. Just quiet, exhausted tears while folding laundry, wondering why her hands shook before depositions but not before hiking solo in the Rockies. She started volunteering one evening a week teaching legal literacy to immigrant teens. And something clicked—not because it paid, but because her voice got steady again. Six months later, she launched a nonprofit that helps young people navigate immigration court. Her income dropped by 40%. Her sleep improved by 200%. Her “stability” changed shape—it became rooted in purpose, not payroll.  

Now, let’s be real: this isn’t about romanticizing risk or pretending money doesn’t matter. It’s about recalibrating your definition of security. Real security isn’t a title on a business card. It’s knowing your values are non-negotiable. It’s building small, concrete buffers—like saving six months of bare-bones expenses *before* you walk away, or testing your idea part-time for nine months while keeping your day job. One woman I coached built a freelance editing business nights and weekends for 18 months—she didn’t go full-time until she had three consistent clients *and* could cover rent without touching savings. That’s not recklessness. That’s respect—for yourself, your timeline, and your reality.  

And yes, you’ll hear the noise: “What if you fail?” “What will people think?” “You’re throwing away your ‘good’ life!” Here’s the truth: the biggest failure isn’t trying and stumbling. It’s looking back at 65 and realizing you spent decades mistaking comfort for safety—and safety for courage.  

Quitting isn’t the end of stability. It’s the beginning of building a different kind—one that holds your values, honors your energy, and lets you wake up and say, “This matters. *I* matter here.”  

Your paycheck doesn’t get to vote on whether your life is worth living with intention. You do.  

So ask yourself gently, honestly: What would I try if I knew I couldn’t fail? Not someday. Not after the next promotion. *Right now.* Not because it’s safe—but because it feels like coming home to yourself.  

That’s not quitting.  
That’s finally arriving.
