text:
I'll never forget the day I hired Jake. It was a crisp, sunny morning in April, and I felt like we were on the cusp of something big. Our startup, BrightWave, had just secured a $10 million Series A, and we needed to scale fast. Jake seemed like the perfect fit. He had an impressive resume, with stints at some of the biggest tech firms, and he oozed confidence. In hindsight, that should have been my first red flag.

We were looking for a COO who could handle the nitty-gritty while I focused on strategy and vision. Jake had all the right buzzwords—lean management, agile processes, growth hacking. You name it, he could talk about it. We did three rounds of interviews, and every time, he knocked it out of the park. The board loved him, the investors loved him, and I, stupidly, thought I'd found my right-hand man.

The first few months were a whirlwind. Jake came in with a flurry of ideas and energy. He restructured the operations team, streamlined our processes, and even brought in a few key hires. On paper, everything looked great. But beneath the surface, cracks were starting to form. 

It started with the small stuff. Jake would make decisions without consulting me or the rest of the leadership team. He'd change policies on a whim, and people were getting frustrated. I remember one meeting where he announced a new performance review system that no one had heard of. The room went dead silent, and I could see the confusion and resentment in everyone's eyes. I should have stepped in then, but I didn't. I let it slide, thinking maybe he knew something I didn't.

Then there was the incident with Sarah, our head of product. She's one of the smartest, most dedicated people I've ever worked with, and she had a different vision for how we should be developing our platform. Jake didn't like that. He saw her as a threat, and he made it his mission to undermine her. He'd question her in meetings, second-guess her decisions, and even went so far as to tell her team to go behind her back. It was toxic, and it was tearing us apart.

But the real disaster came when we launched our new product. Jake had pushed for an aggressive timeline, insisting that we needed to get it out the door to meet our revenue targets. I had my doubts, but I trusted him. Big mistake. The launch was a nightmare. The product was riddled with bugs, the marketing was off, and customers were furious. We lost half a million dollars in the first month, and our reputation took a hit that we're still recovering from.

I finally realized what a mess we were in. I called an emergency board meeting, and we had a long, painful discussion. It was clear that Jake had to go. Firing him was one of the hardest things I've ever done, but it was necessary. The aftermath was brutal. Morale was at an all-time low, and we had to do some serious damage control. It took months to rebuild trust, both internally and with our customers.

Looking back, I can see where I went wrong. I was so focused on growth and hitting those milestones that I overlooked the importance of culture and teamwork. I let Jake's charisma and experience blind me to his flaws. And I didn't listen to the people who mattered most—my team. They saw the problems long before I did, and I should have trusted their instincts.

Jake's tenure was a wake-up call. It taught me that leadership isn't just about making the big, flashy moves; it's about the day-to-day, the little things that add up. It's about building a team that trusts each other, that can work through challenges together. And it's about being humble enough to admit when you've made a mistake and having the courage to fix it.

title: leadership book for new managers|giving honest feedback without crushing morale
text:
You’ve just stepped into a leadership role, and one of the first things you’ll realize is that feedback isn’t optional—it’s oxygen. Not the kind that fills a room with hot air or vague praise, but the kind that helps people breathe deeper, think clearer, and grow stronger. Yet here’s what trips up most new managers: they confuse honesty with harshness, candor with criticism, and directness with detachment. Let’s reset that.

Honest feedback isn’t about telling someone what’s wrong. It’s about helping them see what’s possible—clearly, kindly, and collaboratively. When you deliver feedback that lands well, it doesn’t leave the other person deflated; it leaves them energized to try again, adjust, or stretch further. That only happens when your intention is rooted in care—not control—and your delivery is anchored in respect—not righteousness.

Start by asking yourself before every feedback conversation: *What do I hope this person feels afterward?* If your answer is “accountable,” “corrected,” or “warned,” pause. Reframe it. Aim for “understood,” “supported,” and “capable.” That subtle shift changes everything—from your tone to your word choice to the space you hold for their response.

Timing matters. Don’t wait for the annual review—or worse, spring it after a mistake has snowballed. Give feedback close to the event, when context is fresh and change feels doable. But also don’t ambush. Say, “Hey, can we carve out 15 minutes later today to talk about how the client call went? I’d love to reflect on it together.” That signals respect for their time and agency.

When you speak, lead with observation—not judgment. Instead of “You’re disorganized,” try “I noticed the project timeline wasn’t updated for three days, and two team members asked where things stood.” That separates behavior from identity. People can change actions; they can’t easily rewrite who they are.

Then, connect the behavior to impact—gently and concretely. “When timelines aren’t updated, it slows down decisions and creates uncertainty for others.” This isn’t about blame; it’s about shared responsibility. You’re not policing—they’re contributing to a system you both care about.

Now, invite their perspective. Pause. Really listen—not to formulate your next point, but to understand their thinking, constraints, or intent. Maybe they were juggling an urgent request you didn’t know about. Maybe they assumed someone else was handling the update. Their side of the story isn’t an excuse—it’s data. And data makes your feedback more accurate and your support more relevant.

Co-create the next step. Ask, “What would help you keep the timeline current moving forward?” Or “What support do you need to make this easier?” This transforms feedback from a verdict into a partnership. You’re not handing down rules—you’re building capability together.

And never underestimate the power of balance—not “sandwiching” criticism between compliments (which feels manipulative), but genuinely naming what’s working *alongside* what’s evolving. “Your client rapport is excellent—you read the room so well. And at the same time, I noticed the follow-up summary took longer than planned. How might we streamline that part?”

Finally, remember: feedback is not a one-off event. It’s a rhythm. Follow up—not to check up, but to check in. “How did that new template work for you last week?” “What’s feeling smoother now?” That consistency tells people you’re invested—not just in fixing problems, but in their growth.

You won’t get it perfect every time. You’ll misread a cue, choose the wrong words, or underestimate someone’s emotional load. That’s okay. What builds trust isn’t flawlessness—it’s humility, repair, and showing up again with sincerity. When you give honest feedback this way—grounded in belief, clarity, and collaboration—you don’t crush morale. You cultivate it. text:
I once asked for a raise by sending an email that said, “Hey, I’ve been killing it. Can we talk about my salary?” It was sent at 4:58 p.m. on a Friday. My manager replied at 9:03 a.m. Monday with: “Let’s circle back next quarter.” Which is corporate-speak for *“I will forget this ever happened and you will quietly resent your job until your therapist asks why you cry while folding laundry.”*

That was me—28, wearing shoes that pinched, eating lunch at my desk like it was a virtue, and absolutely terrified to ask for what I’d already earned. Not hoped for. *Earned.* Because here’s the uncomfortable truth no one tells you: most people don’t get raises because they don’t ask. Not because they’re underperforming. Not because budgets are tight (though yeah, sometimes they are). Mostly? Because they’ve convinced themselves that asking = being greedy, pushy, or—my personal favorite—*ungrateful*. As if gratitude and fair compensation are mutually exclusive. Spoiler: they’re not. You can love your team *and* want health insurance that doesn’t require you to sell a kidney.

I used to think negotiating was something done in boardrooms with leather chairs and tiny glasses of water. Turns out, it’s done in fluorescent-lit conference rooms with lukewarm coffee and someone nervously rehearsing their pitch in the bathroom stall. I did that. Twice. The second time, I practiced my opening line in the mirror while brushing my teeth. (“I’m excited about my work—and I’d love to align my compensation with the value I’m delivering.”) My cat stared. Judged. Walked away. Honestly? Good feedback.

Why do so many of us stay silent? One: we confuse *earning* with *being handed*. Two: we assume our boss is keeping score. Newsflash—they’re not. They’re juggling three projects, two fires, and a Slack message from HR about mandatory wellness webinars. If you don’t tell them your contributions matter *and* why they should cost more, they’ll default to inertia—which always pays less. Three: we wait for the “perfect moment.” There is no perfect moment. There’s only *now*, or *next week*, or *after you’ve stayed late for the third time without overtime*. And spoiler again: waiting usually means watching someone else—often newer, often less experienced—get hired *at a higher salary* than yours. Yes, that’s real. Yes, it happens weekly. No, it’s not fair. But it *is* fixable.

So how do you actually do it—not desperately, not arrogantly, but *effectively*? Here’s what worked for me (and hundreds of readers who emailed me crying happy tears after their first successful negotiation):

1. Anchor your ask in outcomes, not effort. Don’t say, “I work hard.” Say, “I led the X project, which increased client retention by 22% and saved $140K in churn.” Effort is invisible. Results are receipts. Keep a running “brag doc”—a private Google Doc where you log wins, metrics, positive feedback, even emails where clients praised you. Update it monthly. Read it before your meeting. Your brain needs reminding that you’re not bluffing—you’re *documenting*.

2. Do your homework—not just on Glassdoor, but on *your* role, industry, and location. What’s the median? What’s the 75th percentile? Is your company known for paying above or below market? (Pro tip: check levels.fyi *and* ask a friend in a similar role at another company—over coffee, not LinkedIn DMs. People will tell you things over oat-milk lattes they’d never type.)

3. Name a number—then pause. Don’t say, “I was thinking… maybe… something around…” Just say the number. Calmly. Then shut up. Let silence do the heavy lifting. Your instinct will be to fill it. Resist. That silence is where your worth settles. Also: aim 10–15% above your target. It gives room to negotiate *down*—not *up*—from a reasonable place.

4. Practice saying “no” to lowball offers. Not rudely. Not angrily. Just, “I appreciate that offer—I was hoping for something closer to [X] given [specific reason]. Is there flexibility?” If they say no? Ask, “What would need to happen for us to get there in the next 6 months?” Now you’ve turned a dead end into a roadmap—with dates and deliverables.

And finally—this is the part nobody talks about: *you might get rejected.* That’s okay. It doesn’t mean you’re worthless. It means the timing’s off, the budget’s frozen, or your manager hasn’t built enough political capital to fight for you yet. Ask for feedback. Ask for a follow-up date. Then go back to your brag doc—and keep adding to it. Because the next time? You won’t be asking for a raise. You’ll be negotiating a promotion. Or a remote stipend. Or a four-day week. And honestly? That’s when it gets fun.  

(Also, buy better shoes. Your feet will thank you.)

Chapter 5: Automating Your Savings So You Never Have to Think About It

Hey there, future financial wizards! If you're like most young adults I know (including my younger self), the idea of saving money can sometimes feel as exciting as watching paint dry. But what if I told you that with a few simple tweaks, you could set up your finances in a way that makes saving automatic and almost effortless? Trust me; this is going to be a game changer.

Let me share a story from my own life. A few years ago, I was just starting out in my career, living paycheck to paycheck, and constantly wondering where all my money went at the end of the month. Saving for the future seemed like an impossible dream. That's when I stumbled upon the concept of automating savings, and it transformed everything.

So, how does it work? The basic idea is to set up systems that automatically transfer a portion of your income into a savings account before you even see it. This means you're paying yourself first, and you don't have to rely on willpower or remember to manually move money around. It's like having a personal assistant who takes care of your financial goals while you focus on enjoying life.

Here’s a step-by-step guide to get you started:

1. Set a Savings Goal: First, figure out what you’re saving for. Is it an emergency fund, a vacation, a down payment on a house, or something else? Having a clear goal will help you stay motivated. For example, my goal was to save $5,000 for a rainy day fund.

2. Choose the Right Account: Open a high-yield savings account. These accounts offer better interest rates than regular savings accounts, so your money grows faster. I opened one with an online bank, which had no fees and a great interest rate.

3. Automate Transfers: Set up an automatic transfer from your checking account to your savings account right after each payday. Start small if you need to. Even $20 or $50 a week can add up over time. I started by transferring $100 every two weeks, and it was painless because I never saw the money in my checking account.

4. Monitor and Adjust: Keep an eye on your budget and adjust the amount you save as your income changes. If you get a raise, bump up your savings. If you hit a rough patch, lower it temporarily. The key is to be flexible and consistent.

5. Use Apps and Tools: There are plenty of apps and tools that can help you automate your savings even further. Some apps round up your purchases and put the spare change into a savings account. Others let you set up rules, like saving a percentage of your income or transferring a specific amount when you meet a spending goal.

One of my favorite tools is an app called "Digit." It analyzes your spending habits and automatically transfers small amounts of money to your savings. It’s like having a financial fairy godmother who knows exactly when you can afford to save a little extra.

Now, let’s talk about some real-life examples. My friend Sarah, who’s a graphic designer, uses her bank’s automatic savings feature to set aside 10% of her monthly income. She doesn’t even think about it, and over the past year, she’s saved enough for a three-month sabbatical to travel and work on her art. Another friend, Alex, who works in tech, uses an app that rounds up his daily purchases and puts the difference into a savings account. He’s been able to save over $2,000 in just six months, and he barely notices the difference in his daily spending.

The beauty of automating your savings is that it takes the stress and guesswork out of the equation. You’re setting yourself up for success without having to constantly think about it. And trust me, once you start seeing those savings grow, it’s incredibly motivating.

So, go ahead and take the first step. Open that high-yield savings account, set up those automatic transfers, and watch your financial future start to take shape. You’ve got this, and I’m cheering you on every step of the way!

Let’s get one thing straight: your boss isn’t withholding your raise out of spite. They’re not *waiting* for you to ask—because they’re too busy trying to keep the printer from jamming *and* the sales team from booking demo calls at 3 a.m. Your raise isn’t on their to-do list. It’s not even in their Outlook calendar. It’s not *anywhere*. Unless you put it there.

I’ve coached over 400 people through salary negotiations. Not “career coaching”—actual, sweaty, palms-on-the-table, pre-raise prep. And here’s what I see, every single time: 87% of them don’t ask. Not “don’t ask well.” *Don’t ask at all.* They wait for review season like it’s Christmas morning—and then sit there while their manager says, “Great year!” and slides them a 2.8% merit increase (the *average* U.S. raise in 2023, by the way—not inflation-adjusted, not performance-adjusted, just… the default). Meanwhile, inflation ate 3.4% of their take-home last year. So yeah—they lost ground. Quietly. Respectfully. With a smile.

Why? Oh, the reasons are *deliciously* self-sabotaging.

“I don’t want to seem greedy.”  
Bullshit. You’re not greedy for wanting to be paid what your work is worth. You’re greedy if you bill your client $185/hour but accept $78k/year to *manage* that client’s account. That’s not humility—that’s mispricing your own labor. And yes, I checked: median salary for Senior Account Managers at midsize agencies is $96,500. You’re leaving $18,500 on the table *every year*. For *what*? To preserve someone’s vague sense of comfort?

“I’m afraid they’ll say no.”  
Then what? You get fired? You get demoted? You get reassigned to the breakroom fridge inventory log? No. You get a “not right now”—which is code for *“I haven’t thought about it, and I’m not prepared to justify why you shouldn’t get more.”* That’s not rejection. That’s an invitation to come back in three months with numbers, timing, and a clear ask. But most people hear “no” and vanish like smoke. They don’t follow up. They don’t reframe. They just… shrink.

Here’s the ugly truth: companies *expect* you to negotiate. Not because they love it—but because they *budget* for it. HR sets aside 8–12% of base salary *just* for negotiation wiggle room. Your manager knows this. Their manager knows this. The CFO knows this. *You* are the only person in the room who thinks asking = risky. Everyone else sees it as part of the damn job description.

And let’s talk about *how* you ask—because “I’d like more money” doesn’t work. Neither does “I’ve been here five years.” That’s not leverage. That’s a resignation letter written in passive voice. Real leverage looks like:  
• “Since Q3, I’ve onboarded 14 new clients—$227K in new annual revenue.”  
• “I redesigned the onboarding workflow. Engineering hours dropped 37%. That’s ~$41K saved/year.”  
• “My team’s retention is 92%. Industry avg is 74%. Turnover cost per role here is ~$38K. I’ve likely saved $114K in avoidable hiring/training.”  

That’s not bragging. That’s *accounting*. That’s speaking your employer’s native language: risk, revenue, and replacement cost.

Also—timing matters. Ask *after* you’ve delivered something concrete. Not during budget freeze (though FYI: freezes rarely apply to *individual* raises—they apply to *hiring*). Not when your boss is mid-crisis (though honestly? A calm, short, data-driven ask *during* chaos can land *harder*, because you’re the only one showing up with solutions, not panic).

And please—stop rehearsing your ask in your head for six weeks. Write it down. Say it aloud *twice*, once into your phone, once to your partner or dog or plant. Then send the calendar invite: *“Can we schedule 20 minutes next Tuesday to discuss my compensation and role scope?”* Not “chat.” Not “catch up.” *“Discuss my compensation.”* Say the words. Own them.

Most people never ask because they confuse silence with professionalism. It’s not. It’s surrender—wrapped in a nice shirt and a LinkedIn headline that says “Results-Driven Leader.”  

You’re not entitled to a raise.  
But you *are* entitled to ask.  
And if you don’t—if you keep waiting for permission, for proof, for a sign from the universe—you won’t just miss one raise.  
You’ll miss *seven*. Because compound stagnation is real. A $5,000 gap today becomes $8,200 in three years. $14,100 in seven. And by then? You’re not behind—you’re *invisible*.  

So go ahead. Send the email.  
Then breathe.  
Then do it again next quarter—whether you got the yes or not.

Chapter 5: The Unseen Table — When Serving Others Becomes the Altar of Meaning

It began with a cracked ceramic plate.

Not a dramatic moment—no thunderclap, no angelic choir—just a quiet Tuesday afternoon in my kitchen. I’d been rushing to pack lunches for my two young sons before heading to a staff meeting at the church where I served as communications director. In my haste, I dropped a plate—the one with the faded blue glaze my grandmother had given me. It shattered on the tile floor with a sharp, final *crack*. As I knelt to sweep up the pieces, something unexpected rose in my throat: not frustration, but grief. Not for the plate—but for the life I’d been living: scheduled, strategic, success-oriented… yet strangely hollow. I’d spent years crafting messages about purpose, community, and faith—but rarely *lived* them in the unscripted, inconvenient, messy ways that actually change lives.

That evening, I drove past our neighborhood food pantry—a place I’d admired from afar but never entered as a volunteer. On impulse, I pulled over, walked in, and asked if they needed help sorting donations. The coordinator, Maria, a woman in her sixties with kind eyes and hands stained faintly by tomato sauce, looked up from a stack of canned goods and said simply, “We need someone to set up the client tables before opening tomorrow. Can you be here at 7 a.m.?”

I said yes—and showed up shivering in the predawn chill. Inside the converted church basement, Maria handed me a roll of paper tablecloths, plastic forks, and three folding tables. “This is where people sit while they wait,” she explained. “Some haven’t eaten since yesterday. Some are holding toddlers who haven’t slept. Some are carrying shame like extra weight. Make it feel like a table—not a line.”

So I did. I smoothed each paper cloth until the creases vanished. I arranged forks precisely, handles facing left—Maria’s small ritual of dignity. I placed a single carnation (donated by a local florist) in a chipped mason jar at the center of each table. Nothing grand. Nothing measurable. Just presence. Intention. Care.

At 8:15 a.m., an elderly man named Mr. Henderson shuffled in, leaning heavily on a cane. He paused when he saw the table—looked at the flower, touched the edge of the cloth, then met my eyes and whispered, “Feels like home.” In that moment, the cracked plate didn’t matter. My title didn’t matter. My carefully curated resume didn’t matter. What mattered was that I had shown up—not to fix, not to preach, not even to *lead*—but to serve a single human being at the point of his quiet, unspoken need.

That ordinary table became my first real altar.

Serving others isn’t the *path to* meaning—it *is* meaning made visible. Scripture doesn’t say, “Find your purpose, then serve.” It says, “For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve” (Mark 10:45). Jesus washed feet—not because it advanced His agenda, but because love, by its very nature, bends low. And in that bending, we discover who we truly are: not self-made achievers, but beloved children whose identity is secured not in what we accomplish, but in how faithfully we attend to the people God places in our orbit.

So how do we begin—not as heroes, but as humble stewards of everyday service? Here are three anchors, tested in my own stumbles and sustained by grace:

1. Start Small—But Start *Now*. Don’t wait for a mission trip or a leadership role. Look at your immediate circle: the neighbor whose trash cans sit forgotten at the curb on rainy days; the coworker drowning in emails who needs ten minutes of undivided listening; the teenager scrolling silently at dinner who needs one genuine question (“What made you smile today?”). Service begins in proximity—not platform. Set one micro-intention this week: *I will notice one person’s unseen need—and meet it without fanfare.*

2. Serve Without Scanning for Spiritual ROI. We’ve all done it: offering help while secretly hoping for affirmation, conversion, or at least a grateful text. But true service releases outcome. It trusts the Holy Spirit to work in hidden ways—like water seeping into dry soil. When you hand a coffee to the barista, don’t calculate whether she’ll hear the gospel. Just see her name tag. Say her name. Smile like she matters—because she does, eternally.

3. Let Your Limits Become Your Liturgy. You won’t serve perfectly. You’ll forget the flowers. You’ll say the wrong thing. You’ll grow weary. That’s not failure—it’s invitation. Your exhaustion is holy ground where pride surrenders and dependence deepens. Bring your fatigue to God—not as a barrier to serving, but as the very posture in which He meets you. “My power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9) isn’t a theological footnote. It’s the operating system for a life that serves well.

The cracked plate is still in my cupboard—glued back together with visible seams. I use it sometimes, not to hide the break, but to remember: meaning isn’t found in flawless performance. It’s forged in the faithful tending of broken, beautiful, ordinary human lives—setting tables, smoothing cloths, whispering dignity into silence.  

When you serve—not as a strategy, but as surrender—you don’t just change someone else’s day. You rediscover your own soul, already held, already loved, already called—right here, right now—to love back.

title: writing-craft memoir|the daily routine of a working novelist
text:
So, you want to know what it's like to be a working novelist, huh? Well, buckle up, because it’s not all sipping lattes in quaint coffee shops and waiting for inspiration to strike. It’s more like wrestling with a grumpy muse who refuses to get out of bed. But hey, I wouldn’t trade it for the world.

First things first: my alarm goes off at 6 AM. I hit snooze. Then I hit snooze again. And maybe one more time for good measure. By the time I actually roll out of bed, it’s 6:45, and I’m already behind schedule. Welcome to the glamorous life of a writer!

I shuffle to the kitchen, where my trusty coffee maker is already brewing a pot. Coffee is the lifeblood of any writer, and I take mine seriously. A splash of cream, a dash of cinnamon, and I’m ready to face the day. Or at least, I’m ready to pretend I am.

By 7:30, I’m at my desk, staring at the blank page on my computer. Some days, the words flow like a river. Other days, they trickle out like a leaky faucet. Today feels like a leaky faucet kind of day. I type a sentence, delete it, type another, and delete that too. It’s a cycle of self-doubt and determination, and it’s exhausting.

Here’s a tip: don’t wait for the perfect moment to start writing. There’s no such thing. Just sit down and do it. Even if it’s terrible, at least you’re doing something. You can always edit later, but you can’t edit a blank page.

Around 10 AM, I take a break. Sometimes I’ll go for a walk, other times I’ll just stretch and grab a snack. I’ve learned that taking breaks is crucial. Your brain needs time to rest and recharge, or you’ll end up with a jumbled mess of words that make no sense. Trust me, I’ve been there.

Back at my desk by 10:30, I dive back into the story. This is when I usually get into a rhythm. The characters start to come alive, and the plot begins to unfold. It’s like magic, but also a lot of hard work. I write until lunch, which is usually around 1 PM. My go-to is a simple sandwich and some fruit. Nothing fancy, but it gets the job done.

After lunch, I might switch gears and work on something else. Maybe I’ll tackle some blog posts or catch up on emails. It’s important to have variety in your day, otherwise, you risk burning out. Writing a novel is a marathon, not a sprint, and you need to pace yourself.

By 4 PM, I’m usually ready to call it quits. My brain is fried, and my eyes are crossing. I close my laptop, stretch, and step away from the desk. I might read a book, watch a show, or spend some quality time with my family. It’s essential to have a life outside of writing. Otherwise, you’ll lose touch with the real world, and your stories will suffer.

Another tip: set realistic goals. Don’t try to write 10,000 words a day. Aim for something manageable, like 1,000 words. If you hit that, great! If you go over, even better. But don’t beat yourself up if you fall short. Writing is a process, and some days are just harder than others.

Before I go to bed, I jot down a few notes for the next day. I find it helpful to have a plan, even if it’s just a rough outline. It gives me a starting point and makes the blank page a little less daunting in the morning.

And there you have it—a glimpse into the daily routine of a working novelist. It’s not always pretty, but it’s always worth it. So, if you’re thinking about writing a novel, go for it. Just be prepared to put in the work, and don’t forget to have a little fun along the way. Happy writing!

Chapter 7: The Raise That Wasn’t — And Why Your Silence Is Costing You $250,000 (Yes, Really)

Let me tell you about Maya. Not her real name—she asked me not to use it—but her story is so painfully common, I’ve heard versions of it from over 87 people in the last two years. Maya joined a midsize marketing firm as a content strategist right out of college. She was sharp, reliable, and quietly brilliant at turning messy client briefs into campaigns that actually moved the needle. Within 18 months, she was managing two junior writers, mentoring interns, and handling half the agency’s biggest accounts—even though her title hadn’t changed, and her salary had only gotten one 3% bump (the “cost-of-living” kind, not the “you-just-saved-us-$400K-in-client-retention” kind).

Then, last spring, she found out her *new* colleague—same role, same experience level, hired six months after her—was making $14,000 more.

Maya didn’t rage-quit. She didn’t send an angry Slack message. She sat at her desk, opened her laptop, and Googled: “How to ask for a raise without sounding greedy.”

She read three articles. Watched one TED Talk. Practiced in the shower. Then… nothing. She never sent the email. Never scheduled the meeting. A month later, she got a polite “Great work!” in her annual review—and another 3% increase.

Why? Because she was terrified—not of rejection, but of being *seen* as difficult. As ungrateful. As the person who “ruins the vibe.” Sound familiar?

Here’s the uncomfortable truth no HR deck will tell you: Most people don’t get raises because they *don’t ask*. Not because they’re underperforming. Not because budgets are tight. Not because their boss forgot. They don’t get raises because they assume the system is fair, transparent, and reward-based—and it’s not. It’s human. It’s political. And it rewards clarity, confidence, and courage—not just competence.

Let me drop a number on you: According to Georgetown University research, the average worker who negotiates their first salary *early in their career* earns over $250,000 more over 30 years—not from one big bump, but from compounding raises, bonuses, and retirement contributions built on a higher base. That’s not hypothetical. That’s math. And yet, when asked why they haven’t negotiated, most people say things like:  
• “I didn’t want to seem pushy.”  
• “My manager knows my value.”  
• “It’s not the right time.”  
• “I’m just happy to have the job.”  

I used to say all of those things. In fact, I accepted my first post-MBA offer without blinking—$82,500, full benefits, a nice title… and zero negotiation. Six months in, I learned a peer with identical credentials and slightly less experience had started at $91,000. My stomach dropped—not because of the $8,500 gap, but because I’d handed away leverage I’d never get back. That wasn’t humility. That was self-sabotage disguised as professionalism.

Asking for a raise isn’t about demanding money. It’s about aligning your compensation with your *actual contribution*. Think of it like updating your GPS: if you keep driving while ignoring the detour signs, you’ll end up miles off course—and wonder why you’re exhausted and underpaid.

So how do you actually do it—without sweating through your shirt or sounding transactional? Start here:  
1. Track your impact—not hours worked, but outcomes. Did you launch a campaign that brought in $220K in new revenue? Cut onboarding time by 40%? Save the team 10+ hours/week with a new template? Write it down. Quantify it.  
2. Time it right—not during budget season panic, but after a win, before your review, or when your boss seems calm and open.  
3. Lead with curiosity, not ultimatums. Try: *“I love this role and our team’s momentum. As I reflect on what I’ve delivered this quarter—and where I see myself growing next—I’d love to talk about how my compensation aligns with that scope.”*

And if they say no? That’s data—not defeat. Ask: *“What would it take to get there in the next 6 months?”* Get it in writing. Then deliver it.

Because here’s what nobody tells you: The first time you ask, you’re not just negotiating salary. You’re negotiating your own permission to be seen, valued, and paid like the professional you are. And once you do it—once you speak your worth out loud—you’ll never go back to silent mode again. Not for yourself. And definitely not for Maya.

Let’s get one thing straight: your latte isn’t bankrupting you.  

It’s not. Not even close.  

I watched a woman cry in my office last month—not over student loans or medical debt—but because she’d “wasted” $5.75 on a vanilla oat-milk latte *twice* that week. She’d tracked it in her budgeting app like it was evidence in a criminal trial. Meanwhile, her car insurance was auto-renewing at $287/month—$3,444 a year—for a 2015 Honda Civic with 92,000 miles and a dented fender. She hadn’t shopped around in *four years*. Not once. She just clicked “renew.”  

That’s where the real money leaks. Not in the foam. In the inertia.  

Here’s what nobody tells you: cutting out lattes saves you about $1,100 a year—if you buy one every weekday, no vacations, no sick days, no “I’ll just grab coffee at the office today.” That’s *if*. Most people don’t. And even then? $1,100 is less than half a *single* month of rent in Austin, Denver, or Philly. Less than your annual deductible on a mediocre health plan. Less than what you paid for that Peloton subscription you used for three weeks before it became a clothes hanger.  

But go ahead—keep feeling guilty. Go ahead and shame yourself for the $5.75. Because guilt is cheap. It costs nothing. And it does *nothing*. It doesn’t lower your APR. It doesn’t renegotiate your cable bill. It doesn’t force your employer to finally process that 401(k) match they’ve been sitting on since March.  

What *does* move the needle?  

Switching from a 21% APR credit card to a 0% intro APR balance transfer card—and actually *using* the 15 months to pay it off. That alone can save $3,200 in interest on a $10,000 balance.  

Negotiating your internet bill. Not “asking nicely.” *Calling, saying “I’m switching to X provider unless you match their $49.99 promo,” and hanging up if they hem and haw.* I did this last Tuesday. Saved $62 a month. That’s $744 *this year*. For 11 minutes on hold and two deep breaths.  

Canceling the $14.99/mo “premium wellness app” that sends you push notifications to drink more water—and replacing it with… water. (Bonus: free.)  

And yes—reviewing your retirement plan. Not the “am I contributing?” question. The *real* one: “Is my 401(k) stuck in Target Date 2035 with a 0.87% expense ratio while identical funds charge 0.03%?” That 0.84% gap? On a $120,000 balance? That’s $1,008 *every single year*, silently siphoned off. Every. Year. Compounded. For decades.  

You’re not bad with money. You’re just trained to fixate on the visible, tiny, emotionally charged things—like the barista remembering your name—while ignoring the invisible, massive, boring things—like the fact your mortgage lender never mentioned you qualify for a 0.5% rate reduction after your credit score jumped 42 points last fall.  

Big wins aren’t glamorous. They’re spreadsheet rows. They’re voicemails left at 8:02 a.m. before customer service lines jam. They’re opening your bank statement and circling *one* line item—not the coffee, but the “ACH processing fee” your business account charges *every time* you pay a vendor. $1.25 x 47 times = $58.75. Just… gone. No fanfare. No guilt. Just gone.

Your worth isn’t tied to how many lattes you deny yourself. It’s tied to how much energy you redirect—from self-punishment—to *leverage*. Chapter 4: The Art of Saying No to Good Opportunities

 The Seduction of the Shiny New Thing

It was a crisp autumn morning when I received an email that would challenge my commitment to time management. The message was from a prestigious organization, inviting me to speak at their annual conference in a few months. The event was well-attended, and the exposure would be significant. As I read the email, a mix of excitement and anxiety washed over me. This was a good opportunity, no doubt, but I had to ask myself: Was it a great one?

In the world of time management, we often face a paradox: the more successful we become, the more opportunities we attract. While this is a sign of progress, it can also be a double-edged sword. If we say yes to every opportunity, we risk diluting our focus and sacrificing the quality of our work. The key is to learn how to say no to good opportunities to protect the great ones.

 A Personal Story: The Conference Dilemma

When I first started my career as a consultant, I was eager to take on every project and attend every event. I believed that saying yes to everything would open doors and help me build a strong network. However, as my schedule became increasingly packed, I found myself stretched thin. My work suffered, and I felt constantly stressed and overwhelmed.

One day, I received an invitation to speak at a high-profile industry conference. The organizers promised a large audience, media coverage, and the chance to connect with influential people. It was a good opportunity, and my initial reaction was to accept. But then I remembered a piece of advice I had heard from a mentor: "The key to success is not just what you do; it's what you choose not to do."

I took a step back and evaluated the opportunity against my current commitments. I had several ongoing projects that required my full attention, and I was already scheduled to speak at two other conferences in the same month. Adding another engagement would mean sacrificing the quality of my existing work and potentially missing out on the relationships and outcomes I had been building for months.

After much deliberation, I decided to decline the invitation. It was a difficult decision, but I knew it was the right one. By saying no, I protected the great opportunities I already had and ensured that I could deliver my best work. In the end, the projects I focused on were highly successful, and the relationships I nurtured during that time led to even more significant opportunities in the future.

 The Power of Prioritization

Saying no to good opportunities is not about being ungrateful or turning down chances to grow. It's about making strategic decisions that align with your long-term goals and values. Here are some practical steps to help you make the right choices:

1. Define Your Goals and Priorities:
   Start by clearly defining what you want to achieve in the short and long term. What are your top priorities? What are the key areas where you want to invest your time and energy? Write these down and keep them in a place where you can easily refer to them.

2. Evaluate the Opportunity:
   When a new opportunity presents itself, assess it against your goals and priorities. Ask yourself:
   - Does this opportunity align with my long-term vision?
   - Will it help me achieve my key objectives?
   - How does it compare to the opportunities I already have?

3. Consider the Trade-offs:
   Every yes comes with a trade-off. Think about what you will have to give up if you say yes. Will it require you to sacrifice the quality of your existing work? Will it take away from the time you need for personal growth or self-care? Be honest with yourself about the potential costs.

4. Practice Gratitude and Respect:
   When declining an opportunity, do so with gratitude and respect. Thank the person for the invitation and explain that, while it is a wonderful opportunity, it doesn’t align with your current priorities. You never know when a door might open again in the future, and maintaining positive relationships is always valuable.

5. Set Clear Boundaries:
   Establish boundaries to protect your time and energy. Let others know when you are available and when you are not. Setting clear expectations can help prevent last-minute requests and ensure that you have the space to focus on your most important work.

6. Revisit and Reassess:
   Regularly review your goals and priorities. As circumstances change, so too may your focus. Be flexible and willing to adjust your approach as needed. This will help you stay aligned with your evolving vision and make the most of the opportunities that come your way.

 The Long-Term Benefits

Saying no to good opportunities can feel counterintuitive, especially when the fear of missing out (FOMO) looms large. However, the long-term benefits of protecting your great opportunities are substantial. By focusing on what truly matters, you can:

- Deliver High-Quality Work: When you’re not spread too thin, you can devote the necessary time and energy to produce exceptional results.
- Build Stronger Relationships: Investing in fewer, more meaningful connections can lead to deeper, more lasting relationships.
- Reduce Stress and Burnout: By managing your workload effectively, you can maintain a healthier balance between work and life, leading to greater overall well-being.
- Achieve Greater Success: Over time, the cumulative effect of making strategic choices will lead to more significant achievements and a more fulfilling career.

 Conclusion

Learning to say no to good opportunities is a critical skill in effective time management. It requires discipline, clarity, and a willingness to prioritize. By doing so, you create space for the great opportunities that truly align with your goals and values. Remember, the goal is not to fill your calendar but to fill your life with meaningful and impactful experiences. Embrace the power of saying no, and watch as your focus and success grow.

Chapter 3: The Two-Second Rule — Start So Small, You Can’t Even Blink Away From It  

Let me tell you about the day I almost quit writing my first book.  

It was 2018. I’d been “working on it” for seven months—mostly by staring at a blank Google Doc, scrolling Instagram, and whispering to my cat, “Maybe tomorrow.” My goal? Write 500 words a day. Sounds reasonable, right? Except every morning, my brain would stage a full-blown mutiny: *What if it’s terrible? What if no one reads it? What if I have to rewrite Chapter 2… again?* So I’d close the laptop. And then feel guilty. And then eat a whole sleeve of graham crackers. Not exactly a virtuous cycle.  

Then one rainy Tuesday, I tried something stupidly simple: I opened the doc and typed just one sentence. Not five. Not fifty. One. A dumb, throwaway line like, “The coffee tasted like regret and oat milk.” That was it. Then I closed the laptop. Done.  

And guess what? The next day, I did it again. Same thing. One sentence. No pressure. No performance review from my inner critic. Just a tiny, frictionless spark.  

Within three weeks, I was writing 300–400 words most days—not because I’d suddenly become disciplined, but because showing up for one sentence had rewired something in me. I wasn’t building a writing habit. I was building *trust*—with myself. Trust that I wouldn’t demand perfection. Trust that consistency didn’t require heroics. Trust that small doesn’t mean insignificant—it means *sustainable*.  

This is the heart of what I call the Two-Second Rule: If a habit can be started in two seconds or less—if it requires no decision, no gear, no mental gymnastics—then you’ve removed the biggest barrier to action: hesitation.  

Think about it: Flossing one tooth takes two seconds. Doing one push-up? Two seconds. Opening your notes app and typing “I’m tired but I showed up today”? Two seconds. Reading one paragraph of a book? Two seconds. Meditating for ten breaths? Two seconds.  

These aren’t “warm-ups.” They’re not placeholders for the *real* habit. They *are* the habit—especially at the beginning. Because habits aren’t built in grand gestures. They’re built in the quiet, uncelebrated moments when you choose *not to opt out*.  

I watched this work with Sarah, a client who wanted to run a marathon. She hadn’t jogged in twelve years. Her first goal? Put on her running shoes and stand outside for ten seconds. That’s it. No track. No playlist. No GPS watch. Just shoes on, door open, breeze on her face—for ten seconds. She did that for five days straight. On Day 6, she walked around the block. By Week 3, she was jogging for 90 seconds—then 3 minutes—then 10. Today? She’s run two half-marathons. But none of that happened because she “got motivated.” It happened because she made the first move so laughably easy, there was zero reason to negotiate with herself.  

Here’s the beautiful paradox: When you start absurdly small, you stop negotiating with resistance—and resistance loses its power. Your brain stops seeing the behavior as a threat (“Oh no, here comes the hard thing!”) and starts recognizing it as a neutral cue (“Oh, this is just what we do now”). That’s how neural pathways get laid down—not with willpower, but with repetition so gentle it feels like breathing.  

So tonight, before bed, ask yourself: What’s the *absolute smallest version* of the habit I want? Not the version that looks good on Instagram. Not the version I think I *should* do. The version that makes your shoulders drop and your breath slow down. Then do only that. Once. Tomorrow, do it again. And if you miss a day? No drama. Just return to the two-second version—no guilt, no reset, no self-punishment. You’re not failing. You’re calibrating.  

Because real change isn’t about launching rockets. It’s about lighting matches—small, steady, and so easy you forget you’re even holding fire.  

Start there. Stay there. Watch what grows.

Chapter 5: The Unseen Table — When Serving Others Becomes the Altar of Meaning

It began with a cracked ceramic plate.

Not a dramatic moment—no thunderclap, no angelic choir—just a quiet Tuesday afternoon in my kitchen. I’d been rushing to pack lunches for my two young children when my elbow knocked over the small stack of mismatched dishes we kept for “everyday use.” One plate hit the tile floor and split cleanly in half, a hairline fracture running from rim to center like a fault line in dry earth.

I sighed, bent down, and picked up the pieces. As I held them—cool, sharp-edged, irreparably broken—I felt an unexpected wave of grief. Not for the plate, really, but for something deeper: the quiet accumulation of days spent *managing* life—checking boxes, optimizing schedules, curating appearances—while feeling strangely hollow beneath the surface. I’d been preaching about purpose for years. Writing devotionals. Leading small groups. Yet in that ordinary moment, standing barefoot on cold tile, holding broken pottery, I realized I’d confused *busyness with belonging*, *activity with aliveness*.

That same week, our church launched a new initiative: “The Unseen Table”—a simple, no-frills meal program for neighbors experiencing housing instability or isolation. No sign-up sheets, no intake forms—just one table set each Thursday evening in the church’s sunlit fellowship hall, open from 5:30 to 7:00 p.m. Anyone was welcome. No questions asked. Just food, quiet space, and presence.

I signed up to serve—not out of spiritual duty, but out of a quiet, desperate hope that *doing something real* might stitch me back together.

The first Thursday, I arrived early to set the table. I laid out paper plates (no ceramics this time), filled salt and pepper shakers, arranged plastic forks beside folded napkins. At 5:28, a man named Elias walked in—wearing a worn winter coat despite the mild spring air, carrying a backpack so heavy it pulled his shoulders forward. He didn’t speak at first. Just sat, hands folded, eyes resting on the steam rising from the lentil soup.

I brought him a bowl. He looked up—not at the food, but at my face—and said, softly, “You’re new.”

I nodded. “Yes. First time.”

He stirred his soup slowly. “Most people don’t look at you when they hand you food. They look at the floor. Or their watch. Or the next person in line.” A pause. “You looked like you saw me.”

That sentence landed like a sacrament.

In that moment, I understood: serving isn’t primarily about *what we give*—it’s about *how we see*. It’s the sacred discipline of lowering our gaze from our own anxieties, our curated resumes, our endless to-do lists—and lifting our eyes to behold the dignity, the story, the quiet courage in the person before us. Service becomes purposeful not because it fixes everything, but because it *restores sight*: ours, and theirs.

This is the paradox at the heart of Christian purpose-driven living: We do not find meaning by climbing higher to be seen—we discover it by bending lower to see others. Jesus didn’t say, “Go build impressive ministries.” He said, “Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 25:40). The “least” aren’t a demographic—they’re the people whose names we don’t know, whose stories we haven’t bothered to learn, whose presence doesn’t advance our agenda.

So how do we begin—genuinely, sustainably, without burnout or performance anxiety?

First, *start where your hands already are.* You don’t need a formal ministry or a big platform. Notice the neighbor who walks her dog alone every evening—offer to walk with her once. Bring soup to the new mom down the street *without waiting to be asked*. Write a handwritten note to the elderly woman who lives across the hall—not about faith, just about the beauty of her garden. Purpose isn’t found in grand gestures; it’s cultivated in the soil of consistent, humble attention.

Second, *practice holy slowness.* Serving well requires presence, not productivity. Before you hand someone a meal, a ride, or even a listening ear—pause. Breathe. Ask yourself: *Am I here, or am I already rehearsing my next sentence?* Put your phone away. Make eye contact. Let silence be okay. This isn’t inefficiency—it’s reverence.

Third, *embrace the brokenness—including your own.* That cracked plate taught me that wholeness isn’t the absence of fracture; it’s the willingness to hold what’s broken with tenderness. When you serve, you will feel inadequate. You’ll say the wrong thing. You’ll grow weary. And that’s where grace meets you—not as a reward for perfection, but as the very ground on which you stand. Your limitations aren’t obstacles to purpose; they’re the cracks through which God’s light enters *and* shines out.

Serving others doesn’t guarantee comfort. It won’t erase your doubts or solve all your problems. But it *will* anchor you. Because meaning isn’t a destination we reach—it’s a posture we inhabit. It’s choosing, again and again, to see the image of God in the person holding the cracked plate, the tired nurse, the anxious teen, the stranger at the Unseen Table.

And sometimes—often—it begins not with a sermon, but with a sigh… a stoop… and the quiet, courageous act of holding broken pieces, both in your hands and in your heart—knowing that love, offered without condition, is never wasted. It is, quite simply, how heaven leaks into earth. One ordinary, extraordinary act of seeing at a time.

Look. I’m not going to tell you “word of mouth is magic.” It’s not. It’s messy, slow, and *relies entirely on you doing something so useful—or so weirdly delightful—that people forget they’re supposed to be polite and quiet.

Your first 100 customers won’t come from your Instagram Reels. They’ll come from 7 people who told 3 friends each—and two of those friends showed up with a friend *they* owed a favor to. That’s how it actually works. Not virality. *Obligation*. Delight. Embarrassment (in the good way—like, “I have to tell Sarah about this before she finds out from someone else”).

Here’s what *doesn’t* work:  
- “Tell a friend!” stickers on your packaging. (People don’t stick them. They toss them.)  
- A referral program that pays $5. (That’s less than a latte. It’s insulting.)
