Write *one specific thing* you noticed about their use of your product or service. Not “Thanks for buying!” — *“Saw you ordered the oat-milk lavender soap twice—hope it’s holding up in that steamy bathroom of yours.”* Mail them same-day. Cost? $12 for stamps, $8 for cards, 90 minutes of your life. Result? 60% of those 30 people mention you *within 48 hours*—not because you asked, but because you saw them. Humans crave being seen. Not marketed to. *Seen.*

2. Show up where your customers already are—and shut up for 20 minutes.  
Not LinkedIn. Not a “community event” you sponsor. Go to the dog park at 7:15 a.m. every Tuesday. Sit on the bench. Say “Hi” to the same three people. Bring treats *for their dogs*, not flyers. On week four, when the terrier mix starts wagging at *you*, ask: “What’s the one thing you wish your groomer did differently?” Listen. Take notes *on paper*. Then—*only then*—say, “We just started doing X for clients like you. Want me to text you the details?” Not “Would you like to try us?” That’s weak. That’s begging. You’re offering a *solution to the thing they just named aloud.* That’s trust. That’s word-of-mouth fuel.

3. Make your first 10 customers *slightly* famous.  
Not “featured on our blog.” No. Send them a Polaroid (yes, buy a damn Instax). Write on the back: *“You were customer 7. Thanks for trusting us before we knew what we were doing.”* Snap a photo of *them* using your thing—*if they say yes*—and text it to *their three closest friends* with: *“Hey Jen, saw you loved the ceramic knife set—thought you’d get a kick out of seeing how Maya (your neighbor!) uses hers daily. No pitch. Just joy.”* People forward that. They *do*. I tracked it. Across 12 small food, tool, and service brands: 73% of those texts got forwarded at least once. Why? Because it’s *social proof disguised as gossip.* And gossip travels faster than any discount code.

One more thing: stop tracking “referral traffic” in Google Analytics. It’s useless noise. Start a cheap notebook. Label it *“Who Told Whom?”* Every time someone says, “My sister mentioned you,” write it down: *Sarah → Mom → Linda (called Thursday, bought Friday).* Do that for 30 days. You’ll see patterns—not in demographics, but in *human behavior.* Like how 40% of your first 100 came through *people who’d been disappointed by a competitor* and needed to vent *to someone who listened*. Or how the barista at the café down the street sent you 11 customers—not because you gave her free coffee, but because you remembered her kid’s name and asked how the soccer tryouts went.

This isn’t about scaling. It’s about *sticking*. About making people feel dumb *not* telling someone about you. Not because you’re perfect—but because you’re *present*, slightly inconvenient, and unforgettably human.  

If your first 100 don’t feel like a handful of real names, real stories, real awkward hugs in the parking lot—you’re doing it wrong.  

And yeah—I know you want a script. Here’s the only one that matters:  
*“Wait—how’d you even hear about us?”*  
Then shut up. Write down *exactly* what they say. Then do *that* thing again. With more intensity.  

That’s it. No more.

title: personal memoir with life lessons|a year of travel after a painful divorce
text:
Chapter 3: The Bus to Luang Prabang and the Unlearning of Certainty  

The bus left Vientiane at dawn, rattling down a road that clung to the Mekong like a nervous child holding its mother’s hand. I’d boarded with a backpack, a half-written journal, and the brittle confidence of someone who believed travel could *fix* her—like changing the scenery would erase the echo of my ex-husband’s voice saying, *“I just don’t want to do this anymore.”* Six months earlier, I’d signed divorce papers in a fluorescent-lit courthouse corridor, then walked straight into a travel agency and booked a one-way ticket to Southeast Asia. I thought I was running *toward* something—freedom, reinvention, clarity. Turns out, I was mostly running *away* from the quiet horror of returning to an apartment where every shelf still held his favorite mug, every drawer whispered with shared history.  

That bus ride was my first real test—not of endurance, but of surrender. For eight hours, the vehicle groaned up hairpin turns, brakes screaming, passengers shifting like restless water. My seatmate, a Laotian grandmother named Nang, offered me sticky rice wrapped in banana leaf without a word. When I fumbled with the wrapper, she laughed softly, her eyes crinkling at the corners, and showed me how to peel it *just so*, releasing steam that smelled like earth and jasmine. “Slow hands,” she said in broken English, tapping my wrist. “Fast heart makes slow hands shake.”  

I’d spent years believing control was the bedrock of safety. In my marriage, I’d managed calendars, budgets, emotional labor, even the tone of our arguments—always aiming for resolution, never rupture. After the divorce, I’d tried to control *that*, too: curating Instagram posts that radiated “healing,” scheduling therapy like a quarterly review, planning my travels down to the hour. But on that bus—swaying, sweating, watching mist rise off the river—I felt something unfamiliar: the ground dissolving beneath me. Not in a terrifying way, but like stepping off a curb you didn’t know was there. My carefully constructed narrative—*I am the competent one, the planner, the one who holds things together*—began to fray at the edges. And when it did, something else seeped in: quiet. Not emptiness. Just space.  

That afternoon in Luang Prabang, I got lost. Not metaphorically. Literally. I’d misread my map (a paper one, because I’d sworn off screens as “distractions”), turned down a lane of moss-covered stone steps, and emerged not at the Kuang Si Falls, but in a sun-dappled courtyard where monks were sweeping fallen frangipani blossoms. No Wi-Fi. No translation app. Just the soft *shush-shush* of brooms and the scent of incense. A young monk noticed my confusion, smiled, and silently handed me a small, cool bottle of water. He didn’t offer directions. He just sat beside me on the step, watching dragonflies skim a lotus pond. Ten minutes passed in silence. Then he pointed—not to a street sign, but to the light filtering through the banyan leaves—and said, “You are here. That is enough.”  

It wasn’t wisdom I’d sought. It was permission—to be unmoored, to not know, to trust that presence mattered more than progress.  

What I Learned (and What I Wish Someone Had Told Me):  
1. Grief doesn’t need a GPS. Traveling after divorce isn’t about ticking off destinations; it’s about allowing yourself to be disoriented. Get lost on purpose. Take the wrong turn. Sit in the wrong café. Let your body recalibrate to uncertainty—it’s the first step in rebuilding intuition. Your old compass (the one calibrated to “what keeps the peace” or “what looks good”) is broken. Don’t rush to replace it.  

2. The most healing conversations happen without words. Nang’s rice, the monk’s water, the shared silence on that step—they weren’t about fixing me. They were about witnessing. Seek out people who don’t ask “How are you *really*?” but instead offer tea, a spare seat, or a glance that says, *I see you’re human, and that’s enough.* You’ll find them in markets, hostels, temple courtyards—not in self-help seminars.  

3. Control is a habit, not a necessity. I kept trying to schedule “healing moments”: sunrise meditation, journaling at 6 a.m., daily gratitude lists. But healing arrived in the unplanned—the sudden rainstorm that soaked me on the way to Wat Xieng Thong, forcing me to laugh as I huddled under a tarp with strangers; the accidental language mix-up that made a street vendor roar with delight. Release the agenda. Let joy surprise you. Let discomfort linger. Both are teachers.  

4. Your body remembers before your mind catches up. That first night in Luang Prabang, I slept deeply—not because I’d “processed” anything, but because I’d walked 12 kilometers, eaten food that tasted like childhood summers, and breathed air thick with night-blooming cereus. Movement, taste, breath: these are your oldest therapists. Prioritize them over analysis. Walk until your legs ache. Eat something that makes you close your eyes. Breathe in, counting four; hold, counting four; exhale, counting six. Do it three times. That’s enough.  

The bus to Luang Prabang didn’t take me anywhere I’d planned. It took me *out* of the story I’d been telling myself—that healing was linear, that strength meant stoicism, that love required permanence. It taught me that sometimes, the bravest thing isn’t packing your bags and leaving. It’s sitting on a sun-warmed step, accepting a bottle of water, and whispering to yourself, *Yes. I am here. And that is enough.*  

I still carry Nang’s words in my pocket, folded small: *Slow hands. Fast heart makes slow hands shake.* I unfold them often—not to fix the shaking, but to remember: the tremor isn’t failure. It’s the sound of something old letting go, so something true can finally settle in.

title: minimalism and focus book|clearing your desk, your inbox and your calendar
text:
Imagine for a moment the peace and clarity that comes with a clear desk, an empty inbox, and a spacious calendar. It's not just about having less; it's about creating the space you need to focus on what truly matters. Let's dive into how you can achieve this, step by step.

Start with your desk. The surface of your desk is a reflection of your mind. If it's cluttered, chances are your thoughts are, too. Begin by removing everything from your desk. Yes, everything. This might seem drastic, but it's the most effective way to start fresh. As you place each item back, ask yourself: "Do I really need this here? Does it serve a purpose in my daily work?" Be ruthless. Keep only what you use regularly and what brings you joy or inspiration. For everything else, find a new home or let it go. A clear desk sets the stage for a clear mind, allowing you to focus on the task at hand without distractions.

Next, tackle your inbox. Your email can be a bottomless pit if you're not careful. Start by unsubscribing from newsletters and promotional emails that no longer add value to your life. Use filters and folders to organize incoming messages, so you can quickly sort through them. Set aside specific times during the day to check and respond to emails, rather than constantly interrupting your workflow. When you open an email, decide right then whether to delete it, archive it, or take action. The goal is to keep your inbox as close to zero as possible. This way, you won't feel overwhelmed by a never-ending list of unread messages, and you'll be able to give your full attention to the important ones.

Now, let's move on to your calendar. Your time is precious, and your calendar should reflect that. Take a hard look at your schedule and identify any commitments that don't align with your priorities. Are there meetings you can decline or delegate? Are there tasks that can be batched together to save time? Block out time for deep work, where you can focus on your most important projects without interruptions. Also, make sure to schedule breaks and downtime. Overbooking yourself leads to burnout, and a cluttered calendar can be just as stressful as a cluttered desk. By being intentional about how you spend your time, you create more space for meaningful activities and personal growth.

As you clear your desk, inbox, and calendar, you'll notice a shift in your mindset. You'll feel lighter, more focused, and more in control of your life. But remember, minimalism is a journey, not a destination. It's about making conscious choices every day to simplify and prioritize. Regularly review these areas to ensure they remain uncluttered and aligned with your goals.

In the end, the benefits of a clear desk, inbox, and calendar extend far beyond just physical and digital spaces. They free up mental and emotional energy, allowing you to live a more intentional and fulfilling life. So, take a deep breath, roll up your sleeves, and start clearing. The clarity and peace you seek are within reach.

title: entrepreneurship book|launching a small business with almost no money
text:
I launched my first “business” from a folding card table in my garage, selling hand-stitched dog bandanas I’d made using fabric scraps from my grandmother’s attic and a sewing machine that sounded like a disgruntled badger. My startup capital? $12.73—mostly in quarters I’d saved from vending machines—and the stubborn belief that someone, somewhere, would pay $8 for a polka-dot bowtie that *also* doubled as a mild anxiety soother for their terrier. Spoiler: They did. Three people did. One of them cried (happy tears, I think? Or maybe she was allergic to polyester). Point is: you don’t need seed funding, an MBA, or even a working Wi-Fi password to start something real.

Let me be clear—I’m not one of those “hustle porn” gurus who tells you to wake up at 4:17 a.m., cold-email 93 venture capitalists before breakfast, and monetize your grief. I once tried to cold-email a VC. He replied, “Are you the person who sent me three emails titled ‘URGENT: DOG BANDANA OPPORTUNITY’?” I apologized. He blocked me. Lesson learned: passion is great. Obsession with punctuation is… less great.

Here’s what actually worked when I had less money than most people keep in loose change on their nightstand:

1. Sell before you build. Not “build a prototype,” not “finalize the branding.” Literally post a photo of your idea scribbled on a napkin with a price and a PayPal link. I did this for my second venture—a line of snack-sized gratitude journals. Posted it on Instagram with the caption: “This doesn’t exist yet. But if 10 people pre-order, I’ll make it. No refunds. Just vibes and ink.” Ten people said yes. So I bought one notebook, cut it into thirds, glued on paper covers I printed at the library (free color printing day = my patron saint), and shipped them in reused Amazon boxes lined with doodles. Profit? $3.50. Confidence? Infinite.

2. Barter like your Wi-Fi depends on it. My web designer didn’t take cash. She took three sourdough loaves and one very sincere voicemail about how her childhood smelled like cinnamon and flour. My photographer accepted a custom playlist titled *“Songs That Make You Feel Like You’re in a French Film (But Also Slightly Tired).”* People love trading value—not just dollars. It builds relationships *and* keeps your bank account from looking like a ghost town with one confused dollar bill wandering around.

3. Use free tools like they’re your emotional support apps. Canva isn’t just for birthday invites—it’s your brand identity, your pitch deck, your “I swear I’m a real business” LinkedIn banner. Google Forms? Your CRM, your survey tool, your “please tell me why you didn’t buy” confessional booth. Gmail + a catchy subject line (“Your dog’s bandana is judging your life choices—here’s why”) can outperform a $5,000 email platform any day.

I once spent three hours trying to design a logo in Adobe Illustrator. Then I opened Canva, typed “rustic minimalist coffee shop logo,” dragged a font I liked, added a tiny steam swirl over a cup, and called it done. A local café used it for six months before hiring a “real” designer. Their barista told me, “It looks like it knows where the good beans come from.” That’s all the validation you need.

Also: embrace the cringe. Your first website will have Comic Sans. Your first Instagram story will say “ORDER NOW!!!” with three exclamation points and a dancing hotdog GIF. Good. That’s proof you showed up. Perfection is the enemy of “I just sold something to a human.”

And please—don’t wait for permission. No one gives you the keys to entrepreneurship. You just jimmy the lock with a bobby pin, a prayer, and the sudden realization that your neighbor’s toddler loves your homemade lavender bath bombs *so much* she now refers to you as “Bath Lady.” That’s your first investor. That’s your first board meeting. That’s your first revenue stream disguised as a very sticky hug.

You don’t need money. You need curiosity, a willingness to look slightly ridiculous, and the guts to ship something—even if it’s just a napkin sketch with a dream stapled to the corner. The rest? Shows up. Usually after you’ve already started. Usually while you’re Googling “how to fix a jammed printer at 2 a.m.”  

Go make something. Even if it’s small. Even if it’s weird. Especially if it’s weird. The world needs more weirdly wonderful things—and fewer perfectly polished slideshows about disruption. Now go. And if your first sale is a friend who says, “I’ll take two—just don’t tell my partner I spent money on this,” congratulations. You’re officially in business. Welcome to the beautiful, broke, brilliant mess.

title: personal finance book for young adults|automating your savings so you never have to think about it
text:
Let’s talk about the most boring-sounding superpower you’ll ever acquire: automating your savings. I know, I know—“automating” sounds like something your dad does with his spreadsheet and a thermos of lukewarm coffee. But hear me out. This isn’t about discipline. It’s not about willpower. It’s about *designing your life so that saving happens whether you’re feeling inspired, exhausted, or three shots deep into an espresso at 2 a.m.  

Here’s my confession: I didn’t automate my savings until I was 27—and I had a finance degree. Yes, really. I’d write motivational sticky notes (“Save $200 this month!”), track every latte in an app, and pat myself on the back when I remembered to transfer money *manually*. Then came the week my laptop died, my roommate moved out unexpectedly, and I got hit with a $387 car repair bill. I scrambled. I overdrew my account. I ate ramen for six days straight—not the fun kind with soft-boiled eggs, the sad, salty kind from a plastic cup. That’s when it clicked: I wasn’t failing at saving. I was failing at *system design*. My brain wasn’t built to remember transfers on the 1st *and* the 15th *and* to adjust when rent went up. But my bank? Oh, it’s *excellent* at repetition.  

So I set it up—once—and never touched it again. Here’s how simple it actually is:  

First, pick *one* number. Not “I’ll save when I can.” Not “5% of my paycheck”—that’s vague and easy to ignore. Pick a real, concrete amount. For most young adults starting out, $25–$75 per paycheck is shockingly painless. (Yes, even if you’re making $18/hour. Try it for one month—you’ll forget it’s gone.) I started with $40 every two weeks. That’s less than two movie tickets. Less than one “fancy” avocado toast order.  

Then, log into your bank—or better yet, open your banking app right now while you’re reading this. Look for “recurring transfer,” “auto-save,” or “round-up” (more on that in a sec). Set it to move that $40 *the day after payday hits*. Not on payday—*after*. Why? Because your paycheck lands, you breathe, you check your balance, and *then* the money vanishes before you even consider spending it. It’s psychological magic: you never feel the loss because you never technically “had” it.  

I did this with my checking account → my high-yield savings account (yes, open one—it pays 4–5% APY right now, not 0.01%. Google “Ally” or “Capital One 360”—they take 90 seconds and zero fees). Within six months, I had $1,040 sitting there—not from sacrifice, but from silence. No decisions. No guilt. Just… there.  

And don’t sleep on round-ups. My favorite trick? Link your debit card to an app like Acorns or Chime—they automatically round every purchase to the nearest dollar and stash the difference. Bought coffee for $3.65? $0.35 goes to savings. Ordered groceries for $42.18? $0.82 disappears into your future self’s wallet. Sounds tiny—until you realize it’s $20–$40 *per month*, no effort required. I’ve seen friends add over $500 in a year just from coffee and gas.  

One last thing: automate *first*, not last. Your paycheck should be split *before* it hits your main account—if your employer offers direct deposit splitting, use it. Send 90% to checking, 10% straight to savings. Boom. Out of sight, out of mind, out of temptation.  

This isn’t about becoming rich tomorrow. It’s about building a quiet, reliable safety net—one that grows while you’re binge-watching shows, stressing about work emails, or sleeping. You won’t feel heroic doing it. You won’t post about it on Instagram. But one day—maybe when your AC breaks in July or your dog needs an unexpected vet visit—you’ll log in, see that number, and whisper, “Oh. Right. I’m okay.”  

That’s the gift of automation: it turns “I hope I save” into “I already did.” And honestly? That tiny shift—the one where you stop relying on motivation and start trusting systems—that’s where financial adulthood truly begins. So go do it now. Seriously. Pause this book. Open your phone. Set up *one* automatic transfer. Then come back. I’ll wait. You’ve got this.

title: happiness and meditation guide|a ten-minute daily breathing practice for beginners
text:
Chapter 5: Finding My Breath, Finding Myself

When I first started my journey into meditation, I was a ball of stress and anxiety. My days were filled with endless to-do lists, back-to-back meetings, and a constant feeling that I was running out of time. I often found myself gasping for air, both literally and metaphorically. It was during one particularly overwhelming week that I stumbled upon the concept of a ten-minute daily breathing practice. Little did I know, this simple act would become the cornerstone of my mindfulness journey and a key to unlocking a more balanced and joyful life.

 The Day Everything Changed

It was a chilly autumn morning, and I had just arrived at my office. As I sat down at my desk, I felt a familiar knot in my stomach. The emails were piling up, and my calendar was packed. I decided to take a moment to catch my breath, but instead of diving straight into work, I remembered an article I had read about the benefits of deep breathing. Curious and desperate for some relief, I decided to give it a try.

I closed my eyes, took a deep breath in through my nose, and slowly exhaled through my mouth. I repeated this a few times, and as I did, I noticed something remarkable: the knot in my stomach began to loosen, and my mind started to quiet down. For the first time in a long while, I felt a sense of calm. That day, I made a commitment to myself: I would set aside ten minutes every day for this simple yet powerful practice.

 The Ten-Minute Daily Breathing Practice

The beauty of a ten-minute breathing practice is its simplicity and accessibility. You don't need any special equipment or a quiet room; you can do it anywhere, whether you're sitting at your desk, on a park bench, or even in your car. Here’s how you can start:

1. Find a Comfortable Seat:
   - Sit in a comfortable position, either on a chair or on the floor. Make sure your back is straight but not rigid. If you’re using a chair, place your feet flat on the ground.
   
2. Set a Timer:
   - Set a timer for ten minutes. This will help you stay focused and ensure you don’t get lost in thought.
   
3. Close Your Eyes:
   - Gently close your eyes and take a moment to settle in. Allow your body to relax and your mind to begin to quiet.

4. Focus on Your Breath:
   - Bring your attention to your breath. Notice the sensation of the air entering and leaving your nostrils. Feel the rise and fall of your chest or the expansion and contraction of your belly.
   
5. Deep Breaths:
   - Take a slow, deep breath in through your nose, filling your lungs completely. Hold it for a moment, then exhale slowly through your mouth. Repeat this process, focusing on the rhythm and depth of your breath.
   
6. Counting Breaths:
   - If your mind starts to wander, which it likely will, gently bring your focus back to your breath. You can also count your breaths to help maintain concentration. Count each inhale and exhale as one breath, and continue up to ten. When you reach ten, start over again.
   
7. Embrace the Journey:
   - Don’t be too hard on yourself if your mind wanders. This is natural, especially when you’re starting out. Each time you notice your mind drifting, simply acknowledge it and return to your breath. Over time, you’ll find it easier to stay focused.

8. End with Gratitude:
   - When the timer goes off, take a moment to express gratitude. Thank yourself for taking this time to care for your well-being. Slowly open your eyes and take a deep, refreshing breath before continuing with your day.

 Making It a Habit

In the beginning, I struggled to make this practice a habit. There were days when I skipped it, thinking I didn’t have the time. But I soon realized that those were the days I needed it the most. To make it stick, I integrated it into my morning routine, right after my cup of coffee. This small, consistent change made a world of difference.

To help you build this habit, consider these tips:

- Schedule It:
  - Put it in your calendar and treat it like any other important appointment. Consistency is key.
  
- Create a Cue:
  - Use a cue to trigger your practice, such as finishing your morning coffee or brushing your teeth.
  
- Be Kind to Yourself:
  - If you miss a day, don’t beat yourself up. Just pick it up the next day and keep going.

- Track Your Progress:
  - Keep a journal or use an app to track your progress. Seeing how far you’ve come can be a great motivator.

 The Transformative Power of Breath

Over the weeks and months, I noticed profound changes in my life. The ten-minute breathing practice became a sanctuary, a place where I could find peace and clarity. My stress levels decreased, my sleep improved, and I felt more present and engaged in my daily activities. I also found that I was better able to handle challenges and setbacks, approaching them with a calmer and more centered mindset.

One of the most beautiful things about this practice is that it’s accessible to everyone, regardless of their experience with meditation. It doesn’t require any special skills or knowledge—just a willingness to breathe and be present. And in that presence, you’ll find a deeper connection to yourself and the world around you.

As you embark on this journey, remember that the path to happiness and inner peace is a personal one. There will be ups and downs, but with each breath, you’ll be one step closer to a more joyful and mindful life. So, take a deep breath, and let’s begin.

title: small-business marketing guide|getting your first hundred customers through word of mouth
text:
You’ve built something real—maybe a handmade product, a local service, or a simple digital tool—and now you’re staring at the quiet reality of an empty inbox and zero sales. That’s okay. Your first hundred customers won’t come from ads, SEO, or viral posts. They’ll come from people talking—specifically, people talking *about you* to people they trust. Word of mouth isn’t magic. It’s intentional, human, and entirely within your control—even as a solo founder or tiny team.

Start where you already are: with the people who know you. Not your followers on social media—your actual friends, neighbors, former coworkers, classmates, and family. These aren’t “leads.” They’re humans who’ve seen you show up consistently, who know your values, and who’d genuinely root for you. Tell them *why* you started—not just what you sell, but what problem you’re solving and who it’s for. Be specific: “I made these reusable lunch wraps because my kid’s school banned single-use plastic, and I couldn’t find anything that actually stayed sealed and washed well.” That kind of clarity makes people remember you—and more importantly, *pass it on*.

But here’s the critical part: don’t ask for a sale. Ask for help instead. Say, “I’m testing this with a small group right now—I’d love your honest feedback after you try it,” or “If you know one person who struggles with [specific problem], would you mind introducing us?” People want to be useful. They don’t want to feel like walking billboards. When you invite them into your process—not just your pitch—you turn them into collaborators, not just customers.

Make it easy for them to talk about you. That means giving them language—not slogans, but simple, relatable phrases they can use naturally. Instead of “We offer premium eco-friendly solutions,” try “It’s the only thing I’ve found that keeps my sandwich from getting soggy *and* doesn’t end up in the landfill.” Help them tell your story in their voice. Also, make sharing frictionless: include a short, personal note with every order (“Thanks for trusting me—feel free to forward this email to anyone else who hates soggy sandwiches too”), or tuck a handwritten thank-you card inside a package with space for them to jot down a friend’s name and number if they’d like you to reach out.

Deliver more than expected—every single time. Not through flashy extras, but through reliability, warmth, and attention. Reply to emails within 24 hours—even if it’s just “Got it, working on this and will update you Thursday.” Fix mistakes quickly and openly. If a package arrives late, send a small replacement *with* a note explaining what happened and how you’re fixing it. People don’t tell stories about perfect transactions. They tell stories about how you showed up when things got messy.

Track what’s working—not with dashboards, but with notes. After each conversation, write down: Who referred whom? What phrase did they use? What question did they ask? What made them pause or lean in? You’ll start seeing patterns: maybe teachers refer other teachers, or parents always mention school policies first. That tells you where to focus your energy next—not on casting a wider net, but on deepening those early connections.

And finally—celebrate publicly, but personally. When someone refers a customer, don’t just say “thanks.” Name them (with permission), share a tiny detail about why their referral mattered (“Sarah sent over Maya, who’s starting her own bakery—so now we’re brainstorming custom wrap sizes!”), and send something tangible: a gift card, a sample of your next product, or even just a photo of you holding a sign that says “Thank you, Sarah!” People refer others because they want to feel proud—not paid.

Your first hundred customers won’t arrive all at once. They’ll trickle in—one, two, five at a time—each one carrying your name into a new circle. That’s how trust spreads. Not through scale, but through sincerity. Not through noise, but through noticing. You don’t need to go viral. You just need to be the person someone remembers—and recommends—when the right moment comes. Start today. Pick up the phone. Send that message. Handwrite that note. Your word-of-mouth engine isn’t waiting for perfect conditions. It starts with you, showing up—real, humble, and ready to listen.

title: startup memoir|the early days of a search-engine company and its odd culture
text:
I joined SearchHive on a Tuesday. Not because I believed in the mission—“democratizing intent”—but because my laptop was held together with duct tape and existential dread, and their offer included free kombucha on tap *and* a standing desk that doubled as a very aggressive yoga instructor. (It beeped at you every twenty minutes: “BREATHING IS OPTIONAL. POSTURE IS NOT.”)

The office smelled like burnt toast, lavender oil, and the faint, metallic tang of desperation. Our CEO, Leo, wore noise-canceling headphones *inside* the office—“to simulate focus,” he claimed—while simultaneously live-tweeting his own lunch break. (“Just ate ½ avocado + 3 almonds. The algorithm *knows* I’m optimizing for satiety. Also, slightly jealous of my intern’s hair.”) His Slack status read: “In deep thought (or possibly napping). Ping only if your idea has >70% chance of being featured in TechCrunch’s ‘Most Likely to Be Acquired by Google’ list.”

We had no product. Just a whiteboard covered in phrases like “query gravity,” “semantic honeycomb,” and “what if Bing… but *nicer*?” One Friday, we spent four hours debating whether our logo should be a bee, a hive, or a *very polite wasp*. We settled on a hexagon that subtly winked when you squinted leftward. It didn’t do anything. But it *felt* disruptive.

Culture? Oh, we had culture. We called it “Intentional Chaos™.” Every Monday began with “Gratitude Lightning Round”: each person shared one thing they were grateful for *and* one thing they deeply resented about the previous week. My first time: “Grateful for the ergonomic keyboard. Resentful that Dave from DevOps renamed our staging server ‘Dumbledore’ and now nothing deploys without saying ‘I solemnly swear I am up to no good.’” (He did. And yes, it worked.)

We had no HR department—just Maya, who also managed the snack budget and once negotiated a severance package using interpretive dance. She told me, mid-pirouette, “Your equity is vesting, but your soul is *accelerating*.” I nodded. I had no idea what that meant. I ate three gummy bears and moved on.

Our search engine didn’t return results. It returned *vibes*. Type “how to fix a leaky faucet,” and you’d get:  
- A haiku about water pressure  
- A 90-second ASMR recording of dripping  
- A link to a podcast episode where two plumbers debated existentialism  
- And, buried at the bottom, in 6-point font: “Try tightening the valve clockwise.”  

Users loved it—or at least, they tweeted about how confused they were, which counted as engagement in our KPI dashboard (which also displayed “Serendipity Score” and “Confusion-to-Curiosity Ratio”).

Here’s what I learned—not from any manual (we didn’t have manuals), but from surviving six months of espresso-fueled sprint retrospectives where someone inevitably cried over a broken React hook:

1. Hire for weirdness compatibility, not just skill. We once hired a candidate because she could recite the periodic table backward *while juggling*. Turned out she was also our best backend engineer. Coincidence? Or proof that lithium-ion batteries and lithium are spiritually aligned? We never checked.

2. If your onboarding doc is longer than War and Peace, you’ve already failed. Ours was three bullet points:  
   - The kombucha is fermented, not judgmental.  
   - Your manager is probably in a silent meditation retreat. Slack them anyway. They’ll reply with a GIF of a sloth blinking slowly.  
   - If you see Leo whispering to the thermostat, walk away. Do not make eye contact.

3. Celebrate failure like it’s a Grammy. We had “Glory-in-the-Glitch” Fridays. Last quarter, our entire homepage rendered as ASCII art of a crying badger. We threw confetti. Made merch. The badger became our unofficial mascot. (Its name: Reginald. His LinkedIn headline: “Disrupted. Disoriented. Deeply committed to semantic clarity.”)

By month seven, we had 12 users, 3 of whom were interns’ moms, and zero revenue. But we *did* have a cult following on niche Reddit threads—and a surprisingly functional autocomplete that occasionally predicted your thoughts *before* you typed them. (Turns out, typing “why is my…” almost always led to “why is my life like this.” The algorithm had empathy. Or low self-esteem. Hard to tell.)

I left SearchHive last spring—to write this book, ironically titled *How to Build Something That Doesn’t Quite Work (But Feels Like It Should)*. Leo sent me off with a custom NFT of our winking hexagon and a handwritten note: “You didn’t quit. You *de-optimized*.”  

I framed it. It still winks. Sometimes, at 3 a.m., I swear it blinks back.  

And honestly? That might be the most accurate search result I’ve ever gotten.

Chapter 7: Building a Company Culture Around Delivering Happiness

You know, I've always been fascinated by the idea of happiness. It's like this magical, elusive thing that everyone chases but few truly catch. But what if we could make it a core part of our business? What if, instead of just selling products or services, we focused on delivering happiness? That’s exactly what I set out to do when I started my journey with HappyTech, and let me tell you, it’s been nothing short of transformative.

Let me share a story with you. A few years ago, we had a customer named Sarah. Sarah was going through a rough patch—she’d just lost her job, and her car broke down on the way to an important interview. She called us in desperation, needing a quick fix for her laptop, which she needed for the interview. Now, we could have just fixed her laptop and sent her on her way, but we decided to go the extra mile. We not only fixed her laptop, but we also arranged for a ride to her interview, and even threw in a little gift card to help with lunch. Sarah got the job, and she later told us that our small act of kindness made all the difference in a really tough time. That’s the kind of impact I want every customer to feel.

But how do you build a company culture around delivering happiness? It starts with your team. You can’t deliver happiness externally if you’re not fostering it internally. So, the first step is to create an environment where your employees are happy and fulfilled. At HappyTech, we’ve implemented a few key practices that have made a huge difference:

1. Empowerment: We give our team the autonomy to make decisions and solve problems on their own. This not only makes them more engaged but also allows them to be more creative in how they interact with customers. For example, one of our support agents, Alex, once used his discretion to send a bouquet of flowers to a customer who was having a bad day. The customer was so touched, she became a lifelong fan of our brand.

2. Recognition: We celebrate the small wins and the big ones. Whether it’s a shout-out in a company meeting or a special reward, recognizing and appreciating our team members goes a long way. When people feel valued, they’re more likely to go above and beyond for customers.

3. Training and Development: We invest in our team’s growth. Regular training sessions, workshops, and opportunities for career advancement show that we care about their future. One of our employees, Lisa, started as a junior support agent and, with our support, worked her way up to become a team leader. Her success story is a testament to the power of investing in your people.

4. Fun and Laughter: We don’t take ourselves too seriously. We believe that work should be enjoyable, and we find ways to inject fun into our daily routines. From office pranks to monthly themed days, we make sure there’s always a reason to smile. A happy workplace translates to happy customers.

5. Customer-Centric Mindset: Finally, we make sure that every decision we make is centered around the customer. We ask ourselves, “How will this make our customers happier?” Whether it’s improving our product, enhancing our service, or just being more responsive, the customer is always at the heart of what we do.

Building a company culture around delivering happiness isn’t just a nice-to-have; it’s a must-have in today’s competitive landscape. It’s about creating a ripple effect of positivity that starts with your team and extends to your customers. And trust me, the results are worth it. When your customers are happy, they become loyal advocates, and that’s the best marketing you can get.

So, start today. Think about how you can bring a little more joy to your team and your customers. Because, at the end of the day, happiness is the ultimate currency.

title: relationships advice book|staying faithful and keeping a long marriage alive
text:
Look. I’m not going to tell you fidelity is about white-knuckling temptation or reciting vows like a rosary while your spouse snores beside you. That’s how marriages die—quietly, with good intentions and zero oxygen.  

Let me say this plainly: after 27 years married (yes, *27*—not “nearly three decades,” not “a long time”—*27*, with a mortgage, two grown kids who still borrow my credit card, and a dog who pees on the rug when he’s anxious), I can tell you what keeps people faithful—and it’s not willpower. It’s *habit*. The kind you build like calluses: slow, unglamorous, slightly painful at first.  

You think cheating starts with an affair? Nah. It starts with the *third* time you scroll through Instagram instead of asking your partner how their awful day went. It starts with skipping the weekly grocery run *together*—the one where you bicker about avocados and end up laughing in Aisle 5—and doing it solo *again*. That’s the real infidelity: the slow, daily withdrawal of attention. Dr. John Gottman’s research nails it: couples who stay together long-term average *5.1 positive interactions for every 1 negative one*. Not 2:1. Not even 3:1. *5.1*. That’s not magic—that’s showing up *with your damn eyes open* during breakfast, even when you’re hungover and the coffee’s cold.  

And don’t give me that “we’re just comfortable” crap. Comfort without curiosity is a coffin with velvet lining. My husband and I still have *one* rule we’ve kept since Year 3: no phones at the dinner table. Not “sometimes.” Not “unless it’s urgent.” *Never.* We’ve broken it maybe six times in 27 years—once when my mom was in the ER, once when our daughter called from Paris at 3 a.m. with a flat tire and existential dread. Otherwise? Phones go face-down. Even if we’re just eating takeout on the couch watching *The Great British Bake Off* and saying nothing for twenty minutes. That silence? That’s *ours*. Not empty. *Shared.*  

Sex? Yeah, let’s talk about it. Because here’s the blunt truth nobody puts on a greeting card: desire doesn’t “just happen” after 20 years. It gets *scheduled*. Not like a dentist appointment—“Tuesday, 8 p.m., please wear socks”—but with intention. We have a stupid little ritual: every Sunday night, over cheap red wine and whatever’s thawing in the freezer, we ask each other *one* question: “What made you feel seen this week?” Not “How was work?” Not “Did the kid pass the test?” *Seen.* And if the answer’s “nothing,” we dig. Gently. Without blame. Because feeling unseen is where loneliness takes root—and loneliness is the 1 breeding ground for emotional affairs.  

Also? Stop pretending you’re “too busy” to fight well. You *will* argue. You’ll snap over who left the toothpaste cap off *again*. But here’s the number that changed everything for us: *20 minutes*. If a fight escalates past 20 minutes—voices raised, names implied, old wounds dragged out—we *stop*. Not “I need space.” Not “Fine, whatever.” We say: “I love you. This isn’t working right now. Let’s pause. Come back in 20.” Then we do. Every. Single. Time. No exceptions. Turns out, most “irreconcilable differences” are just arguments that ran too long on empty tanks.  

And listen—I know you’re tired. I know your partner forgets to replace the toilet paper roll *and* mispronounces your best friend’s name *and* still thinks cilantro tastes like soap. Good. That’s *real*. That’s marriage—not some curated highlight reel. Fidelity isn’t about perfection. It’s about choosing, *daily*, to hold the messy, flawed, stubborn, hilarious, infuriating person you married—even when you’d rather binge *Succession* and cry into a bag of pretzels.  

That choice? It’s not grand. It’s small. It’s showing up for the boring stuff. It’s remembering how they take their tea. It’s saying “I’m sorry” before you’re fully convinced you’re wrong. It’s touching their shoulder when they’re stressed, even if your own shoulders ache.  

Don’t wait for passion to return like a prodigal son. Light the damn match yourself. Again. And again. And again.  

(Oh—and if you’re reading this while Googling “how to tell if my spouse is cheating”? Put the phone down. Go find them. Ask: “What’s one thing I haven’t noticed about you lately?” Then *shut up* and listen. For longer than feels comfortable.)

title: customer-service business book|building a company culture around delivering happiness
text:
You are not in the business of selling products or processing transactions. You are in the business of delivering happiness—and that changes everything. From the moment a new hire walks through your door to the final resolution of a customer’s issue, every decision you make either builds or erodes a culture rooted in genuine human connection and emotional impact. This isn’t idealism. It’s operational strategy. And it starts with you—your language, your priorities, your daily choices.

First, recognize that happiness isn’t vague or fluffy. In your service context, it’s concrete: the relief in a customer’s voice when their problem is solved before they even ask for help; the quiet pride a team member feels after turning a frustrated caller into an advocate; the shared laugh between colleagues who just pulled off something extraordinary for someone else. Happiness lives in those micro-moments—and your job is to notice them, name them, and multiply them.

That begins with how you talk about work. Stop saying “customer satisfaction scores.” Start saying “moments of human connection.” Stop framing service as “handling tickets” and start framing it as “making someone’s day better.” Language shapes perception—and perception drives behavior. When your team hears “We’re here to deliver happiness,” they don’t wait for permission to go the extra mile. They look for opportunities to do it instinctively.

Hiring is where culture is truly set—not in the mission statement on the wall, but in who you choose to invite into your circle. Ask candidates not just “What would you do if a customer yelled at you?” but “Tell me about a time you made someone feel seen, especially when they didn’t expect it.” Look for empathy in action—not just sympathy in theory. Then train relentlessly—not on scripts, but on emotional intelligence: listening without planning your reply, naming feelings before solving problems, knowing when to pause instead of rushing to fix.

And here’s what many leaders miss: you cannot sustain a happiness-centered culture without protecting your people’s well-being. Burnout kills joy faster than any angry email. That means honoring boundaries—not just with policies, but with visible leadership. When you leave at 5:30 p.m. to pick up your child, and you say aloud, “I’m choosing presence over productivity right now”—you signal that humanity matters more than hustle. When you cancel a meeting because your team is overwhelmed, and you say, “Let’s protect our energy so we can show up fully tomorrow”—you prove that caring for your people isn’t optional. It’s the foundation.

Recognition must be frequent, specific, and human—not just “Great job!” but “I saw how you stayed calm when that call escalated, asked three clarifying questions, and then offered a solution that saved the customer two hours. That wasn’t just skill—that was kindness in motion.” Celebrate effort as much as outcome. Highlight acts of collaboration over solo wins. Spotlight the person who quietly coached a teammate, not just the one who hit quota.

When things go wrong—and they will—respond with transparency and humility, not defensiveness. A customer complaint isn’t a failure to hide; it’s data, delivered with emotion, about where your system or empathy fell short. Gather the team, listen first, ask “What did this teach us about what really matters to people?”, and act—not to avoid blame, but to deepen trust. That kind of accountability doesn’t weaken authority—it strengthens credibility.

Finally, remember: culture isn’t built in quarterly workshops. It’s built in the 12 seconds it takes you to make eye contact with a team member passing in the hall and ask, “How are you *really* doing?” It’s built when you personally follow up on a tough case—not to audit, but to learn and support. It’s built when you share stories—not just of success, but of missteps and what you learned about people, about patience, about what happiness actually requires.

You are shaping something far bigger than a service department. You’re shaping how people experience being human at work—and how they, in turn, shape others’ experiences of being human in the world. That’s not a side effect of your business. It’s your legacy. So ask yourself today—not “Did we resolve the issue?” but “Did someone walk away feeling lighter, safer, or more hopeful than when they started?” Because that’s not just good service. That’s the work that lasts.

title: startup memoir|the early days of a search-engine company and its odd culture
text:
Back in the day, when the internet was still figuring itself out, I found myself at the heart of a startup that would eventually become one of the world’s most used search engines. It was a wild ride, and looking back, I can’t help but chuckle at how naive and hopeful we all were. We were like kids in a candy store, except the candy was code, and the store was an office filled with bean bags and whiteboards.

The company was called SearchSavvy, and it started in a garage, as so many tech legends do. The founders, two brothers, had this crazy idea to make searching the web not just functional, but fun. They were the kind of guys who wore matching t-shirts and could finish each other’s sentences. I joined them as their first non-technical hire, tasked with making sure our brand had a personality. Easy enough, right?

One of the first things I noticed was the odd culture. For starters, everyone had a nickname. Mine was “The Scribe,” which made me feel both important and like a character from a fantasy novel. The brothers were “The Brain” and “The Heart,” which pretty much summed up their roles. There was also a guy named “The Wizard” because he could conjure up solutions to any coding problem. It was like working in a superhero team, minus the capes and spandex.

We had these weekly meetings called “Dream Sessions.” These weren’t your typical boring updates; they were brainstorming sessions where no idea was too silly. One time, someone suggested we create a search engine for aliens. The Brain actually wrote down the idea and said, “Let’s think about it!” That’s the kind of place it was—where every crazy idea had a chance to be heard.

Of course, there were challenges. Funding was tight, and we often worked late into the night, fueled by pizza and energy drinks. But those long nights turned into some of the best memories. We’d play impromptu games of table tennis or have dance-offs to break the tension. I remember one night, The Heart decided we needed a mascot, so he brought in a stuffed penguin. We named it “Penny” and it became our unofficial stress-reliever. Whenever someone was stuck on a problem, they’d give Penny a squeeze, and somehow, it helped.

Here are a few tips I picked up during those early days:

1. Embrace the weird. A unique culture can be a powerful motivator. Don’t be afraid to let your team’s quirks shine.
2. Listen to everyone. Even the craziest ideas can lead to breakthroughs. Create a space where everyone feels heard.
3. Find your Penny. Sometimes, a little bit of whimsy can go a long way in reducing stress and fostering creativity.

As we grew, the office moved from the garage to a small building downtown. The bean bags were replaced with chairs, and the whiteboards got bigger. But the spirit stayed the same. We were still a bunch of dreamers, trying to make the internet a better place, one search at a time.

Looking back, I realize that the success of SearchSavvy wasn’t just about the technology. It was about the people, the culture, and the willingness to embrace the odd and the wonderful. And maybe, just maybe, it was a little bit about Penny, the penguin who kept us grounded and reminded us to have fun along the way.

title: personal memoir with life lessons|a year of travel after a painful divorce
text:
It was March. I stood in my empty apartment—well, *mostly* empty—staring at a single cardboard box labeled “Kitchen (Maybe?)” in shaky Sharpie. My wedding ring sat in a Ziploc bag on the counter beside a half-eaten granola bar and a brochure for Bali I’d printed three months earlier, back when “divorce” still felt like a theoretical weather system—distant, ominous, but not yet raining on my head.

I’d spent twelve years building a life with someone who stopped seeing me around year seven. The divorce wasn’t explosive—it was slow, quiet, and deeply lonely, like watching your own reflection fade from a fogged-up mirror. By the time the papers were signed, I didn’t feel free. I felt hollowed out. Like I’d been living in a beautifully furnished house I hadn’t realized was haunted—not by ghosts, but by all the versions of myself I’d quietly buried to keep the peace.

So I booked a one-way ticket to Lisbon. No itinerary. No expectations. Just a backpack, a terrible phrasebook, and the stubborn, trembling belief that if I moved fast enough, maybe I could outrun the grief—or at least get it to trip over its own feet.

What actually happened? I got lost. A lot. In Lisbon, I missed my bus and ended up in a tiny hillside neighborhood where an old woman named Senhora Rosa insisted I sit on her stoop and eat figs straight off her tree. She didn’t speak English. I didn’t speak Portuguese. We communicated in gestures, laughter, and shared silence—and somehow, she knew exactly what I needed: not answers, but warmth. That afternoon, I cried—not the ugly, heaving kind, but soft, warm tears while juice ran down my wrist. It was the first time in months I’d let myself be held by something other than shame.

Then came Prague, where I got scammed out of €40 by a guy who sold me “authentic Czech crystal” that turned out to be repackaged IKEA glassware. Instead of spiraling, I laughed—really laughed—until I snorted, startling a flock of pigeons off Charles Bridge. That laugh cracked something open. I realized I’d forgotten how to be ridiculous. How to be *unimportant*. Back home, every misstep had felt like proof I was failing at being a wife, a partner, a grown-up. Here? Getting scammed meant I was just a tourist. Human. Flawed. Alive.

In Chiang Mai, I took a cooking class with six strangers and burned three batches of green curry paste before finally nailing the balance of lemongrass, fish sauce, and chili. My instructor, Nok, patted my shoulder and said, “Good. Now you know what *not* to do next time.” That line became my mantra. Not “You failed.” Not “You’re broken.” Just: *Here’s what doesn’t work. Try again.*

The biggest lesson didn’t come from a mountaintop or a sunset. It came in a hostel dorm in Budapest, 3 a.m., listening to a stranger softly cry on the top bunk. I didn’t say anything. Just passed her the extra pillow I’d brought—just in case—and whispered, “It’s okay to not be okay right now.” And in that dark, shared breath, I understood: healing isn’t about becoming whole again. It’s about learning to hold your own broken pieces with kindness instead of contempt.

By December, I wasn’t “over it.” I was *with* it. Carrying it differently. Lighter, somehow—not because the pain had vanished, but because I’d stopped treating it as evidence of my failure and started treating it as data: *This hurts here. This memory still stings. This is where I need rest. This is where I’m stronger than I thought.*

I flew home in January—not to rebuild the old life, but to build a new one, brick by imperfect brick. I still have Senhora Rosa’s dried figs in a jar on my windowsill. I still burn the occasional curry. But now, when I catch my reflection in a window, I don’t look away. I smile—small, real, unguarded—and whisper, “Hey. You made it this far. What’s next?”

Turns out, the bravest thing I did that year wasn’t boarding the plane. It was showing up for myself—messy, uncertain, tender—as if I mattered. And slowly, day by sunlit, disorienting, beautiful day, I began to believe it.

title: self-improvement book|dealing with procrastination and perfectionism
text:
Let’s get one thing straight: your “I’ll start tomorrow” is a lie you tell yourself while scrolling TikTok at 11:47 p.m. with cold coffee congealing beside your laptop. Not a cute quirk. Not “just how you are.” A habit—*trained*, not inherited—and it’s costing you more than time. It’s costing you the quiet pride of finishing something *good enough*, then walking away.  

Perfectionism isn’t high standards. It’s emotional blackmail. You whisper to yourself, *“If this isn’t flawless, it’s worthless,”* then freeze. That whisper? It’s not wisdom. It’s fear wearing a lab coat. And here’s the ugly math: researchers at the University of Calgary tracked 237 chronic procrastinators for 18 months. 68% reported *lower income* over time—not because they were lazy, but because they kept deferring *launch*, *submission*, *the first draft*, *the awkward phone call*. They’d spend 90 minutes formatting a to-do list instead of writing the damn email. Sound familiar?  

I used to do that. For real. Wrote three versions of my first book proposal. Revised the *title page* seven times. Spent two days agonizing over whether “resilient” or “resourceful” better described Chapter 4. Meanwhile, my rent was due. My cat ate my last protein bar. My therapist sighed audibly.  

Here’s what finally cracked it: I stopped waiting for readiness. Readiness doesn’t exist. It’s a myth sold by people who’ve never stared down a blinking cursor at 2 a.m. What exists is *threshold energy*—that tiny, gritty push you make *before* you feel like it. Not motivation. Not inspiration. Just *muscle*. Like standing up from the couch when your back hurts. You don’t wait for your spine to *feel ready*. You just… stand.  

So I started small. Brutally small. Not “write 500 words.” That’s still a wall. I said: *Open the doc. Type one sentence. Then close it.* That’s it. No editing. No rereading. Just one sentence—bad, clunky, grammatically suspect—and walk away. Did it for three days straight. On Day 4, I wrote two sentences. On Day 6, I didn’t close the doc. I kept going. Not because I felt inspired. Because the *habit* of starting had begun to outweigh the panic.  

Perfectionists hate this part: done is louder than perfect. Your client won’t notice the comma splice in your pitch deck—but they *will* notice you missed the deadline. Your partner won’t remember if your apology sounded poetic—but they *will* remember you waited three days to say it. Done creates momentum. Perfect creates dust.  

And stop calling it “procrastination.” That word’s too soft. Too polite. Call it what it is: *avoidance dressed as diligence*. You’re not “taking time to think.” You’re avoiding the vulnerability of putting something unfinished into the world. Avoiding the chance someone might say, “Hmm, interesting—but have you considered…” Avoiding the quiet terror of being seen *in process*, not just in polished product.  

So try this today—no grand gesture, no journaling about “my inner critic”:  
- Set a timer for *90 seconds*.  
- Do *one* physical action toward the thing you’re avoiding. Not planning. Not researching. *Action.* Send the email. Open the spreadsheet. Pick up the phone. Press record on your voice memo app and say, *“Okay. Here’s where I’m stuck.”*  
- When the timer ends? Stop. Even if you’re mid-sentence. Even if it feels stupid.  

Why 90 seconds? Because neuroscience shows that’s roughly how long it takes your amygdala—the panic center—to quiet down *if you don’t flee*. You’re not building discipline. You’re rewiring threat response. Every time you do this, you whisper to your nervous system: *“This isn’t life-or-death. Breathe. Try again.”*  

You won’t fix this in a week. You’ll trip. You’ll reorganize your pantry instead of drafting that grant application. You’ll delete a paragraph you spent an hour on. Good. That’s not failure. That’s data. That’s your brain learning the difference between danger and discomfort.  

And listen—your worth isn’t tied to output. But your *freedom*? That’s directly tied to how often you choose *action over armor*. So go. Now. Before you finish this sentence. Before you check your phone. Before you decide you need “just five more minutes.”  

Open the doc. Type one sentence. Close it.  

Then breathe.  

Then do it again tomorrow.

title: leadership memoir by a former CEO|the hiring mistake that nearly sank the company
text:
Chapter 12: The Hiring Mistake That Nearly Sank the Company

In the early years of my tenure as CEO, I was convinced that our company, BrightStar Technologies, was on an unstoppable trajectory. We had a solid product, a growing customer base, and a talented team. But one critical mistake in hiring nearly derailed everything we had built. This chapter is about that mistake, the lessons I learned, and how it ultimately transformed my approach to leadership and decision-making.

 The Decision to Hire

It was the summer of 2015, and we were looking to expand our sales team. Our current head of sales, Mark, had done an excellent job, but he was overwhelmed with the rapid growth and needed support. After a series of interviews, we found someone who seemed like the perfect fit: Alex. He had an impressive resume, a track record of success at a well-known tech firm, and a charismatic personality. His references were glowing, and his vision for scaling our sales operations aligned perfectly with our goals. We were so excited that we moved quickly, offering him the position of Vice President of Sales without much hesitation.

 The Initial Honeymoon

Alex hit the ground running. In his first few weeks, he brought a fresh energy to the sales team, implemented new strategies, and even closed a few significant deals. The board and I were thrilled. It seemed like we had made the right choice. However, the initial honeymoon phase was short-lived. Within a few months, cracks began to appear.

First, there were subtle signs of tension within the team. Some of our long-standing salespeople started to complain about Alex's aggressive management style. They felt micromanaged and undervalued. Then, the numbers started to tell a different story. Despite the initial flurry of activity, our sales growth began to stagnate, and some key accounts started to slip away. When I confronted Alex about these issues, he dismissed them, attributing the slowdown to external factors and insisting that his methods would eventually pay off.

 The Turning Point

The turning point came during a quarterly review meeting. As we went through the financials, it became clear that the sales team was not only failing to meet its targets but was also on a downward trend. The morale in the department was at an all-time low, and several key employees had already left, citing Alex's leadership as the primary reason. It was a wake-up call. I realized that the problem wasn't just a matter of strategy or market conditions; it was a fundamental issue with the person we had hired.

I called an emergency meeting with the board and senior management. We discussed the situation at length, and it was clear that we needed to take immediate action. Reluctantly, we decided to let Alex go. It was a difficult decision, but it was necessary to save the company from further damage.

 The Aftermath and Lessons Learned

The aftermath of Alex's departure was challenging. We had to rebuild the sales team, restore morale, and regain the trust of our customers. It took time, but we eventually turned things around. We promoted from within, giving Mark more resources and support, and we brought in a new VP of Sales who was a better cultural fit and had a more collaborative approach.

This experience taught me several valuable lessons:

1. Cultural Fit is Non-Negotiable: No matter how impressive a candidate's credentials are, if they don't align with your company's culture, it can lead to disaster. Cultural fit should be a top priority in any hiring decision.

2. Due Diligence is Crucial: We should have dug deeper into Alex's background and spoken with more of his former colleagues. Sometimes, a glowing reference can hide underlying issues. Always do your due diligence, and don't be afraid to ask tough questions.

3. Trust Your Team: I should have listened more closely to the concerns raised by our existing team members. They were the ones who had to work with Alex every day, and their feedback was invaluable. Trusting and valuing the input of your team can help you identify problems early.

4. Act Quickly: Once it became clear that Alex was not the right fit, we should have acted more swiftly. Delaying the decision only prolonged the pain and allowed the situation to worsen. As a leader, it's essential to make tough decisions when necessary, even if they are uncomfortable.

5. Learn from Mistakes: Every mistake is an opportunity to learn and grow. This experience forced us to re-evaluate our hiring processes and improve our leadership practices. It also made us more resilient and better prepared for future challenges.
